- THE MASTER OF THE HOUSE. He cannot walk, he cannot speak, Nothing he knows of books or men, He is the weakest of the weak. And has not strength to hold a pen; He has no pocket and no purse, And never yet has owned a penny, But has more riches than his nurse, Because he wants not any. He rules his parents by a cry, And holds them captive by a smile— ' A despot, strong- through infancy, A king, from lack of guile, He lies upon his back and crows, Or looks with grave eyes on his-mother— What can he mean? But I suppose They understand each other. In doors or out, early or late, There is no limit to his sway, For, wrapped in baby-robes of state, - He governs night and day. Kisses he takes as rightful due, And, Turk-like, has this slave to dress him His subjects bend before him, too. I'm one of them. God bless him! Jon-s DENNIS.

OUR COUNTRY. Not only where the fields are thick with grain, And countless cattle pasture on the plain; Not only where the earth is full of ore, %. And laden fleets ride off the happy shore; Not only in the summer of success, But in the depths of cruel weariness, Mid arid rocks, on unproductive sands, And in the heart of God-forgotten lands, Have men been found to glory in the song, "My country always, whether right or wrong." And if one heart can warm with generous fire For home so cheerless, and for life so dire. How many British hearts perforce must flame At the mere mention of their country's name! The name above all others in the roll Of names that nerve the heart and stir the soul; , The name that, whispered in a Briton's ear, Makes weakness brave and banishes all fear. Ours is no country bounded by the waves That lap her rocks and haunt her ocean caves: She reaches far and wide beneath the sea, And all her children, scattered though they be, • Clasp hands unseen around the earth, and feel A common gladness in the commonweal; And where her ensign flashes in the sun, All british hearts are wont to beat as one: Just as the triple crosses there combined, All float with equal motion on the wind; E 7. For neither white, nor blue, nor dazzling red, Can droop unnoticed while the rest are spread; Nor can a single one away be borne By any gale that leaves the rest untorn. Oh, Britain ! dearest land in all the world,' To save thy flag from being soiled or furled, Who of thy sons would not be proud to die, And, dying, would not breathe a bitter sigh That he had only one good life to throw Between his country and his country's foe! The rich and poor alike would lavish all, And give their last in answer to thy call; The sick would rise; the halt, with loud acclaim, - Would leap to arms if Britain's summons came To bid them guard the priceless treasure bought With blood and sorrow when their fathers fought. .--Canell's Saturday Journal.

Customer: " But aren't the trousers too long ?" Tailor: "Too long? Dey is made to fit a man exzekly your size, If your legs happen to be a drib e short, you must quarrel mit nature—not de tailor." Papa—" Glad to see you to-morrow evening. My daughter Alice will sing, and Beatrice will recite to us a new poem she composed. We sup at nine." Young man —" Thanks. You're very kind. Most happy. Fil be with you at nine." " Have you anything else old?" said an English lady at Rome to a boy off whom she had bought some an- tiquities. "Yes," said the young urchin, thrusting forward his hat, which had seen some dozen summers, "my hat is old." The lady rewarded his wit. "Grandma, have you seen the coinage the Government are now making—three pieces to a penny ?" asked a youn hopeful home for the holidays. "No," said the old lab& with much interest; "what are they like?" "Two farthings and a halfpenny," answered the grace- less youngster. An old Dutch tavern-keeper, who had his third wife thus expressed his views of matrimony: "Veil, you see, de first time I married for love. Dat was goot, Then I married for beauty. Dat was goot, too, about as de first. Ills time I married for money, and dis is petter as poth." A small west country farmer, when canvassed by a, newspaper agent, refused to subscribe to his journal on the ground that his (the farmer's) father had taken in the Magnet for more than twenty years, and so had left his son far more newspapers than he should ever get through in his life. At the time when Sir W. Armstrong's heavy guns were awakening such interest in military circles, two Irishmen were in conversation on the subject. "Pat," says one, " howiver do they make them cannons without a jine ?" " Arrah !" exclaimed rat, "sure, its aisy to understand ye wor rared in a bog ! Doesn't iverybody know that they get a round hole an' pour a lot ow iron raund it?" To ALL WHOM IT MAY CONCERN.—Don't talk too much. Learn how to be silent. Not that people should always keep the tongue still, it is made for use. But there are times when silence is the best and most effec- tive reply. When a boor speaks roughly or uncivilly to you, when you are asked an impertinent question, when a sneer is conveyed under cover of an inquiry for in- 'formation, or when, having appealed to you on a question .of taste, your opinion is met with ridicule—the best -answer in these or like exigencies is masterful silence. Silence bespeaks self-command, and nothing is at times So effective as the silence which springs from contempt. AN INCIDENT IN THE HISTORY or Nonwron.—Kett's re- bellion is perhaps the most noteworthy 'event in the his- tory of Norwich during the age of the Reformation. The alienation of the Church lands to the courtiers of Henry VIII. and the encroachments on the part of the new proprietors upon the privileges of the common people, which tfrey had acquired by a kind of right of usage under the generally easy government of the c.332onasteries• 'had caused a deep and by no means uncle- --rve,u'se (intent. The first outbreak was at Wymond- -1,,,,.ti-m" ,u ,„n Norfolk; and Robert Kett, a tanner of that ',vas acknowledged as leader of the rebels. His iGreer marched to Norwich, and encamped on Mouse- Heath, a tract of moorland on the plateau near the on the left bank of the Wensura. Their head-quar- ters were at an old tree, called the Oak of Reformation. For some time they were masters of the city, the Royal I troops being at first repulsed with loss, when Lord Shef- field and several others were killed. The Earl of War- I wick, however, arrived with a stronger force, and a smart encounter took place. The fight was not on the heath, but in a neighbouring valley, which the rebels had adopted as their field of battle in consequence of an old saying. Like Delphic oracles, however' it proved double- edged. A great slaughter there was, but of their own party, notwithstanding their stout resistance at first; for, as Fuller puts it, "rage was conquered by courage, number by valour, rebellion by loyalty, and in the flight and pursuit two thousand at the least were slain." Kett, his brothers, and many others, were taken prisoners. Then came the punishment, which was a notable one. The chief culprit was hanged in chains on the top of the castle, his brother on Wymondham steeple; nine of the others were hanged and quartered at the Oak of Re- formation, and altogether about 300 suffered death in or about Norwich.—Front Our Own Country for October. PHYSIC EY PROXY.—During the war about 20 Con- federate prisoners were at Fort Mc.Henry, stored away ia a fodder loft, under guard. One day Captain Ned Bridges was playing an innocent game of cards when the sick call was sounded—the signal for ailing soldiers to re- port at the surgeon's office to be examined. " Lieutenant," said Captain Bridges, turning to a young soldier, "an- swer sick call for me, and let us finish this game. Go down there and personate me, and tell the doctor you want another box of his liver pills." The obliging lieu- tenant marched out and proceeded with the other soldiers, under the escort of the guards, to the surgeon's office. When the name of Captain Bridges was called, the lieu- tenant's face appeared at the little office window. "Doc- tor," he began, "them pills you give me helped me up considerably, but I want another box, I think another box will fix me up all right." "Didn't those pills cure you?" asked the doctor abruptly, looking over his spec- tacles at the bogus Bridges. "No; but another box will fix me, I think." "Well, well," said the doctor half to himself, "I'll have to change the treatment on you." Thereupon he picked up a graduating glass, and from various bottles mixed the most infernal mess that mortal ever saw. The lieutenant shuddered. When the villainous compound was made up, the doctor stirred it vigorously and viciously, and holdin. it out, said, "Drink that." The lieutenant took hold of tfie glass. Cold chills ran up and down his spine. "Doctor," he stammered, "I'd—l'd er heap ruttier take the pills." "Drink it 1" stormed the Doctor, and in the excitement the medicine went down the lieutenant's throat. When the lieutenant returned to the fodder-loft he was very glum. When the game of cards grew monotonous, Captain Bridges turned and asked, " Lieutenant, git them pills ?" " Naw !" " said the captain, " you needn't be so snappish about it. What did the doctor say ?" "He said he was going to change the treatment on you, and if you don't get well it ain't my fault, for I've taken the nastiest dose for you that ever I saw. "—Atlanta Constitution. A gentleman whilst looking out of the window of a house near Kingston, in the island of Jamaica, heard a negro talking to a donkey. The conversation ran as follows—" You not go on, sar? Dat a fact. eh, sar? Well, sar, I bet you a bit' I make you go! Eh, sar, what you say—dat a bet? Well, den, done sar." The animal appeared to accept the wager, as he laid back his ears to the fullest extent, threw out his fore legs, and evinced no intention of moving. The negro then came behind the donkey, and grasping his tail, proceeded to twist it round with all his force. The animal at once gave in, and started off at a brisk trot. The negro was preparing to follow, when the gentleman hailed him, and said, "So you have won your bet. But how will you get paid ?" "Oh, massa," hel answered, with a grin, "my missy gib me dis"—producing from his pocket a "bit" which is a colonial coin worth about fourpence—" to buy him a feed of corn when we get to Kingston! I gib him notink now, and just spend de bit on lilly drop of sometink good for tomack." MARY RUSSELL MITFORD'S DOG.—My pet is neither very good nor very handsome. I did not choose him; he chose me. He sought me, followed me, loved me, would be loved, and was loved. There is no resisting preference and affection, come from where they may; so he is my pet. Mossy was a large black dog, of the very largest and strongest kind of greyhounds; very fast, and honest, and resolute—past example; a magnificent and noble-looking creature. There never wao such a dog! His temper was, beyond comparison, the sweetest ever known. Nobody ever saw him out of humour; and his sagacity was equal to his temper. Under a fir tree,. marked with his initials, he lies. We covered his *dead body with flowers. Everybody so sorry—everybody loved him—" dear saint!" as I used to call him, and as I do not doubt he now is! No human being was ever so faithful, so gentle, so generous, and so fond. I shall never love anything so well. My own beloved Mossy, heaven bless you! Farewell, my own best beloved! Gvd bless you, my Mossy! I cried when you died, and I can hardly help crying whenever I think of you. All who loved me loved Mossy.—Life of Mary Rarstil Max's BUSINESS IN LlFE.—Men's proper business in this world falls mainly into three divisions :—First, to' know themselves and the existing state of the things they have to do with; secondly, to be happy in them- selves and in the existing state of things; thirdly, to mend themselves and the existing state of things as far as either are marred and mendable. These, I say, are the three plain divisions of proper human business on 'this earth. For these three the following are usually, substituted and adopted by human creatures :—First, tt, be totally ignorant of themselves and the existing state of things; secondly, to be miserable in, themselves and 7 in the existing state of things; tlairdl3r,..to let themsel and the existing state of things alone (at least in the way of correction). The dispositions which induce us to manage thus wisely the affairs of this life seem to be: —First, a fear of disagreeable facts, and conscious shrinking from clearness of light, whidi, keeps us from examining ourselves, and increase gradually into a spe- cies of instinctive terror at all truth, ancrlbre of glosses, veils, and decorative lies of every sort.. secondly, a general readiness to takede/ight in anything post, future, far off, or schnewhere eNe, rather than in things now, near, and here;. leading as gradually to piece our plea- sure principally in the' exercise of the imagination, and to build all oar satisfaction on things as they are not. Which power being one not accorded to the lower ani- mals, and having indeed, when disciplined,a very noble use, we pride ourselves upon it, whether disciplined or not, and pass our lives complacently, in substantial dis- content and visionary satisfaction.—Ruskias "Modern

Painters." RIGHT DEVELOPMENT OF MAN'S FACTILTIRS.--In the make and nature of everyman, however rude-and simple, whom we employ in manual labour, there are some powers for better things; some tardy imagination, torpid capacity of emotion, tottering steps of thought, there are, even at the worst; and in most cases it is all our own fault that they are tardy or torpid: But they cannot be strengthened, unless we are content to take them in their feebleness, and unless we prize and honour them in their imperfection above the best and most per- fect manual skill. And this is what we have to do with all our labourers; to look for the thoughtfla part of them, and get that out of them, whatever we lbse for it, whatever faults and errors we are obliged ta take with it. For the best that is in them cannot manifest itself but in company with much error. Understand this clearly: You can teach a man to draw a straight line, and to cut one; to strike a curved line, and to carve it; and to copy and carve any number of given lines or forms, with admirable speed and perfect precision; and you find his work perfect of its kind; but if you ask him to think about any of those forms, to consider if he can- not find any better in his own head, he stops; his execu- tion becomes hesitating; he thinks, and tem to one he thinks wrong; ten to one be makes a mistake in the first touch he gives to his work as a thinking being. But you have made a man of him for all that. He was only a reacnine before—an animated tool. And observe, you i are put to stern choice n this matter. You must either make a tool of the creature, or a man of him. You can- not make both. Men were not intended to work •c7ith the accuracy of tools, to be precise and perfect in all their actions. If y?u will have that precision out of them, and make their fingers measure degrees like cog- wheels, and their arms strike curves like compasses, you must unhumanise them. All the energy of their spirits must be given to make cogs and compasses of them- selves. All their attention and strength roust go to the accomplishment of the mean act. The eye of the soul must be bent upon the finger-point, and it, soul's force must fill all the invisible nerves that guide t, ten hours a day, that it may not err from its steely precision, and ' so soul and sight be worn away, and the whole human being be lost at last—a heap of sawdust, so far as its in- tellectual work in this world is concerned; saved only by its heart, which cannot go into the form of cogs and compasses, but expands, after the ten hours are over, i into fireside humanity. On the other hand, f you will make a man of the working creature, yon cannot make a tool. Let him but begin to imagine,.to think, to try to ; do anything worth doing, and the eng,ine-turned pr?- cision is lost at once. Out come all his roughness, all his , dulness, all his incapability; shame upon shame, failure upon failure, pause after pause; but out comes the whole majesty of him also; and we know the height of it only when we see the clouds settling upon him. And, whether the clouds be bright or dark, there will be transfiguration behind and within them.—Ruskin. tion and anoint the passage with lard, and when the cow pains herself his assistants should, when he gives the word, pull quickly and firmly together downwards, and in the direction of a line drawn midway between the hips and the hock. They should take plenty of titre, and never pull except when the cow is paining herself. As soon as the cow has calved the calf should be taken round to the head of the cow for ten minutes. Licking 1 the calf will do both cow and calf good, and if the calf be removed in ten minutes or so the cow will not be un- settled. If milk fever is feared it is a good plan to ' leave the calf with the cow for three or four days. As soon as the cow is in labour some oatmeal porridge should be made, and a pailful, in which from 31bs. to Sibs. of treacle has been mixed, should be given to the cow luke-warm, as soon as she has calved. The cow should not be milked clean for the first two days, but after that every drop should be taken. The cow should be in good store condition when she calves, but for ten days be- fore calving she should be sparingly fed—a little sweet hay, scalded bran, treacle and water in winter, and she should have exercise daily. In summer the cow should, when dried for calving, be put in a bare, well sheltered, and well shaded pasture, where she will have to work hard to supply her wants, and she should be put in a covered yard or large airy box a few hours before calving. Very fresh cows may, with advantage, be bled in the nose a day or two before calving. Should an artery be cut, the bleeding may be stopped by dash- ing plenty of cold water on the cow's head. After , calving, and till after the ninth day, when the second cleansing usually comes away, the food in winter should I consist of sweet hay and bran mashes, given in great moderation. The bran should be scalded, and the water warmed. In summer the cow should, till after the ninth day, be housed at night, but after the third day she may be turned out for a few hours morning and evening, but she should not be allowed access to cold water till after the third day. She should have bran tea aria a little sweet hay and grass for the first three days after calving, and if she has had a hard time in calving, oatmeal gruel and cod-liver oil will help to get up her strength. Malt improves the appetite and helps the di- gestion. Cows should always have access to rock salt and to field soil. For medicinal purposes always have at hand a good supply of linseed and cod-liver oil, Epsom salts, ground ginger, :whisky, and sound ale. For sore udders, laudanum and cream. For straining after calv- ing, apply carbolic oil with a sponge tied to the end of a stick. Should a cow show signs of milk fever (unsteadi- ness of gait, a wild expression, and a sudden falling off in the flow of milk are the chief signs) administer promptly a pint of whisky and a pound of Epsom salts, and get her to walk about, if possible; encourage the circulation of the blood in every way. Should she re- fuse to walk, though still on her feet, take from three to four quarts of blood from the jugular vein. If she goes down and is unable to rise, keep her body covered with sacks of hot bran day and night, and put clothes dipped in cold water on her head, draw the milk every hour, and keep the cow propped up on each side with straw."

GLTURF. _

High prices are being realised for German horses by German breeders. During last year over 1,400 horses were exhibited for sale at Stuttgardt, the highest price realised being £l3O, and the lowest £2 15s. The number of horses at present in Wurtemberg is set down at 96,885, and the bulk of the better class are sold for export to Switzerland. The breeders of draught horses have had a busy and profitable season, no fewer than 600 Clydesdales having* been shipped from Glasgow for Canada, United States, Brazil, Australia, and New Zealand; while to the same countries, but particularly to the United States, over 100 Shire horses have been taken. A demand has also begun

in America for Suffolk horses. OPEN' BUILDINGS FOR LIVE STOCK.-46 R." writes "Recently I was over a farm where a valuable stock of cattle are kept, and where, contrary to the usual prac- tice in this district, a few buildings have been erected, open to the south. In one of these were a lot of heifer calves. They had been playful whilst the sun was up, and on going in for the night were in a state of profuse perspiration, their coats being wet with sweat. Of late the nights have set in very cold, with frost. Recently, accompanied by one of my children, we walked five miles to a railway station in the evening, and arrived there in a state of perspiration. Having a short time to wait, I put on my overcoat, and also cloaked my daugh- ter, against her will. On the train coming up, the child wanted the carriage windows left open, but after thirty miles' ride in the night air she was wishing for another cloak, in a closed railway carriage. Now, I would ask all who have the care of live stock, how would it be with those calves before the morning? Would it be a sensible procedure for any parent to put his children to bed, sweating from their evening's play, on a winter's night, with one wall of their bedroom taken out? If not, why

not? If wrong in the case of children, how can it be right in the case of calves? They may bear it, but they cannot thrive as well. It is not a question of coddling, but a question of common sense. Let there be plenty of ventilation, but save the animals from chills and draughts." YEARLING COLTS.—The average yearling colt wintered in the yard or in the fields in the north is usually a sorry looking subject. Bony, puny, the skin covered with matted hair; it has been indeed a struggle with him for life. it is midsummer before he becomes at all decent looking as to flesh, and never recovers from the cruelty that made a walking skeleton of him between weaning time and the spring. Such matters usually make the mare do double work in the summer—raise a colt and labour every day on the farm. The consequence is the colt has had little milk, and that fevered. It soon learns to eat grass, indeed, but this is at the expense of dis- ordered digestion, from which the colt never recovers. The mare also, from being over-taxed, may have become the victim of dropsy and other serious disorders. And yet how many, otherwise kindly and God-fearing men, are there who think they have performed their whole duty to the animals of the farm. The stinting process never made money in any department of industry. It never pays with any farm animal, and least of all with colts in their first year. It has filled the country with weedy, weak, undersized horses and continued from generation to generation, the horses, plug type of horse is fixed, entailing loss year by year. We have written more than once that whatever of real flesh an animal loses in winter is a dead loss. It is not necessary to reiterate the arguments why this is so. The fact shows for itself. Shall you have other colts to raise this summer? Are you of the class that has followed the starving policy, both as to feeding and exposure? Turn over a new leaf and begin anew. Feed so as to develop the frame, however indifferent it may be from bad breed- ing and lack of the necessary shelter. Weed out all the plug mares of the farm and get better ones as soon as ,v9tl are able. One strong mare that has been well fed land handled from eolthood will do the work of two ill- kept starvelings, and require but little more food than the one ought to have. Work the mares up to nearly the time of foaling. It will not be amiss. Once they have foaled, give them a rest during the heat of summer. It will pay both in the colt and in the future value of the mare. ENSILAGE EXPERlMEN'TS.—Experimentg in the making of ensilage have this yearbeen conducted at several of the farms in this district on a small scale, and large land- owners—both in the Fvlde, in the north of the county, and in the Chorley Division—have repeated on a larger scale the ensiling of green fodder. Earl Bective has for the past few years experimented, and, in a speech a few days ago, he thus alludes to a subject with which we hope again specially to deal in the Agricultural Columns of this journal :—" I am pleased to find that the subject of ensilage is beginning to be thoroughly studied, and, I am sure, to a certain extent, appreciated by the farmers of the district. Those who like myself have used ensil- age have obtained great benefit from it, and I might tell you that I saved about £2OO last year by using it. To my mind, the ensilage question is still in the embryo state. There is ensilage and ensilage. I have visited most of the silos in the district during recent years. Taking into consideration our damp an cold climate, there are some products I have met with that I would not feed to stock in winter, having due-regard to the health and constitution of the animals. It fmnot enough to say that after a winter's trial the animals appear none the worse. Possibly enthusiasts will not seem change in one or two years, but where sour and dampensilage is fed close attention should be paid to the live stock; and,, in my humble opinion, such ensilage should never be fed to mulch cattle in the depth of winter without meal being added. On the other band, I have met with silage that closely approximated to hay, whilst partaking-, in a great measure of the succulent properties of grass, the juices of the grass, when chewed in the mouth, having the taste' of sugar. This, with a little meal, seems a safe and good food even in the depth of winter. The most sensible use of ensilage fora district like ours appears to be. made of it at the Holker Farm of the Duke of Devonshire. Here the silos aro never opened until the spring-of the year, when the roots- are given out, anclthe silage-supplements the roots until the spring growth of grass sets in. There can be no, doubt that ensilage is valuaZle adjunct to the Britisfe farmer ; the dangerlavill be in expectingtoo much from it. To subserve thebest ends, it must he made with ..i.ttneent, and it must be used with judgment." FOOD' A/fD FEEmNo.—During- its life and in the 'per- formance of its vital functions, the fresh of an animal continually being wasted, and theproducts of that waste appear hr the excretions. The bodies of animals may be regarded as composed of aibunvinoid mattes,. fat, mineral salts, and water. The aiUuminoid matter con- tains nitrogen as its, eharacterietie• constituent, and4al.-- ;huminoid waste consists of a nitrogenous substance,. urea and some compound allied to it. The amount' of urea which-an animal* excretes may therefore be used'as, 3 measure of 'its anurninoid or flesh' waste. It appears, iin the urine of the animal ; and henceby estimating-,the amount of nitrogen contained in theurine, it is poseible• to determine the amount of flesh which must have been! wasted in order to, produce it. If' the amount of flesh waste is smaller than the albuminoid or flesh-forming matter whiath the aninsal has digested from its food,.the animal must- be laying on food. Thus it is possible,. by the analysis of the urine, to determine what is the gain or loss of fleeli in the-animal body under various cendi- tions. It is found that the flesh waste of an animal' is greater whenit is in good conditian -that when it is in a. poor condition. To make good thieiiacreased waste, an increased amount of albuminoid matter as food must be given. An animal in; good conditierrmay lose flesh from, living on diet which enabled it to make flesh when in ea poor condition-, just as a strong man would lose :flesh on a diet on which a weak man gained flesh. A certain period 'arrives-in feeding in which the, albuminoid mat- ter in the food* and the flesh waste' of the body come • inteaequilibrium: An increase in the albuminoid matter of the food would thencletermine eagain of flesh in the-ani- mal body, but the gain' would not correspond to the in- crease of albuminoid matter in Cie fbod, for the amount of flesh waste-also increases and only a small part of the albuminoid food' is capable of being: fixed as flesh on the body-of an animal. To enable an animal in poor condition to improve and gain flesh the alieurninoid constituents of its food must be slowly increaeed! To increase the al- buminoid matter quickly would be to waste that valhable material,.for lb is only as animala. improve in condition that they are able to make geed !use of their increased , diet. Considering an animal's- food to consist of two! things--albuminoid and carbo-hydrates—the smaller the proportion of albuminoid the- larger must be that of carbo-hydrates. Experience shows that animals are. kept in poor condition when the ratio between the al- buminoid matter and the carbo-hydrates is a wide 'one for example, I pint of albuminoids t 0,13 of caxbo-dydrates in thefodder of a store-ox is sufffcient to keep ibia poor condition, but it does not gain flesh or fatten on it. the ratio is gradualiy narrowed the animal puta on flesh, and improves. in condition fer. each increase,- of alleue minoid matter. if the ratio is widened the animal loses flesh. If albuminoid matter were entirely withheld,, then, no matter how much carbo-hvdrates the, animal' might eat, it would starve and die just as soon as if it had' eaten nothing. Thus fatesugar, and staech,if given alone, do not retard the death-moment of an animal,. be- cause nothing has been given to make good, the con- tinuous flesh waste of the animal. A certain amount of fat given along with the albuminoid food has a very favourable effect, and enables the animal to do with less albuminoid matter; it diminishes the albuminoici waste. Carbo-hydrates do the same, and it is important for feeders to know what is the best proportion between the albuminoid matter and carbo-hydrates a, each point of an animal's growth, so as to be able to feedeconomically. —AP. A. HINTS ON THE TREATMENT Or IN-CALF COWS.—Mt. Robt. E. Turnbull has been writing a very interesting series of articles on the selection and management of dairy cattle. In his last article dealing with in-calf cows, he says :—" In-calf cows should be liberally bedded. Cows calving in the winter season should be put in a well-ventilated, well-bedded loose box, as soon after being dried as possible, an the nearer the calving box is to the dressing-room window af the farmer the better. ulinoltf thel e rheadgh cattleman way a sI s tsahnoc eu d s shouldit If the cow is likely to,calve in the night the owner or be sciavlef n untilis coming feet are in sight. A hempen rope, with a noose at one end, should be attached to each foot above the fetlock, and then the ropes should be twisted together. The head herdsman should keep the feet of the calf in the right posi.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

Tnn WINDOW.—CaIIa ./Ethiopica (Lily of the Nile), with its beautiful green, glossy leaves and white, trumpet- shaped flowers, is one of the best window plants, and is grown in thousands by florists near our large towns to furnish the rooms of the rich as well as for decorating churches at Eastertide. The plants may now be fresh potted in three parts loam and one leaf mould, or they may be top-dressed with the same material after the inert surface soil is removed, and a little decayed manure may ha added to the compost. The off-sets, or suckers, should be detached, and, if required, may be potted into the smallest-sized pots they can be got into. They re- quire a liberal supply of water at all times, and more especially during their season of active growth, when manure water would also be most beneficial. Tnn FRONT GARDWQ, --Single Dahlias have been in fine form the past three weeks, and if we are not visited by frost they will continue so for a similar length of time. The plants are so easily raised from seeds that anyone having a hot-bed early in the year to place a pot or pan of seed in might with care see his plants flower well the same year, and after they are destroyed by frost the tubers should be taken up and stored in the usual way. Amongst named varieties we like Paragon best, and think everybody should have a plant of it The Cactus Dahlia Juarezii is a remarkable semi-double flower en- tirely distinct from any other variety in form, and the colour is rich crimson. Constance is a white Cactus, and New White Cactus is said to be a great novelty from Oporto resembling Juarezii more than any other. These and the single ones are far superior for cutting purposes than the clumsy doubles, and now that prizes are offered to them at our horticultural exhibitions we expect them to be more generally cultivated. The late sorts of Michaelmas Daisies are rapidly developing their Bowers, and as they are not affected by wind, rain, or ordinary frost, we may expect to see some of their gaily-coloured flower heads after the season 'with which their name is associated is past It is a little remarkable that out of the 70 or 80 species only two or three are any other colour than blue or shades of it- FRUIT GATT/ERING.—The second early varieties Of fruit must be frequently examined in order to ascertain if they are ready' for gathering. We have in a previous paper given some rules that might serve as a guide in gathering, or rather to know when together, early kinds; butthey are not applicable to theseand later ones, inas- much as the pips must be much browner, and the fruit, when taken in the hand and raised, gently, should part readily from the tree. It has beers frequently observed that a portion of the crop from a tree will shrivel and the others will remain plump, which proves that one lot -was rituch riper than the others. It is, therefore, a good plan to go over the trees at intervals' of a week or a fort- night, just as the weather may happen to be fine and sunny,or dull and cold. It is unnecessary to try all the fruit to.discover whether it is fit to pia, and it requires but littlirexperience to tell at a glance which is ready. Wicker baskets of any description are unsuitable for fruit-picking purposes, as from their flexibility they give way, andithe fruit that is in contact with the sides will ho covered with impressions from the willow, or cane which the baskets are made of. For the same reason baskets are also. obfectionable for the purpose' of conveying fruit to market, and we would prefer light boxes such as those in' which oranges are packed. A suitable-sized box with a. handle across might be made of the same material for the purpose of gathering, and with the as- sistance °Pan S-shaped wire hook it may be suspended from the Ihdderortree, so that the hands may be free. A light zinc pailiis also much hotter than a basket to gather the fruit is. Ali apples and pears intended Upkeep must be carefully handled, and not shot from one vessel to another as is frequently draw. The fruit at the' time may not exhibit indications of this rough treatment beyond de- pressions over its surface, but in a few days if the skin is removed the pulp will be brown and in an incipient state of decay. Dry- weather should be selected' for gathering fruit intendbd"tokeep. At first it should be laid out in es:thin a layer as space will permit to avoid excessive eweating and 'facilitate inspection, as fruit that has been pieked,by birds or has other wounds or blemishes will soon show symptoms of decay, and they can be picked , out and the sound' ones may then be packed' closer to- gether or, to- economise space, placed in orange boxes, which may be packed one above the other, care being teiien not to-fill the boxes too full, so that the bottom of one may not press on the contents of the other. When it is necessary to examine them, provide One empty box to,start witb,.and empty with the hands the' fruit from one-into the other; until the whole is overhauled. As a rule fruit keeps best in an upstair room', such apart- ments being drier than those on the ground floor, and the leading points to be observed in fruit- keeping are citmess, with, a coed steady temperatme- and careful handling of the-fruit..

Saucepans, ; and all Domestic Washing.— Advt. % Charity is tile salt of riches, without which they cor- rupt thereselims. He who is-slowest in making a promise • is apt to be the most faithful in the performance-of it. It was a son of Erin who asked the meeting to 'excuse him from sailing on a committee because, he expected to be unexpectedly called away. A lawyer-engaged in a case toxmented a witness so much withiquestions that the poor fellow at last cried for water. "There," said the judge, "1 thought you would pump him dry." If people fix their attention upon what is wrong, it looms up ..lefore them in exaggerted and untrue propor- tions, and renders them wholly unable to cope with it -; if they were more occupied withlthe rigltit, the good, and, the beautifui, however, they would be in a calmer and' happier frame of mind, and wculd be far better fitted to remedy the evilsA they would deplore, in looking down upon and lamenting the dust at their- feet they forgetto look upwards, and so do not see the glory of the sun overhead and Illuminating all] around, them. GREAPNEDI,OII A Mutt —4.n.Englieh lady, ona visibto Scotland, attended public worship in a parish church. In the same pew were abou, a dozen persons—farmers, their wives, and herdsmen. Shortly before the beginning of the sermon a large snuff-mull was passed to the occupants of the pew. Upon the Indy visitor declining to take a pinch, an old man who was evidently a shepherd whispered, in a very significant manner, "Pak' the sneeshin, mem ; tale the sneeshin'. Ye dinna ken our meenister ; ye'll need it aforehe's dune !" The foundation of all education, from the time a child 1 begins to learn, is thoroughness. Whatever is attempted must be carried out thoroughly, until the learner becomes !,master of the subject. Thoroughness is the groundwork of all good habits of mind, and a child's mind is as much a bundle of habits as its body. For this purpose it is well to strengthen the memory by insisting upon children learning something by heart every day; it cultivates the retentive powers of the mind, and is a help to spelling accurately, as the eye accustoms itself to the appearance of words.;

div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

INDIAN GAME. Considerable attention has of late been given to a variety of fowls that are common in one district of England, but are very little known outside of that dis- trict. We speak of the breed called by some Indian Game, and by others Cornish Game. The latter cogno- men at once denominates the part of the country where they are found, the south-western corner of England, whence has come another of our most useful varieties, the Minorca. The latter is one of the best breeds we possess for laying properties, and the Indian Game ex- cels in table properties, so that the Cornish breeders are in a fair way to supply all our needs in the direction of domestic poultry. It is very evident that though the name Cornish Game may be given to this race of fowls it owes its origin to the Eastern hemisphere, whence come all our fowls. Probably the Cornish coast, being the first at which ves- sels call on their way home, or rather did call in the old days, gave the residents there an opportunity of picking up rarities, and in this way the Indian Game would be at first introduced, soon to make its way by its own intrinsic merits. What part of India they are native to may be gathei•ed from the following letter, published some time ago in one of the poultry papers. In it the writer says :—" I have returned from a good six years' sojourn in India, that land of 'milk and honey, gold and silver, rico and curry.' While in Hazaubaugh (a thou- sand gardens), a town in the north-west provinces of Bengal, I carrid across a splendid breed of large, hand- some game fowls, cherished by the natives for their beauty and fighting propensities. I have travelled the greater part of India, but in no part except the Hazen- baugh district did I see a game fowl of any description. I am thoroughly convinced, after a close study of the game fowl in India, that they are of a pure breed, and not made from the Malay or any other breed, and that they are natives of the soil on which Ilprst saw them— viz., Flazaubaugh, Bengal. My description of the male bird is—head broad; neck thick, with good reach; shoulders broad, square, and well set; good chest; legs well set, wide apart, and not too long • colour, willow; comb, single. The hen is a beautiful Pheasant-like bird, rather lighter in colour than the hen of the English black-red breed. They are indifferent layers; inclined to sit several times during the year; weight, about six pounds; willow legs; very small comb and wattles. I know that several of these birds have been bought by English soldiers, and taken with them when they left for another station. An officer of a regiment would have no 1, difficulty whatever in bringing a cock and hen home I with him, and I am most decidldaly of opinion that they have come to England in that manner." The same writer considers that the Cornish Game have a touch of Malay in them, and this appears to be a general im- pression. The following description of the breed is supplied by one of the most successful breeders, and may be taken as reliable, so far as they are at the present day. This breeder says :—"The home of the Indian Game is in Cornwall especially, where we believe it was first bred in this. country, and where it is kept in large numbers, having been well established there for the last twenty years. The amount of solid white flesh, generally covered with a thin white, though sometimes with a yel- lowish, skin, makes it a very valuable table fowl. &11 writers are silent as to its origin, nor can the most pro- minent breeders be induced to venture on an assertion on this point; but judging from its appearance, there can be no doubt that it is closely allied to the Malay lit-wing many points in common with that breed ; and in my opinion feathered game have played a part in its production. Let that be as it may, scarcely a more valuable breed exists, nor one that breeds truer to its points. The weight of the adult cock is about 91bs., and that of the hen from &lbs. to 71bs. "The cock is of a very dark partridge colour, with, black breast and hackle: The hen is not unlike a pheas- ant in marking all through, the body nicely pencilled with the hackle darker; in fact, there is no class of marking that approaches nearer to the common pheasant in appearance. The plumage is extremely hard and short, being-next to the feathered variety in the latter respect. The • comb is pea-shaped, i.s., similar to that of the Malay, or like two-peas joined together, one behind the other, and is low and close to the head. The eyes are red, the-beak and legs yellow or orange. The head is rather short, or between that of the Game and Malay; the beak slightly curved and very strong; legs shorter than the ordinary Game, strong in bone; and set wide apart on well-spread feet, armed with strong claws. The back should be well filled, wings short, the butts or shoulder points standing well out from the chest, with strength of muscle; breast broad, deep, and prominent; and the bird should handle very solid and heavy. "Indian' Game hens are not very abundant layers, generally laying from, twenty to thirty eggs in a batch, after which they generally go to nest and sit well; they are excellent- nurses, defending their offspring well, and attending them to a good age. The eggs are of a, rich buff, sometimes almost approaching a chocolate; and those produced by pullets weigh eight to the pound, and from hens seven.' Writing- upon the questton of the table qualities, an anonymous correspondent of the Lies Stock Journal says that this Indian Game fowl "has, however, yet to be recognised as one of the very best of table fowl, not only as a pure breed, but as having the properties which are most desirable for- crossing purposes. Possessed of a marvellous development of breast, in which important particular it is unsurpassed by any other breed of domestic poultry; singularly close in. plumage' skin of an excellent colour, and fine juicy flesh, without an ex- cess of bone, and above the average size—in fact, a heavy bird, much heavier than appearances suggest, Indian , Game has also the advantage of being a remarkably hardy fowl. FOr all practical purposes a profitable table fowl should have a capacity for fattening, or, rather flesh forming, without an undue waste.of food. :It does not follow becausea bird is a large feeder that it will add flesh and prove profitable to the fattener. There is as much difference in the aptitude of the various breeds 'to fatten as there is in egg-production, and the majority of fatteners of poultry in this country generally find this particular branch of poultry farming unprofitable, be- cause they cultivate unsuitable breeds, the fattening element being wanting. " The-conformation of a fowl greatly determines its flesh-forming capacity. Li bird with narrowbr east and short breast bone can never be profitable or even satis- factory as a table fowl, and an abundance of feather or- Offal absorbes a lot of flesh-forming material. It is here. that the individuality of, Indian Game is most striking.. With its broad muscular chest and fine keel, without a. feather more than is necessary, it iapre-eminently a fowl of the minimum of offal, and on this account is most profitable; adding a greater percentage of flesh in pro- portion to the amount ot food consumed than probably any other breed, and Is. therefore entitled to rank as. one of any finest table fowls existing. Here, then, is an em- bodiment of usefulness which,. added to its symmetrical and handsome appearance, should gain it a Lost of ad- mirers. It is net often in the selection of,' poultry, whether for farming or exhibition purposes for profit or solely for pleasure, that One has the choice. of sohappy a combination as is found in Indian Game:" •-a There is a variety known as Aseels, which, is virtually a smaller type of the breed. These are the. highly-bred , fighting fowls of India, and are of so pugilistic a nature I that they are only to be kept by the vent few who can almost give every bird a run to itself: Aseel simply means thoroughbred. SEASONABLE HINTS. So long as the weather keeps as fine and open as we have had it of late the chickens may be allowed to roost in the trees, if they have been accustomed to do so; but the nights and mornings are beginning to feel chilly, and careful watch must be kept in order to check at the out- set all colds and other diseases. For this reason it is most important that the stock be constantly looked over,

for if roup gets a hold at this season of the year it will be very difficult indeed to get it out again. One of the best preventives is to mix in the soft food every morn- ing a small quantity of stimulating powder, such as aromatic compound, and to give the soft food hot and as soon after daylight as possible. This prevents the birds getting their stomachs chilled, and will have the effect of preventing trouble.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF
GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Greening, Brown, Isherwood, Clark, Humphries, Strange, Woods, Bonnell, Jolley, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Harrison, Blackhurst, Eckersley, Wright, Kilshall, Balharry, Owen, Heaton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk).

HOUSE COIMITTEL The House Committee recommended that the following tenders, the consideration of which had been left over, be accepted : groceries, Messrs. J. and T. Edwards; shoes, ttc., Messrs. Roberts and Son ; clogs, Mr. P. Sudlow ; wines and spirits, Messrs. Howson. The Committee reported that Mr. Mines, superintendent of the school, Padgate, had re- ported that there were at present 106 boys and 7.6 girls at the schools, and there was room for 6 boys and 12 girls. The Committee recommended that 53 new beds be obtained for the workhouse to meet the expected demands.—Mr. WOODS, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said there was room for 43 additional inmates in the Workhouse.— Mr. JOLLEY seconded, and mentioned that the tenders ac- cepted were the lowest. The wine and spirits, however, I would in future be supplied in turns by the respective mer- chants, as in the Case of expensive medicines—The minutes were adapted.

THE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE. The School Committee's minutes stated that the superin— tendent reported that the children were all healthy and cheerful. Mr. W. Houghton, of Wargrave, was thanked for a present of a hamper of pears. Mr. and Mrs. Carter ten- dered their resignation of the offices they hold, and it WAS recommended that the resignations be accepted, and that ad- vertisements for their successors be issued. The committee recommended that the tender of Thomas Whittle and Son for the supply of leather be accepted. The superintendent of the schools, agreeably to the directions given by the Guardians, presented a book showing the hours of absence of officers during the last quarter, and a summary of the total thereof; also a statement of the cost of fish supplied in the last quarter for use of officers, in substitution for butcher's meat, which showed the cost of fish to be less than that of meat by 6id per week on the average. The superin- tendent is reminded of the expectation of the Guardians that an annual report of the working of the schools and their cost will be prepared, and that such information as given in the returns named be embodied, and the superin- tendent explains that such a report will be prepared as to the pest year and presented in due course.—The CHAIRMAs. moved, and Mr. WOODS seconded the adoption of these minutes, which was agreed to. • SCHOOL FEES. The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 102 cases, 82 of which were old and 20 new.—Mr. BLACKHURST, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said there had been a great increase in the school fees allowed over the past few weeks, but he did not think there wae any particular increase on the same period of last year.— Mr. JOLLEY seconded, and the minutes were adopted.
DR. JACK'S APPOINTMENT.

A letter frqm the Local Government Board was read em- pressing the approval of that Authority with the arrange- ment come to at a previous meeting of the Guardians with regard to the appointmerit of Dr. Jack as medical officer of No. 1 district.—ln answer to a question the Clerk said that Dr. Jack was preparing to remove into Church-street.

div.head: THH CALLS.
div.p: THH CALLS.

The CLEux explained---t-flai—a-t—the previous meeting he said that the calls of all the townships had been paid with the exctption of a sum due by Houghton, Middleton, and Arbury, but that sum, he afterwards found, had been paid in to the treasurer at the time he spoke. There were, there- fore, really no arrears. (Hear, hear.)
MR. COOPER'S GRATUITY.

On the motion of Mr. JoLuirTse—co—n-ded by Mr. Br.e.cx- HURST, it was decided to pay to Mr. Cooper, vaccination officer, Newton, a gratuity of £lO for extra services rendered by bim.—Tbis gra'uity was awarded to Mr. Cooper several months ago, but owing to a regulation of the Local Govern- ment Board it could not be paid, but that difficulty, the clerk now explained, bad been overcome.
THE POOR-LAW CONFERENCE.-THE DEPUTATION'S
EXPBNSES.

The CHAIRMAN, who had attended the recent Poor-law Conference held in Liverpool, as one of the deputation sent by the Board, gave a brief report of the prwceedings of the conference.—ln answer to Mr. ONVEN,.it was stated that the cost of the deputation was El 9s per member,, the scale of expenses being fixed by the Local Government Board.—On the motion of Mr. HARRISON, seconded by Mr.. OWEN, a vote of thanks was accorded the chairman for his state- ment.

div.head: PROPOSED INCRRASE OF SALARY.
div.p: PROPOSED INCRRASE OF SALARY.

A letter was read from the porteress of the Workhouse, asking for an increase of salary, and mentioning that she had held the office for eight years. It was explained that she at present received £25 a year without rations, and Mr. Harrison gave notice that he would move at the next meet- ing that the salary be increased to £3o.a. year. The relief cases were then proceeded with.

Yl2 kant analise a kiss enny more-than kan the breath of a flower. The only way to deskribe- a kiss is tew take one, and then set down awl alone, out of the draft, and smack yure lips.—Josh Billings. Expect not praise without envy until yoi . are dead. Honours bestowed on the illustrious dead have in them no admixture of envy, for the living pity the- dead, and pity and envy, like oil and vinegar, assimilate net. Those are the best masters and; generally speaking, the best men who ever remember that the master is exactly as much under obligation to the servant as the servant is to the master, and that money alone will not discharge the debt of the latter.. All history teaches that good of every kind has first existed in the conceptions of the best and; wisest men, then been gradually diffused through the- minds of the many, and at length transmuted into the most practical 'and vital realities of life and conduct. The philosopher's dream, if he be a true philosopherebecomes in time the cherished standard of common daily life. One who has put his best abilitiesinto hiswork to-day may well afford to be contented and; satisfied with that so far as it goes; but that does- not prevent him from seeing its deficiencies and, doing better work on the morrow. On the other-hand, a restless discontented spirit will fret and chafe over inperfectiocrs in an impa- tient way that will prevent the clear and calm vigilance needful to insure better things in the future. First Boy—" My mw says I mustn't play with you, because your father is nothing but a shoemaker." Second boy—" So's your father a shoemaker." First boy —"Ma says he's a manufacturer. He makes a thousand pair of shoes to your father's one pair." Second boy— " Then he must be a thousand times worse than my father. I guess I won't play with you any more." One day, when in Florence Paganini jumped into a cab and gave orders to be driven to- the theatre. The distance was not great, but he was late, and an enthusiastic audience- was- waiting to bear him: per- form the famous " Prayer" of Moist on a single string. "How much do I owe ?" he inquired of the driver. "For you," said the man, who had recognised the great violinist, "the fare is ten francs." "What Ten francs? You are jesting!" "1 am:speaking seriously. You charge as much for a place-at your concert." Paganini was silent for a nainute, and then, 'with a complacent glance at the rather toe-witty cabcaan, he said, handing him at the same time a liberal fare, "I will pay you, ten francs when you drive.me-on one wheel!" MR. GLADSTONE AND THE CONVERSIOS OF THE TORIES. —Replying to a letter from the editor of the" Northampton Mercury," accompanying a copy of the report of Mr. Brad- laugh's Wellinborough speech on Lord Randolph Churchill's declarations at Dartford,, Mr. Gladstone writes :—" I thank you for the able statement sent me and for the kind words respecting myself. We have reason, appar- ently, to congratulate ourselves on a marked conversion of the Tories and their leader to a mass of Liberal opinion. It remains to hope chat this conversion may be durable and- effective." ALLEGED WIFE: MURDER—At Wolverbamteton, a nail- maker named Narrimore was arrested on Tuesday morning on suspicion of having caused the death of his wife. The. man is an officer of the Salvation Army, but has not lived, with his wife for some time, and she has been in the habit, of attending meetings of the Church Arm-e. On Monday night the husband fetehed his wife out of her mother's house, and the couple were seen walking together in the. direction of the canal. On Tuesday morning the waman'a dead lacdy was found in the canal. Thee tsre several marks of rough usage and scratches on the hEebund's face. FIRE AT A. LIVERTOOL MUSIC UAL,—About six e'cloe%
,on Monday evening a fire broke out at the—daiet—y-M-u—sie Hall, Liverpool. A hose belonging to the place was turned on, and the fl'ameaut out. The fire had broken out in the

_ --- back of the stage in the neighbon7Lood of the gas meter. One of the employes, however, bail sufficient presence of mind to tarn the gas off at the main, and thus saved what would certainly have been a Barlow conflagration.. As it was, the back of the scenes and some property were burned, but the amount of the damage has not yet been ascertained, nor is it known whether the building and contents were in- sured. The performance at the hall was not proceeded with at night. SBRICMS GAS EXPLOSION, IS MANCIIES.7EIL-- A serious gas explosion occurred early on Friday morning in Marylebone-street, Manabester, The occupant of the house in which the explosion took place is Mr. John Sewell. At about seven o'clock he noticed a strong smell of gas proceeding frara the front parlour. He went into the room and applied a light to the chandelier. An exple, sion immediately followed, and Mr. Swell was knocked to the floor and badly burned about the face, head, and the right hand. The force of the explosion displaced a great portion of the brickwork of the front window and loosened all the framework. Several of the windows at the back of the house were completely shattered, while the walls and ceilings of almost all the rooms in the house were cracked.

div.p: SHOCKING ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT

EARLESTOWN. On Thursday a shocking attempt to commit suicide was made at Earlestown under somewhnt romantic circumstances. Nearly two years ago James Kinsey, a respectable middle-aged nagn, who was em- ployed as chief engineer on the S.S. Orpheus was married to a Miss Ann Mottram, daughter of Mr. John Mottram, a smith at the Viaduct Waggon Works, who lived at 147, Earle-street, Earles- town. For a short time Mr. and Mrs. McKinsey lived together at Walton, Liverpool, and the husband resumed his dutieaen board ship. Unfortunately, however, Mrs. MainseY, it is stated, suffered considerable violence at the hands of her husband, and in consequence she left him and returned to her father's house at Earlestown. This was about nine months ago, and since then she has continued to live there. Mr. McKinsey afterwards visited his father-in-law's house, but the visits were far from friendly. From April last, 111) ' to Thursiay in last week, be was not seen in the neighborhood, but on the day named he again turned up and de- manded admittance. As Mr. Mottram was then engaged at his work, and both Mrs Mottram and her daughter—the visitor's wife—were ill in heel, McKinsey was not admitt.ed. The same afternoon Mr. McKinsey instructed, a local solici- tot's clerk to visit Mr. Mottram's house and try to arrange a meeting between him and his wife. The latter absolutely de • clined to see her husband, and the matter then dropped. On Thursday afternoon, after Mr. Mottram had gone to work, a girl brought word to Mrs. Mottram that her daugh- ter's husband was at a public house a few hundred yards away. The doors were then locked. Not many minutes elapsed before McKinsey appeared at the front door, and directly afterwards a loud report was heard. The shecking discovery was then made that McKinsey had shot himself just below the left ear. He fell headlong across the step, and the walk leading from the garden gate to the front door of the house. The report of a firearm quickly brought a crowd together, and fortunately Dr. J. N. Patterson was one of the first to arrive. The injured man was found lying in- sensible, and by his side was a new six-chambered revolver, four barrels of which were still loaded wth ball cartridges. The bullet was imbedded in his heed, and blood was oozing from the wound. Mc- , Kinsey was taken to the railway station on a stretcher, and was afterwards placed in the guard's van of the 4 p.m. ex- press for Liverpool. He remained unconscious all the time, and his removal was conducted under the arrangements of P.C. Hughes, of Earlestown. He was taken to Liverpool Infirmary. Inquiries have elicited that Mr. Kinsey, at the time of his marriage with Miss Mottram, was a widower with four children, who are still living at Liverpool. In addition to DT. Patterson, Dr. Fouiston, of Earlestown, was also present at the scene of the occurrence, shortly after the shot had been fired. The motive for McKinsey visiting his wife's home with a new revolver appears to indicate premeditation to commit crime of some character. The affair has caused some excit,ment in the neighbourhood. On inquiry at the Liverpool Infirmary, late on Thursday' night, the injured man was found to be in a precarious con- dition.

div.head: ALLEGED ATTEMPT TO DECOY A
div.p: ALLEGED ATTEMPT TO DECOY A

- - GIRL. At St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, before Mr. A. Sin- clair and Mr. Walmsley, a young man who gave the name of Richard Halton, and described himself as a traveller in the wine and spirit trade, living in Boundary-lane, Man- chester, was charged with assaulting Police-constables Reeves and ePllenry ; and further with assaulting a girl named Margaret Myles, aged 13, who lives at Chester.— Superintendent Johnston stated that the girl had been a ser- vant for about three months at reibeheeter, and on Thurs- day she was journeying from that place to Chester, where • her aunt lives. At Preston Station she met prisoner, and , he asked her to go to Manchester with him, and he would " make a lady "of her. Prisener got into the same com- • partment of the train, and on arrival at Wigan they had to change trains. While in the waiting-room at Wigan he assaulted her. Prisoner should have got into a train for Manchester, and the girl should have got into another for Warrington and Chester. They, however, got into a Liver- • pool train, and when nearing St. Helens he again assaulted her. She said she would call a guard, but they got out at St. Helens, and went to a lodging-house in Market-street, where prisoner said the girl was his wife. The girl said she was not. Later in the evening prisoner caused a distur- bance, and the police were called in to put him out. On hearirg the story of the girl, they took him into custody, . and he then assaulted the officers. He (Superintendent Johnston) did not propose to go into the case that day, but would ask for a remand.---The girl, Margaret Myles, of in- telligent appearance, was then put into the box. She said she was travelling on Thursday from Ribchester to Chester, and met prisoner at Preston. He assaulted her at Wigan, and again on nearing St. Helens. They went to a lodging- house together, where he said she was his wife but she con- tradicted him. In reply to the prisoner, the girl said she saw some porters at St. Helene, but she did not say any- • thing to them, or make any complaint. She went to George Ripley's public-house and there had a sandwich given her. He tried to pass her off as-hie sister there, but she said ehe was not. After that they went to a cookshop, and then to a lodging-house.—The Magistrates said the prisoner would be remanded for a week.—Prisoner asked for bail, but Superin- tendent Johnston said he knew nothing about him.—Pri- - sonar: lamin a respectable position. lam a traveller for a spirit merchant, and in a substantial position.—The Bench refused to grant bail, and the prisoner was removed in cus- tody.

THE CONGREGAT lON AL UNION. On Monday evening the Mayor of Norwich (Me.. Gurney) entertained a large number of the ministers and delegates attending the annual autumn meeting of the Congregational Union of England and Wales in the St. Andrew's Hall, Norwich. The business proper of the "Union commenced at Norwich, on Tues— day morning.---The Chairman (the Rev. Edward White, of Kentish Town) delivered his address, the subject of which was "Handling the Soriptures." He maintained that the doctrine of original Christianity had in no respect been superseded by the advance of science. The New Testament was not a ladder which might be kicked down after haying served its turn. He looked upon the Revised.Vsrsion as a distinct and considerable gain to the cause of apostolic Christianity. The-Bible as a whole was an overpowering. reply to all serious objections to the Bible in detail. In conclusion, Mr. White expressed the wish that the year of the Queen's jubilee might witness the ascension of indepene. dency into a new, national authority in religion by planting.: itself more firmly than ever on the authority of God.—. —The Rev. Dr. Allon. of London, moved a resolution.in-- structing the Committee, in the name of the Assembly, to • prepare an appropriate address of congratulation to the Queen on the jubilee of her reign.—Mr. Colman, seconded the resolution, which was adopted, the assembly rising eremasseend singing the National Anthem.—A peas. tion to Parliament in favour of the Sunday closing of prits-• lie-houses was adopted by the assembly.—The Rev. Mr.. Hunter, of Hull; introduced a resolution to the effect." That in view of the decision and action taken by the Committee. of the Union toreceive and hear Mr.Bescher in the event of his presence, in Norwich during the meetings of the Union,. the Assembly desired to express its-regret that it would not have an opportunity of giving hira,a hearty welcome."— Rev. Fleming Williams seconded the resolution., The. Chairman enpressed his delight at the good temper shown. by the mover and seconder of the resolution, whieh he en- tirely reciprocated. He had very strong feelings of respect, foe Mr. Raecher. They did not pass judgment upon any-- one. It was their duty to recogpise the good in every man. Many persons thought that Mr. Beecher had hada good in' flings in England already, and that they might, have their Union meetings without his presence.—(Hisses, "Shame," anti interruptions and cries of "Williams.") The Chairman, in the midst of the interruptions put the resolution and de-- eared it carried, but the decision was challenged by some of thenseerahly.—The Rev. Mr. Snell, of Manchester, .asked if it was utterly impossible that Mr. Beecher conk/ be present on Wednesday or Thursday. If that were not impossible he would move diet a tele- graphic invitation be sent to Mr. Beecher to addressthe Union. (Loud applause).—Aftersome discussions the Chairman remarked that as the last sentence of hi, speech had evidently given offence he frankly withdrew itf although he had no intention of irritating the feelings o- anyono—The Rev. Mr. Snell said that after that withdrawal by tire chairman he was prepared to 7ritbdraw.his amend- ment, which was agreed to by the seconden—Tbe resolution was then carried unaninaously.------The President of Yale :College, the Rey. Dr. Noah Porte, then addressed the assembly. He referred to the fact that at the time of Mr. Beecher's great trial he was chaietnan of the committee which drew up tha report acquitting him of the charges brought against him, and expressed the opinion that there was not a shadow. of- foundation, for those charges, He maintained that the Congregational body in America was as orthodox as any. evangelical body.—ln the evening a ' public meeting took place in St. Andrew's Hall, presided over by Mr. Albert Spicer, of London.—ekt Wednesday's meeting of the Congregational Union a resolution was,. liaised suggesting that the committee should approach other, evangelical bodies with a view to prevent overlapping in. Christian work. At a meeting in the evening it was an- nounced that the London Missionary Society expected a deficit in, income, this year amounting to probably £ls,CalOs The Congregational Union on Thursday received a depu- tation from the Baptist Union. The President of the latter body (the Rev. Charles Williams) suggested that in this aggressive work of the churches there should be net onIT co-operation but also consultations between their county, asseeiations to prevent the building of unnecessary chapels.. The Chairman of the Congregational Union (elle Rev.. Edward White), in his reply, said he had no great zeal for the union of denominations, and he expressed a hope that the zeal of Baptists against infant baptism would not, lead them to zeal against infants. It was annoulaced that the year's contributions to the Jubilee Fund amounted to £32,000, making a total income to date of Ye 374,000.
