TEE 'UNUSUAL EI'ERIENCES OF A PROMINENT
MAN MADE PUBLIC.

The following article from the Democrat aftid Clirogriele, of I/ )chester, NX.,i of so striking a nature and emanates from so reliable a sourte, that it is herewith re-published entire. In addition to the valuable matter it .contains, it will be found excked-

ingly interesting: To the Editor of the Democrat and Chronicle. Sritg—On the first day of June, 1881, I lay at my • residence in this city surrounded by my friends and - waiting for death- Heaven only knows the agony I then endured, for words can never describe it. And yet, if a few years previous, any one had told me that I was to be brought so low, and by so terrible . a disee-se, I should have scoffed at the idea. I had always been uncommonly strong and healthy, had weighed over 200 pounds, and hardly knew, in-my • own experience, what pain or sickness were. Very many people who will read this statement realise at times that they are unusually tired and cannotac- count for it. They feel dull and indefinite pains in various parts of the body and do not understand it. • Or they are exceedingly hungry one day and•Rntire- ly without appetite the next. This was just the way I felt when the relentless malady which had fastened itself upon axe first began, Still I thought it was nothing; that probably I had taken a cold which would soon pass away. Shortly after this I noticed a heavy, and .at times a neuralgic, pain in my head, but as it would come one day and be gone the next, I paid but little attention to it. Then my I . stomach would get out of order and my food often failed to digest, causing at times great inconvenience. Yet I had no idea, even as a physician, that these things meant anything serious, or that a monstrous disease was becoming fixed upon me. Candidly,:l •thought I was suffering from Malaria, and so doc-1 • tored myself accordingly, But I got no better. next noticed a peculiar colour and odour about the • fluids I was passing—also that there were large quantities one day and very little the next, and that a persistent froth and scum appeared upon the sur- face, and a sediment settled. And yet I did not realise my danger, for, indeed, seeing these symp-, • toms continually, I finally became accustomed to them, andmy suspicion was wholly disarmed by the fact that I had no pain in the affected organs or in their vicinity. Why I should have been so

blind I cannot understand. There is a terrible future for all physical neglect, . and impending danger always brings a person to . his senses, even though it may then be too late. I , . realised at last my critical condition and aroused myself to overcome it. And, Oh! how hard I tried I consulted the best medical skill in the land. I visited all the prominent mineral springs in America, and travelled from Maine to California. Still I grew • worse. No two physicians agreedas to my malady. • One said I was troubled with spinal irritation; . another, nervous prostration:; another, malaria, ; another, dyspepsia; another, heart disease; another, general debility; another, congestion of the base of the brain; and so on through ,a long list of com- mon diseases, the symptoms of all of which I really had. In this way several years passed, during all of which time I was steadily growing worse. My condition had really become pitiable. The slight symptoms I first experienced were developed into terrible and constant disorders. My weight had been reduced from•2o7 to 130 pounds. My life was a torture to myself and friends. I could retain no -food.upon my stomach, and lived wholly by injec- tions. I was a living mass of pain. My pulse was uncontrollable. In my agony I frequently fell upon the floor, convulsively clutched the carpet, and prayedfor death. Morphine had little or no effect in deadening the pain. For six days and nights I had the death-premonitory hiccoughs constantly My urine was filled with tube casts and albumen. I •was struggling with 'Bright's disease of the kidneys in its last stages.

While:suffering thus I received a call from my pastor, the Rev. Dr. Foote, rector of -St. Paul's Church, of this city. I felt that it was our last ii.nterview, but in the .course of conversation Dr. Foote detailed to me the many remarkable cures which had come under his observation, by means of ;a remedy which he urged me to try. As a practis- ing ,physician and a graduate of the schools, I .cherished-the prejudice both natural and common 'with all regular practitioners, and derided the idea of any medicine outside the regular channels being the least beneficial. So solicitous, however, was Dr. Foote, that I finally promised I would waive -my prejudice .and try the remedy he so highly recommended. :I began its use on the Ist day of June and took it according to directions. At first it sickened me; but this I thought was a good sign for media my debilitated condition. I continued -to take it; the sickening sensation departed, and I was able to retain food upon my stomach. In a few days I noticed a decided change for the better, as also did my wife and friends. My hiccoughs ceased, arid I experienced less pain than formerly. I was so rejoiced at this improved condition that, upon what I had believed but a few days before was my dying bed, I vowed, in the presence of my family and friends, should I recover I would both publicly and privately make known this remedy for the good of humanity, wherever and whenever I had an opportunity, and this letter is the fulfilment of that TOW. My improvement was constant from that time, and in less than three months I had gained 26 pounds in flesh, became entirely free from pain, and I believe I owe my life and present condition wholly to Warner's Safe Cure, the remedy which I used. Since my recovery I have thoroughly re-investi- gated the subject of kidney difficulties and Bright's disease, and the truths developed are astounding. I therefore state, deliberately, and as a physician, that I believe that more one-half the deaths which occur in America are caused by Bright's disease -of the kidneys. This may sound like a rash statement, but I am prepared to fully verify it. Bright's disease has no distinct symptomsof its own (indeed, it often develops without any pain whatever in the kidneys or their vicinity), but has the symptoms of nearly every other known complaint. Hundreds of people die daily, whose burials are authorised by a phy- sician's certificate as occurring from "Heart Dis- Apoplexy 7. "Paralysis," ease," ""Spinal Com- Rheumatism," "Pneumonia," and other plaints," " common diseases, when in reality it was Bright's lisease of the kidneys. Few physicians, and fewer people, realise the extent of this disease or its diugerons and insidious nature: It steals into the syetem like a thief, manifests its presence by the commonest symptoms and fastens itself upon the , constitution before the victim is aware. It is nearly as hexeditary as consumption, quite as common, and „fully as fatal. Entire families, inheriting it from their ancestors, have died, and yet none power which of the num_ her knew or realised the mysterious was remcviN them. Instead of common symptoms it often shows none whatever, but brings death suddenly from convulsions, apoplexy, or heart dis- ease. As one who has suffered, and knows by bitter experience what he says, I implore everyone who reads these words not to neglect the slightest symp- om of kidney difficulty. Certain agony and possible death will be the sure result of such neglect, and no one can afford to hazard such chances. I am aware that such an unqualified statement as this, coming from me, known as I am throughout the entire land as a practitioner and lecturer, will arouse the surprise -and possible animosity of the medical profession and astonish all with whom I am

acquainted, but I make the foregoing statements, based upon facts which I am prepared ;:o produce, and truths which I can substantiate to the letter. The welfare of those who may possibly be sufferers such as I was, is an ample inducement for me to take the step I have, and if I can successfully warn others from the dangerous path in which I once walked, I am willing to endure all professional ana personal consequences.
J. B. lIENION, M.D.

• FOREIGN NEWS- THE BULGARIAN CRISIS.— THE ELECTIONS.— SERIOUS RIOTS AND LOSS OF LIFE. SOFIA, SIINDAY.—The elections to the Great Sobranje commenced here this morning. About 150 peasants arrived from the surrounding villages and proceeded to the Russian Consulate, where they gave cheers for the Czar and aeleed for his protection. M. Nekliudoff, the Russian Diplomatic Agent, thereupon appeared on the balcony and delivered a short speech. The peasants then proceeded to the polling place and endeavoured to disperse the electoral bureau. The crowd within, howeverrresisted, and an affray ensued., in which sticks and stones were freely used, several of the peasante being wounded. Having been expelled from the courtyard in front of the-pnlling place, they returned to the Russian Consulate, where bread and other nesessaries were distributed to them. About four o'clock the crowd round the Russian Consulate began hooting the peasants in the garden, when one of them threw a heavy piece of wood among the people. His example was Wowed immediately by others, who threw both wood and st, nes. The crowd outside then began to retaliate with stones, and the Monte- negrins and Cavasses in the garden of the Consulate there- upon drew their revolvers and fired about fifteen shots among Vie crowd, who, however, did not fire in return. The gen- darmerie ultimately dispersed the crowd. No one was wounded. It is asserted that the man who first fired is a person frequently seen at the Russian Consulate. Accord- ing to a current report, M. Nekliudoff stated that the eventi of to-day would lead to a-complete rupture of relations be- tween Russia and Bulgaria. On arriving at Shurela Gen. Kaulbars was encountered by a large crowd, who informed him that they bad full conadence in the present Govern- ment; and that they desired the immediate convocation of the Sobranje and the punishment of the conspirators. Another crowd, numbering about 5,000 people, afterwards collected near the windows at which General Kaulbars was seated, and hooted twelve :..Zankovists who went to pay their respects to the General. The latter 'called an oftleer and asked him to disperse the crowd, but he answered that it was not his business and declined to interfere. Late in the evening it was found that all the Ministers and leaders of their party had been elected by overwhelming majorities. About' 400 supperters of the Government have been elected, and about 20 Zankovists. SOFIA, MONDAY.—A deputation waited upon M. Redo- slaveff yesterday evening in order to congratulate the Pre- mier upon the result of the election. A telegram from Dubnitza states that MM. Graneieroff and Zagra, deputies, and M. Dimitreff, the prefect, were murdered by Mace- donians during the elections at that place yesterday. At Irretzt and Slavena, where the population is favourable to Rassia, the elections were not proceeded with. At Buccino an attempt was made to held the elections, but the electoral bureau was several times dispersed by the people, and was at length forced to close the polls. The results of 80 out of 86 divisions are now known, and it is expected that of the whole number 70 or more are in favour of the Government. PHILIPPOPOLIS, MONDAY.—The Macedonian suspected of being concerned in the plot against the Government, who was recently arrested at Eski Luxe, has been examined by the authorities. The prisoner deposed that the Russian Consulates here at Sofia and Rustchuk had organised in , their respective departments four bands under the leadershipl of trusted partisans of Russia which were to meet on the 17th inst. on the height of St. Getorge's in the Balkans, and thence to disperse themselves over the country stirring no a revelt.against the Government, in order to prepare a way for altussian occupation. BVSTOHIIII, MONDAY.—The elections here have resulted in the return of all the Government,eandidates by a large majorlty:l,o24 votes havirg been recorded in their favour, against-SO for their opponents. The authorities are in full possession of full details of the plot discovered'at Eski Zags, which, according to the testimony of the persons arrested, received pecuniary support from Ramie. VIEMIA, WEDNESDAY Mousram.—News from Sofia states that out of 500 deputies whose election has been made known. 480 are firm supporters of tho Government, 26 are followers of M. Zankoff, and 15 of M.:Karavelort. The Great Sobranje will be convoked in a fortnight's time, and will meet at Tirnova. The Government will almost imme- diately issue a formal reply to M.Neklindarsprotastagainet the legality of the elections. TIIIIRSDAY.—A despatch from Sofia states that General Eaulbare has received telegraphic instructions from St. Petersburg expressly ordering him to renounce the idea of continuing his journey through Roumelia, and to return without delay to Rustchuk. iNDIA.—CONTINUED RIOTING. DELHI, SATURDAY—The state of affairs in this town continaes in a critical condition, and reinforcements of dragoons and infantry have been despatched hither from Meerut. The Maloometans have destroyed a small Hindoo temple, breaking the idols in pieces and smearing the place with blood. Twenty 'natives are in the hospital, suffering from wounds of a dangerous character. The injuries sus- tained by Mr.ilatcheti, the district superintendent of police. who was wounded in the riot here last Monday, are seri- ous. Order was maintained by the troops throughout last night. BOMBAY, SATUBDAY.—Serions riots occurred yesterday between the Hindoos end Mahometans at Jeptur. in the Kattywar district. No casualties, however, are reported. Dnutr, SUNDAY. The town is now quieter, and the troops have been withdrawn, but are kept in readiness for immediate action in case of necessity. • BOMBAY, TUBSDAY.—A actions religions riot has occurred at Hashiapur. in the Punjaub. The Mahometans attacked the Hindoo quarters looting and wrecking the houses. A. detachment of the Connaught Rangers, who were en route for Jullundur, weredetainedrhy the authorities to quell the disturbances. A few casualties occurred. FIGHTING IN BURMAH. RANGOON, SATUUDLY.—Quetnappe was looted and burned by the Shans on the 7th inst. The force. ander General White, despatched to the relief of the garrison had an en- gagement with the rebels, who were compelled to retreat to the hills. Their loss is not yet known. The British casuali- ties were one killed and six wounded. RANGOON, MONDAY. Colonel Winsloe'a column. with 130 sick, reached Mahlon, four miles south of Minhla, yes- terday, an I embarked there for Thayetmyo. On the march they had a skirmish with the insurgents, our casualties be- ing one man killed and two men wounded. Mandalay is quiet, but the district is much disturbed by the insurgents. A large gathering of the rebels is reported on the Pangana river, south of Ave. The Tsagam district is ravaged by in- surgent bodies under Hlavo and Minoh. The troops have defeated the insurgents at Yatagya. The rebels are in considerable force in the Minhla district. The Pagan district continues to improve under Mr. Eyre's control.
TURKEY.

t CONSTANTINOPLE, SATURDAY.--it is stated that the delay ; in sanctioning the appointment of Sir W. White as British ; representative at Constantinople was due to Russian in- trigue 3 at the Palace. The date of Sir E. Thornton's fare- well audience of the Sultan has not yet been fixed, and it is inferred in diplomatic circles that the delay is due to the Sultan's desire to gratify Russia and France,who, it is stated, have for some time been endeavouring to cause embarrass- ment,to England in Egypt. ANARCHIST PLOT TO BURN VIENNA. VIENNA, SATURDAY.—The Vienna police discovered and arrested on the 3rd inst. a band of about 20 Anarchists be- longing to the working classes, who were engaged in the manufacture of explosives with the intention, on the night between the 3rd and 4th inst, to set fire to the timber stores and certain public buildings in Vienna, and then to throw bombs among the crowds which would be attracted by the cenflagration. A quantity of dynamite, bombs, and dag- gers were seized by the police. Five kilogrammes of dynamite were also discovered under the railway bridge at Penzing. VIENNA, 6UNDAY.—There is not the least doubt that the design of the Anarchist conspirators far surpassed in extent and diabolia ingenuity anything ever aimed at by Johann Most's followers or by the party of dynamite in London. Had the scheme of the Anarchists succeeded, it may be safely said that Vienna would have been the scene of such wholesale crime and destruc- tion as has not been witnessed for centuries. The police examination of the prisoners has established the fact that the plot was directed from the United States and from London. IMPROVED TRADE IN CAN illA. OTTLWAt TUSSIOS.—The reports from the industrial cen- tres of Canada Weak very favourably of the activity of business at the present time. The railway returns show that the rolling stock is being employed to its fullest capacity.

ANOTHER EARTHQUAKE SHOCK. HLure.x, TEILTRSDAII.—A shock of earthquake lasting ten seconds has been felt at Sydney, Cape Breton Islands. The inhabitants were much alarmed, but no damage is re- ported..

DESTRUCTION OF A TOWN. NEW 1.70RK, TnOLSDAL A despatch from Orange, Texas, reports that a town on the Sabine Pass was totally destroyed by the overflowing of the Sabine river on Tuesday night. Sizty-five lives were lest. A hotel in which were twenty persons was carried away by the floods, and swept into the bay, all the occupants beinz drowned. _

t_ GAMING Ex.rEuxFSCR. —At Bow-stieet Police Court, London, on Monday, John Mills was remanded charged with stealing a watch and money, by means of the confi- dence trick, from Ben. Gibson, a sergeant in the Ck,eshire eonstabalary.—Mr N'aughan, magistrate, to the prosecutor: I think the experience you have had in London will be bene- ficial to you In Cheshire. 1114,SSACLIE OF CHRISTIANS —TIM= VILLAGES BERNED. —The .1 Standard " Paris correspondent telegraphs :—The director of the Catholic Miasions has received a letter Irom Mgr. Puginisr in which the situation of the Christians in Tonking is described as most deplorable. Since writing be has sent the following telegram, which proves that his fears were not unfotanded :—" Tanhos.. Seven hundred Chris- tians have been massacred, 30 Tillages burned, and MOO ChriEtiAna aro earring."

FOOTBALL.

.0. Secretaries ot F,otbtll Clubs are requested to note t.3.t reports of matches. played on Saturday ruust be sent tc thehead ottine, itewsey-street, Warrington. not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY RULES. FARNIVOiarn 'V. WELIMINGTON RANGERS.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Aturday, and after a hard game victory rested with Farnworth by one dropped goal and seven minor points to three minor

points. RUNCOEN ATHLETIC V. SUTTON FREE WINDERERS.—A match between these clubs was played at Runcorn on Satur- day, when the Athletics obtained toe victory, the score be- ing :—Athletics, 4 tries and 7 minors to Fret Wanderers 1 disputed goal and 2 minors. HOWLEIC ROVERS V. HOWLEY RANGERS.— This match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter and resulted in a easy win for the Rovers by four tries, five minors, to nil, or under new rules, four points. The tries were obtained by Thornily, Fairhurst, and Andrews. SANKETZ RANGERS V. Sr. JAMES'S ROVEIC.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and after a very pleasant game the Rangers won by three tries (Massey, Whitfield, Glover), seven minors, to nil. The Ran- gers played a clinking game. as did also the,Rovers. Sr. HELENS V. WAVERTREE.—These two old opponents should have met on the ground of the former. at Denton's Green-lane. A number of spectators assembled, but they were disappointed by the arrival of a telegram stating that the Wavertree club could not get a team. The first and second teams of the home club then played a scratch

match. WAL'ZON V. SCTTON.—These teams met at Walton on Saturday, and a very evenly-contested match ended in fa- vour of Sutton by one goal (three points) and two minors to one try (one point) and three minors. Smon played one man short. R fd‘Cully, 3 Wilson,and A. IWEinnon were the most conspicuous for Suttan, while J Roberts and E Holden did goad service for Walton. LATCIIFORD T. PENDLETON ATECLETIC.—This match was played on the ground of the latter, on Saturday, and after a very rough game ended in a victory for tile visitors by 1 goal, 5 minors, to 1 try and 1 minor. The try was got by J. Acton, and converted into a splendid goal by Jon. Barber. For Latchford Boardman, .1 Acton, J Barber, W Ttylor, J Jackson played a good game, and Barrett did likewise for the

home team. WARRINGTON HORNETS V. WIGAN ROVEIIr. (IST TEAMS.) —These clubs met at Wigan on Saturday, the game result- ing in a win for the Hornets by one goal, one try, and four mi3or points to three tries and eight minors. -Joe Pritchard dropped the goal for the Hornets in a clever way, and Jas. Whittaker got the try. The Hornets team was badly re- presented. This is the fourth match this season; two have been won and, two drawn. WARRINGTON HORNETS T. WIGAN ROVERS (2ND TEAMS.) —These clubs met on Saturday on the Hornets' ground for the erst time this season, the game ending in a win for the Rovers by one goal, one try to one try. The try was got by -Isherwood for the Hornets. The game was rough and fast. B. Wilcock and Cooper at bark played well for the home team; the forwards one and all worked well to-

gether. Ruefteme RECREATION (2ND) V. BIRKENHEAD WAN- DER3IIS.—ThiS match was played on Saturday on the ground of the former, and after a somewhat rough and noisy.game resulted in a win for the "Rece " by. 2 goals, 8 minors, tcel try and 2 minor points. P. Brooks dropped a goal for the" Rees," and J. Lunt got a try, to which H. Grounds (captain) added the major point. Alex. Smith gained the try for the Wanderers, but his side failed to im- prove upon it. EOPerlreOßT, OLYMPIC Y. Leen HOI7SE TRUE BM:O.—The members of the Lowe House True BI nes football cl ab journeyed to Southport, and played a vary evenly-contested match with the Southport, Olympics, the game being played under the new Rugby rules. During the first half no points were scored, .1) ut at the close ef the second half Gill, for the Olympiesernade a capital run and succeeded in carrying the ball over the Blues' goal line. The try was not improved ups, and the game stood Southport Olympic one point to the True Blues nil. WIDNMS RECREATION V. LEVENSHULME —Played at Leyensbulme on Saturday, when after a hard fought and pleasant game the visitors were victorious by one goal (dropped by Grundy) and four minors to one try and fire minors. The following were the teams :—Widnes Recrea- tion cFall back, Barker; three-quarter backs, Grundy. Wailing, and Flynn:; half backs. Norris and Gaskell • for- wards, Clare, Johnson, Curry, Brarnon, Tonkies. Mkririe (captain), Noon, Sumner, and G. Wright. Umpire, Mr. Benjamin Hartley' Levenehnlme: Fall back, W.Vaughan ; three-quarter backe, C. Ryder, d. Parkinson, and T. Bytbell ; half becks A. ,Green and A. Nally; forwards, Larder, J. Robinson: W. Cowan, Hall. W. Barker, C. Fenn, W. East- wood, James Henderson, and J. Knott. Umpire, Mr. E. Perkineon. Referee, Mr. Cowan. RUNCORN RECREATION 'V. ST. AUGUSTINE'e (MARCHES- TER).—The abeye-named clubs met on the groued of the latter on Saturday. Recreation were victorious by 1 goal. 1 try, to the Saints' niL Pennington, Worrell, and Massey played a good forward game, with Booth and G. Pendlebury behind, for the Recreation, and Healy and Forster, forward, and Greenall and the two Hunts, backs, for the home team. After a pleasant game the visitors were entertained to tea in the Church schoolroom. Teams: Recreation—Full back, S Booth; H Pendlebury, W Wistalade, and James Clare, three- qaarter backs; W Woodward and G Pendlebury, half backs; Acton, Pennington, Worrell, Coutn, Massey, Price, Carr, d Green, and Peacock, forwards. Saints—Full back, F Allen; Ramsbottom, Greenall (captain), and Smith. three-quarter backs; d and C Hunt, half backs: Healy, Hough. Farm- worth, Jolly, Fawcett, Watkins, Tonlan, Forster, and McGee, forwards. COCKHEDGE MISSION STAR OF 1:10pE V. CHESHIRE LINES Seegeren Teeer.—This match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the former. The visitors' captain won the toss, and the home team kicked off. Soon after the com- mencement play raged furiously in the'visitors' quarters, the home team at last haying a minor conceded to them. After the drop out the visitors worked a little hetter to- gether, but still they could not get from mid-field. The home contingent again took the ball over the line, Swindells kicking dead. Up to half-time the home team severely pressed their opponents, but still could not score a major point. The second half was a repetition of the first, but in this half the visitors at the hands of Scariabrick managed to secure a try, Shaw's kick at goal being a failure, the bell falling rather short. At the close the home team were de- Glared the winners of a very fast game by 1 try and 6 miners to nil. Ste HELENS RECREATION V. WALEDEN.—These teams met on the groand of the former, on Saturday afternoen, when a very stubbornly-contested game was witnessed by about 2400 spectators. The game was under the new rules for scoring passed by the Football Association a few weeks ago, which accounts a goal three points and a try one, whilst eto notice is taken of the minor points. Parr, the Recrea- tion captain, kicked off, and immediately hostilities com- menced with earnestness. Both sides played with great vignur, tut neither could gain any advantage.. At the close of half time Walkden had succeeded in scoring two minors to nothing. On change of ends the home team soon equal- ised matters by some strong and quick play. Towards the end of the game a splendid struggle took place a few yards from the Recreation goal line. The Walkaen men made re- peated attempts to score, but were prevented by the fine play Of the home teairi. The result was a draw, as follows : Racreatiob three miaor pointe,Walkden two. • SANKEY V. WARRINGTON 2ND.—This match was Played on the ground of the latter on Saturday. Warrington kicked off, and took play to the visitors' 25 flag. Some good scrimmages here took place, and Barton getting the.ball, and being pressed, kicked, and following up secured a try, the same player failing in kicking a goal, the ball striking the post. Woolev was next prominent by a short run, but loos- ing the ball, Barton took a flying kick, the ball bitting the bar, and rebounded into Highly's hands, who drooped over the line, the ball, however, being ruled back. Benin, Bird, and Skidmore were next to the front with a splendid drib- ble. This brought about half-time. Jefferson kicked off for Sankey, and the forwards following well up, prevented a return, the visitors keeping the home team in their own 26 for a considerable time, but they at last broke away and transfered play to the visitors' quarters. Rigby picking the ball up in a scrimmage on the Sankey goal line got Over, but was ruled back. Here the Sankey forwards broke away with a splendid rush, and overcoming all opposition carried, the ball to the Warrington quarters. Time was now called, leaving Sankey the winners of a very hard game by 1 try, 3 minors, to Warrington 2nd nil. Bate at half back for the losers played a grand game, as did also Jolley, a full back. Referee, Mr. A. Allen. SALFORD V. WIDDIES.—PIayed at Salford. A good mus- ter of spectaters assembled to witness the game. which was played under the new rules. Ottiwell kicked off for Salford with the wind and ground in their favour, and after even play in the Widnes half, Slater dropped at goal without effect, a dead ball being reeistered. From a neat pass by Varley, Slater punted the ball over the crossbar, only gain- ing a minor. Farrell then made a splendid rush, taking operations into the Salford quarter, but the borne men, working well together, neutralised the edvanLage, and Var- ley, getting possession, dropped a beautiful goal. Kiddie I resumed from centre, and Smith following up well, an at- tack was made on the Salford citadel, Clegg nicely reliev- ing, and two more minors were gained by fine play on the part of the home team before half time. After change of ends, the game still continued of a fast and exciting des- cription, the dribbling of the forwards of bath teams being much admired. Slater put another drop, which transferred the leather behind the line, and after the full-back had run the ball out a scrimmage was formed, almost on the Widnes line. While in dangerous proximity to the visitors' strong- hold Barlow got possession from a throw out and, strongly running, grounded the ball over the line. Ottiwell failing at the place. Plumpton, Harding, and Farrell worked bril- liantly to score, while Varley, Slater, and Eagles were con- spicuous in the frustrating tactics, arid after two minors were scored in Widnes' favour a grandly contested game ended in a victory for the home team by 1 goal, 1 try, and 2 minors, to Widnes two minors, or according to the new rules, Salford 4 points, Widnes nil. ARDWICE IST V. WARRINGTON "A."—This InitCh was played at Ardwick on Saturday last in the presence of a goodly number of spectators. A start was effected at 330. The first noticeable point was made by O'Brien, who made a capital run, but was brought down by Boardman before he became dangerous. From loose play which followed, Ran- dalls secured the ball and made a capital kick, and Moly- neaux, following well up, obtained possession, through Hall mulling, and obtained a splendid try. The attempt at goal Is, Ashurst, however, proved fruitless. Blakely dropped out
with a smart long kick, which Randslls did not fail to re- turn in his usual competent style. Directly afterwards Whittle gained possession and passed to Appleton, who

dropped ,nlendid goal. Morris recommenced the game, but owing to an infringement of the off-side rule by the home team, the bail was called back and a scrimmage formed, when, owing to a misunderstanding, the visitors were compelled to touchdown. Appleton restarted the game by a beautiful kick, the ball entering•touch from the &id of play, near the 25 yardstag. The Warrington forwards im- mediately afterwards came down the tield in a combined . .
dribble, and Boyle picking up passed to Whittle, the latter
. . securing a try, which point Asimrst•failed to improve. The borne quarters were again invaded by the visitors, and Whittle securing the hall transferredit to Appleton, who.es-

sayed a drop at goal, tut was not so fortunate as in his for- mer attempt, a minor point only being registered. The ball was no sooner brought into play than the visitors' forwards took it over the line, and another minor point was regis- . _
tered. On resuming the game the home 'team now pre;Sed the visitors and Unswerth was compelled to touchdown. By

some good loose play Warrington entered the Ardwiik territory, and Boardman, receiving the ball from Whittle, gained a somewhat easy try; Asburst failing again at goal, although this and his wo previous attempts were very good ones. Pole dropped out, the return being made by Antro- bus, and a good bit of passing took place between Whittle, Antrobus and Appletost, the latter altimately being brought

down near the line. From the scrimmage which ensued, Morris passed to O'Brien, who made -a long run, but was brought down by Telford. With the exception of a few dashing runs by the backs on each side, and another minor noint being registered for the visitors, nothing further of importance occurred totthe call of time, when Warrington were declared the winners by 1 goal, 3 tries, and 3 minors, to Ardwick 2 minors. For the visiton, Appleton, Board- . _ _ .

man, and Whittle weve,the pick of the backs,' whilst Moly- neaux, Dillon, Littlewood, and Telford played a sterling forward game. For the home team, Pole and Morris played a oapital game in the .back department, whilst the pick of the forwards were Eroadfoot (captain), Welster, and Buxton. Teams:—Warrington r. Raudalls, back; .Boardman, Apple- ton, and Crnswortb, three-quarter backs; Whittle (captain) aud Antrobue, half hacks; Molyneaux, Nevins, Littlewood, Boyle, Jones, Ashurst, Eyres, Dillon, and Telford, forwards. Ardwick : Hall, Bank; Pole. O'Brien, and Blackie, three- quarter backs; Morris and Holt, half backs; Broadfoot, Brindle?, Henderson, Moores, Simpson, Webster, Blackley, Buxton, and Barber, forwards. Ruwconw v. Rocenehres HORNETS —The Runcorn team travelled to Rochdale, onCaturday, when they met the Hor- nets, a team who have earned a good reputation by their sterling play. The Runcorn team, however, had been slightly altered from that which played against Salford, Riley and Cawley taking the places of Lunt and Davies. Hastings, the Hornets captain, having choice of ends, chose to play uphill, when W. Hughes started the ball, and in response to the return, Cawley put in a short run, but was put into touch by Bamford. IFrom the line out the ball was taken into the Hornets' half.. Buckley smartly kicking back. W. Hughes securing, a free ,kick, the ball was again sent into the Hornets quarter. Bamford and Speakman exchang- ing kicks. The ball then got among the forwards, who by good play took it nearer the line; and Weight coming through with the ball at his loot was within an ace of scor- ing, hot Buckley touched downejust in time. Hastings ran along the touch line, and getting clear of the .pack looked like getting through. Riley, ehowever, tackled so safely that all his subsequent movements were well watelled. From centre field Faulkner, Clarke and Gatley started a nice dribble, which Nolan frustrated by dropping on thehall near to the line. H. Hughes, however, punted on, the ball going dead behind the line. After the drop met some i long kicking was indulged in by Buckley, Cawley, and Riley, the ball eventually restingein touch in the home half. From the line out another rush mks made into the Hernets' territory. where Nolan exchanged quickly to fEattings, whom Riley again disposed of before he got out of his own half. Wainwright was next to move towards the home line, and by a strong run got in close prozeimity to the line, when relief was attempted by Griffiths, who was smartly collared by Gatley. Buckley, however, relieved the pressure by touching down again which tactics e esorted to again in a very short time. ial In one instance .he ran back some ten yards in order to bring about relief by touching dawn. Speakman and H. Hughes next contributed runs, Speakman only being checked in tithe to prevent him scoring. On half time being aunbunced, the score stood Runoern seven minors, Hornets nothing. The game now became very fast, Hastings making grand efforts to score, as did Nolan and Smith' but theeir movements were too well watched. An .effort was now made by Faulkner and Broady uphill. When up near the home line Andrews gave Speakman a chance, but Smith was down on him before he could get away. From here Nolan got away to centre, Riley dropping en the ball. For a little time play continued in the Runcorn half, the ball exchanging hands rapidly, until Cawley kicking on, Nolan got a free kick. Wylde took the place kick at goal, the ball dropping 'jag upder the bar. Play continued at a fast pace, but neither team secured a wincing point, the game remaining drawn--Rancorn seven minor points to two. At three-quarters Speakman and Riley were in the best form, their collaring and kicking, being good. At half back Andrews and Hugiaes showed much better form than previously this season. The forwards played a" clinking" game, in fact they outplayed the Hornets' forwards corn- ips laryu,nniFnogr atrihde hploemteelyte,ebonithHiansttihnegspa(ccaksaanind) iwnothbeestlo,oshe general play being splendid. Nolan and Bamford played very safely at half. The forwards frequently showed what they were capable of doing if not closely watched. They played very nicely in the open, being expert dribblers. Wil- son. Scholes, and Wylde doing a lot of good work. Teams : —Rochdale Hornets: S Buckley, beck; T Smith, W Hast- ings and J W Griffiths. three-quarter backs; J Nolan and A BIB:ford half backs; B Nuns, J Brierley, J Groves, T Mallien, J Rankin, R Ashworth. W Scholes, E Wylde, and J Wilson, forwards. Runcorn: T Woods, back; H Cawley, W A Riley. and H C Qpeakman, three-quarter backs; H Hughes and H G Andrews, half backs; W Wright, W Hughes, J Lewis, W H Broady, J Gatley, J Barnes, J Clarke, W Faulkner, and G Wainwright, forwards. WARRINGTON V. NEW BRIGHTON. New Brighton for the first time visited Warrington on Saturday, and were very decisively defeated, the scores be- ing—Warrington, 3 goals, 5 tries, and 5 minors; New Brighton, 1 try and 1 minor. The weather was beautifully fine, this being, no doubt, a great inducement to the 3,060 spectators who assembled to witness the encounter. Harry Ashton won the toes, and elected to play with a slight wind in his favour. little before four o'clock the New Brighton captain kicked off, Massey returning, and a few tight scrim- mages took place at half-way. The visitors' forwards showed up best first, and the oval was taken to the borne 25, Gilbert, by good play, taking it back again. Gilbert afterwards gained a lot of ground by propelling the leather down the field to touch. Shortly afterwards the visitors' forwards, by a dangerous rush, cooked like scoring, Walsh saving extremely well. Speakman put in a Nice pass to Barnes, who, in turn, passed to Gilbert, who kicked to touch. From some loose play Jolley got hold, and, knock- ing his opponents aside, grounded the oval over the line, Walsh making a good attempt at goal. The hick out was well returned ley Hough, the ball directly after going to touch in goaL Play settled down to centre from the kick out, until Speakman put in a nice dribb,e to the 25 flag. A piece of excellent play was next witnessed between Turner, Jolley, and Povev, which gained a lot of ground. A nice pass was next sent to Barnes from Gilbert, the little three- quarter dropping amidst great cheering a beautiful goal. Speakman returned the kick out, scrimmages next taking place. Ashton, Davies, Povev, and Heves next showed up prominently with a nice dribbles but the visitors' forwards, beaded by Macmillan, grandly returned the charge. Gilbert now put in a dribble, taking the ball close to line, and smartly picked up and transferred to Barnes, who, in turn, passed to Fair. Turner, who got over, Walsh failing at goal. A. scrimmage followed. and Barnes got he a lying kick, gain- ing ground; and the ball falling into the hands of Massey he kicked it dead. Another dead ball shortly afterwards resulted through the instrumentality of Barnes. Good play was next witnessed on the part of Massey, Walsh, and Barnes, one minor resulting. A good pass by Gilbert to Jolley nearly enabled the latter to score, and the same half back next passed to " Tommy," who wriggled his wee' over; Walsh again failing to notch the coveted point. From the kickout Gilbert returned to touch, and the same player now got in a good run and pass to Povey, who in turn re-passed to Fair. Turner, who, knocking aside his opponents with the greatest ease, obtained another try. Speakman was this time entrusted with the place kick, which was successful. From the kick out Barnes only made a poor return, and the visitors' forwards playing up with greater vigour, confined play to the home 25. ToWnsend now put in a fine run, be- ing only stopped when on the line, and immediately followed a dead ball in favour of the. visitors. Frank Turner kicked, and W. Dillon following well up pre- vented a return, hostilities occurring in the centre. Jolley replied to a good run by Townsend, and then Walsh nicely saved a dangerous rush, and put in a good kick. Jolley again got in a nice run, and, by the aid of Ashton, Davies, and Frank Turner, the ball was taken to the line. From a scrimmage near centre Gilbert passed to Barnes,who dropped his second goalrntt raaenmdo :dips ttahvgeireefisae, tl idea. pl fp l taAi u mf steee .r ti waslAe f call sea odl intervalteheg boaoball play yz b tGh cbee Frank Turner kicked off, the ball falling into touch. The visitors agreeing to play it there, Frank Turner was first to show up prominently, gaining ground by a strong rush, and it is a noticeable thing that this young player may always be depended upon to give back a good pass. The breeze had now freshened considerably, this being of great advantage to the visitors. Townsend got in a good run and kick, Speakman replying. Massey now got hurt through collid- ing with Townsend, and had to retire for a short time. Speakman had to fall back to throe-quarters, Davies taking his place at half. The visitors, finding a man short, quickly took the ball to the lice; but Massey, coming on at this critical moment, stopped their scoring. Play still raged in the Warrington quarters; but Davies eventually moved to half way. The visitors' ferwards again worked the ball back, and *Frank Turner aided his side by removing to half-way. The two three-quarters (Jolley and Barnes) now treated the spectators to a fine bit of passing, Povey gaining ground by a good run. Townsend kicked the ball full into the hands of Massey, who got in a splendid run to 25. Jones now sent a long kick to Walsh, who finely returned, and was loudly applauded for so doing. Speakman taking the bell to the line. Townsend, however, was equal to the occasion, and sent down a good kick, Massey replying by a smart ran. Jones now ran in without opposition, as the Warrington men were under the impression that the whistle had blown, the kick at goal proving futile, as Ashton, Turner, Dillon, and Hughes charged it down. Some good Passing was next indulged in between Speakman, Povay, and Frank Turner, the last named getting a try, Speakman

making a good attempt at goal, but failing. Ashton soon afterwards scored by an unselfish pass from Fair. '1 urner, Speakman again not kicking a goal. Good play by Gilbert and Hough brought a pleas4ntly-contested game—one of the best ever seen on the club ground—to a conclusion. All theWarrington men played an excellent combined game, Walsh at back playing extremely well. Barnes again showed that he was fit for any team in England, the two half-backs and Jolley and Massey also showing superior form. Fair. and Frank Turner, Ashton, and W. Dillon were, perhaps, the best of a fine lot of forwards. Townsend, Jones, and Macmillan were the best of the New Brighton contingent. Warrington team: Goal, Walsh ; three-quarter backs. Massey, Barnes, and Jolley; half-backs, Speakman and Gilbert ; forwards, Ashton, Povey, Davies, Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, Hoagh, Hughes, Reyes, and Dillon. Re- feree, Mr. Naylor, Wigan. ASSOCIATION RULES.

EARLESTOWN V. GOLBORNE.—These local teams met at Golborne, on Saturday afternoon, in the presence of a large number of spectators. The visitors had the best of the game throughout, and won by four goals to two. ST. HELENS ASSOCIATION V. BOOTLE WANDERERS.— The first teams .of these clubs met on the ground of the former, near the Cowley Grammar School, on Saturday af- ternoon. The game was of an exciting character, and the play was very even, but the visitors won by four goals to one. EARLIESTOWN (2ND Tux) v. GOLDORNR (2ND).—The second teams of the Earlestown and Golborne Clubs met on the ground of the first-named, the Mesnes, Earlestown, en Saturday afternoon. There was only a poor attendance of spectators. The match resulted in a victory for Earlestown by six goals to none. RUNCORN V. WIDNES.—The Association teams of these towns played a game on the ground of the Widnes club on Saturday. The Runcorn captain won the toss, and Widnes kicked off at four o'clock, the play being limitel to two 35 minutes. A very even game Was played, neither side hav- ing scored up to three minutes before time. Then Hickson scored by a grand ehot from a free kick, leaving Runcorn the winners of a good game by one goal to nil. LANCASHIRE CuP TIE.—HAYDOCS T. Car RCH.—The meeting of these teams at Haydock on Saturday afternoon, to decide their tie in the first round of the competition of the Lancashire Association Challenge Cup.-excited a lively interest throughout the district, and nearly 1,500 persons attended. The visitors won the toss and -elected to play during the first half with the wind in their favour. S Har- rison kicked off for the home team, and the play at once became of a very exciting character. , The leather Was taken into the Church quarters, but it was well returned by the backs and the struggle raged in mid-field for some time. After about 25 minutes' play the visitors began to assume a strong lead and pressed their opponents, but Taylor, assisted by the backs aad half backs. ,cleverly saved his charge on several occasions. A swift, low shot by W Woad scored the first goal for Church, and a few minutes later, after some splendid passing, the visitors again scored. The home team then visited the other end, and playing with great determination, compelled Thorpe to work actively to secure his charge. During the pressure on the visitors' goal J. Harrison had a chance of scoring, but he sent the leather just outside the posts. No further point was registered up to half time, when ends were changed. The visitors swain pressed their opponents, and secured two additional points after some beautiful play. Subsequently, the Haydock team had hard lines, and claimed a goal, after a free kick in front of the Church posts. The referee, however, •decided against the claim, and disallowed the goal, on the ground that the ball had not touched a clayer after the free kick. Tke play continued exciting up to the finish, when Church had won by four goals to none. Teams: Haydock—John Taylor, goal; Thomas Hatton and Richard Whittle, backs: John Kilner, Thomas Wedgwood, and Thomas king, half backs.; James Blackey and Jobn Moran, right wing; Paul Twist and John Harrison, left wing.; Samuel Harrison. centre. Church—Thorpe, goal: J W•od and B Robinson, backs; W Wood, Gastall, and Taylor, half backs; Fielden and Smith. right wing; Berresford, centre; Gregson and Holden, left wing. NOTES BIP THE WAY.

The first round for the Lancashire Cup closed on Satur- day, the results being as follow :—Loveclough ,laeat Man- chester by five goals to none; Turton beat Lower Darwen nine to two; Padibam v. Blackburn Park-road, not played; Astley Bridge beat Halliwell two to one; Witton beat Black- burn Olympic three to none; Accrington beat Darwen two to one; R.ossendale beat Cherry Tree two to none; South Shore beat Low Moor (Clitheroe) four to two; Preston North End beath Blackburn Rovers seven to one; Beltoa Wanderers beat Wigan fourteen to nose; Bootle beat Raw- tenstall five to one; Higher Walton beat Fishwick Ram- biers four to three; Church beat Haydock four to none; Hurst scratched to Great Lever; lrwell Springs (Bacup) beat Darwen Old Wanderers four to two; Burnley Union Star v. Burnley, drawn game, two each. In the next round the representation of the different centres will be as follows: —Botten district, four; Rossendale, three; Accrington and Burnley district, three or four; Preston district, three' Blackburn, one or two; Liverpool, one. The results of the chief Association matches in England on Saturday were as follow :—ln the Birmingham Cap com- petition, West Bromwich Albion 1 goal, Aston Villa 0; Der- by County 6, Burton Waaderers 1; Burslem Port Vale 7, Market Drayton 0; Wolverhampton Wanderers 0, Birming- ham St. George's 2; Walsall Swifts 3, Great Bridge Unity 0. In the Sheffield Cup competition, Sheffield Wednesday beat Eckingtoa Works 3to 0. Stoke 2, Notts 1; Crewe Alexandra 4., Druids 1; Davenham 2, Oswestry 0; Lialliwell 5, Bursiem Port Vale 0; Notts Forest 2, Staveley 1; Everton 4, Bury 1. A new ground, which will bear comparison with any , in the district, was opened at Birkenhead with the first of I the season's matches between Manchester and Birkenhead, on Saturday. Several thousand spectators were present. The game closed with the victory of Manchester by seven points (three goals and one try) toneone. 1 Broughton met Oldham on the Broughton ground on Saturday, when the game ended in a draw, fear points each.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

At the Listowel Town Commission Court on Saturday, two young men were each fined .E 1 and costs for endeavour- ing to get a publican named James Enright. of Church- street, boycotted for giving stabling to a racehorse that at- tended at the Listowel Steeplechase. A serious affray occurred at Ballydrenan, county Water- ford, on Saturday. A farmer named Ryan and his brother, who had been boycotted, alleged that while going home from Clonmel they were attacked by a party of men. Sticks and stonei. were used, and Jas. Devereux had his sktpll fractured, while Daniel Long was beaten so seriously that little hope is entertained of bis recovery. Further particulars received at Cork with regard to the attack on Lord Cork's quarrymen near Kantark show that the object of the attack was to obtain a quantity of gun- powder, which it was supposed Fitzgerald possessed as , quarryman. The unfortunate man was shockingly beaten, I and was made to swear he would not inform the police of the I raid made on his house.

The police made an important arrest on Monday at Boher- bue, county Cork. A man, stated to be the leader of the Moonlighters of the three counties of .Clare, Cork, and Limerick, and who is identified with most of the county Limerick moonlight raids, was arrested by Sergeant Kirwan, of Botierhne. He was conveyed to Limerick city for identification. 'lwo of his gang were arrested with him.

As a police patrol from Knocknagashed was on duty on Sunday at Meenbauavan, they heard an unusual noisq at some distance from them. They immediately went towards the spot, and came across a party of men killing two bullocks. When the police were seen the whole party decamped in different directions, but one of them was ar- rested.

div.p: ' afterwards plucked up couraee and went to the rescue. He was himself wounded, and declared he had never met else- where mobs so wicked. Truncheons were of no use against them. At the same time it was useless to give the police rifles if they were not to be allowed to use them. Elsewhere in Ireland the authcrities would not have permitted mobs to have their own way as they did in Belfast.—On Monday Mr. Justice Day expressed surprise that the police permitted drnmming parties to go about the streets on the mornings of " anniversaries" directly after midnight was turned. General Montgomery Moore, military commander of the Northern District of Ireland, who witnessed much of the rioting, said the po,sitien was a very peculiar one, which would perhaps never occur again. The respectable ini.abi- tante of the Shankhill neighbourhood had turned against the police. On the night of Saturday, August 8, Belfast was like a pandemonium let loose. He thought the press in Belfast on both sides was very much to blame for what went on. He described as "very inflammatory a passage from a sermon by the Rev. Dr. Hanna, adding that the Roman Catholic clergy were very active in restraining their side, whilst the success that attended the efforts of the Protestant clergy was not so marked. Amongst the note worthy facts elicited on Monday was the statement by a military officer that be witnessed the release of a prisoner by order of a magistrate in response to the clamour of a mob.—At the sitting, on Tuesday, Captain Stokes, resident magistrate, gave evidence in support of the retention of rifles , by the constabulary, but condemned the use of buckshot, as it scattered widely and wounded innocent people. When firing was necessary he would tire ball. On e,ccasions when he saw firing it was absolutely necessary. He had found Catholics generally amenable to reason, but not Orangemen. They seem to have entered into a conspiracy to get rid of the Irish constabulary in order to have a local force they might control.—Major Keogh, resident magistrate, brought from Louth to assist the Belfast magistrates, described the disturbance as a sort of insurrectionary movement against the State authorities rather than party riots. They were due to the Home Rule proposals, and nothing like them need be feared again unless Home Rule were resolved upon.— Mr. Andrew Reed, inspector general of constabulary, gave evidence on Wednesday. He said there was no foundation for the impression that the police force was " packed " on account of religious or political epinions. Mr. Morley had nothing to do with the selection of the constabulary snit at any time to Belfast. The witness denounced as " craven " the charge that the police continued to fire on the crowds , after the necessity for their doing so had passed away, and he complained that much of the dis Tder was due to the ar- ticles and letters which appeared in the Belfast newspapers. Counsel for the Loyal Defence Association having put to the witness a question with reference to the districts whence the extra police were drawn, Mr. Justice Day told him with some warmth that there was not a tittle of truth in the stage gestion that the late Home Secretary and Mr. Reed had en- tertained the "murderous and nefarious design" which ignorant persons had been induced by malicious people to impute to them. At the Belfast inquiry, on Thursday, the Mayor of the borough (Sir E. J. Harland) was examined. He believed that the riots were largely due to the report that the coun- try police had been sent into Belfast to shoot down the Protestants and Loyalists. He himself felt that it was impossible that there could be any truth in this report, but he was sorry to say that it was not discountenanced by some sections of the press. As for the constabulary, they did their work manfully and well.—Mr. Lowther, a local justice of the peace, was afterwards examined. He spoke of the difficulty of finding who was at the head of the police in the streets, upon which Mr. Justice Day remarked," Or at the head of anything else ;" and on the witness pro- ceeding to say, in regard to the stipendiary magistrates, that nothing could be worse than a political magistrate, his Lordship added, "Except a religious magistrate, in the sense in which religion is understood in Belfast."

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

FREE CHURCH SUNDAY ScnooLs.—On Sunday sermons were preached in Victoria-place United Methodist Free Church, in aid of the Sunday schools, the preacher being the Rev. J. W. Chisholm, of Liverpool. ASSAULT AT WHISTON.—On Tuesday week, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, before Mr. W. L. Evans, Alice Rylance, of Platte Bridge, Whiston, was summoned by Elizabeth By- lance, her sister-in-law, for assaulting her on the 28th nit. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the complainant, and the Bench, tibinking the offence proved, bound the defendant over to keep the peace for three months. FRIENDLY SOCIETIES' CHURCH PARADE.—OR Sunday afternoon tkere was an assembly of friendly societies at tbr Old Park, Prescot. The procession was headed by the band of the 2nd Battalion Prince of Wales Own, and consisted of Rechabitee, Oddfellows, Foresters, Hearts of Oak, and mem- bers of other lodges in the district. The service was con- &toted by the Rev. H. A. MacNaghten, vicar, assisted by the Rev. J. Johnstone, minister of the Congregational Churcu. A collection was made on behalf of the parish nurse fund. The arrangements were admirably carried out by M. B. Lawton, Mr. H. Makin, and other gentlemen. 2xn VOLUNTEER BATTALION SOUIM LANCASHIRE REGI- MENT (Prince of %Tales' Own).—To members of this batta- lion the following prizes have been distributed by Mrs. Henry Cross, in the absence of Mrs J. C. Gamble, viz. :- Ist, Private R. Preston, £1 lOs and cup; 2nd, Private J. Leadbetter, LI 5s and meerschaum pipe; 3rd, Private T. Edwards and book; and about 20 other prizes were gained by various members of the corps. Afterwards songs were given by Mr. Baylis, Miss L. Driffield, Miss L. K. Hall and Lieutenant Hall; readings by Mr. W. Jackson, and selec- tions were played by the band, under the conductorship of Bandmaster Arkell. A PRESCOT WATCHMAKER AND HIS AFFAIR6.—At the County Court, on Wednesday, before Judge Thompson, Mr. J. P. Mearns, solicitor, made application for an administra- tion order, regarding ;he affairs of James Dickenson. 4, Rowson-street, Prescot. Applicant said he was a watch movement maker, but trade had been dreadful for the last two or three years, and there was no sign of improvement. His liabilities were £49 12s 11d, and he attributed his diffi- culties to trade depression. During the past twelve months be had averaged only 16s a week. His wife bad been ill, and he had four children. His Honour masie an order for the amount to be paid at 4s a month. Mr. Ormandy, ac-

countant, was appointed trustee. If Dickenson keeps up his payment it will take about twenty years 0 pay the whole amount. TRANSFEES.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions the following licenses were transferred :—Tke White Hart, Eccleston- street, Prescot, from Thomas Howarth, deceased, to Mary Ann Howarth, widow ; Commercial Inn, Appleton, from John Lynch, to John Robinson; beerhouse, Appleton, from Samuel Tickle to Mark Young; beerhouse, 55, Midwood- street, from John Moss to William Cogley ; beerliouse at the Holt, Whiston, from William Jones to John Varley ; beerhonse, Widnes from Hannah Siminaitys to John Camp- bell.--Mr. F. W. Hartley, solicitor, of Lancaster, again appeared before the court and applied for the temporary en- dorsement of a license to sell spirits and beer to be con- sumed off the premises, at a shop situate at 16, Waterloo- road, Widnes, from one Lone Miller to Miss Mary Hagan. The latter stated that she did not really want the license, and the license was accordingly refused.

BOARD OF duAß,Disxs.—:-the fortnightly meeting of the members of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held on Thursday, at the Workhouse, Whiston. Mr. John Lowe presided, and there were present the Rev. Thomas Cham- bers, Messrs. Joseph Jackson, W. Birchall, James Buckley, Joseph Ellison, J. W. Wareing, James Fisher, W. G. Ash- ton, C. B. Johnson, John Kenwright, W. Middleharst, Jas. Burchall, I'VTrrer, E._Syder, T. Eatock, J. Ranson, Thos.

F. Hill, H. Hulme, I'. Heald, W. Swift, J. Leatherbarrow, W. B. Longton, R. A. Graves, P. Longton, and W. Daine. The Workhouse Master (Mr. Hale) reported that there were 452 inmates this week against 465 last week and 420 in the corresponding week of last year. Vagrants relieved 65, against 57 in the corresponding week of last year. He also reported that the Rev. S. A. R. Sylvester, vicar of Roby, _ _

Mr. Berry called attention to the quality of the gas supplied' to Prescot. He said he thought it was the duty of the Baarti to see that the gas sup- plied was of such a character as not to interfere with the health of the town. How were they to know if it was of the right power unless it was analysed by the medical offi- cer P—The Clerk said he did not think it was any duty of the medical officer to analyse the gas. It is for the Local Board to take action and direct that the gas should be tes- ted.—Mr. Whitfield was of opinion that it would be a good thing to have the gas tested in order to prevent smoke and sulphur being emitted from it.—Mr. Berry gloved that the medical officer of health be instructed to analyse the gas, say not less than four times in the year, to see the amount of sulphur emitted, the amount of sulohuretted hydrogen and ammonia, and of course the illuminating power.—Mr. Whitfield seconded the reotion.—Mr. Hewitt said he did not see that the medical officer need object to do the work, and he thought the Beard had power to employ anybody they had a mind to test the gas.—The motion was carried.— Death of Mr. Hatton: Mr. Berry alluded to the death of the late Mr. Hatton. and said ho had an intimate acquain- tance with that gentleman for a period of not lees than 25 years, and he felt sure if ever there was an upright trades. man in the town it was the late Mr. William Hatton. In his death the town had lost a very able and painstaking representative. He moved "That this Board desires to ex- press its sincere sympathy with Mrs. William Hatton and family in their bereavement, and to record the loss the Board has sustained by the death of their member, Mr. William Hatton."—Mr. Dennett seconded the motion, and he was able to endorse all Mr. Berry had said.—The resolu- tion was adopted, and the Clerk promised to send a copy to the widow.—This was the only business.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The troopship Tyne, grounded when leaving Sheerne4 for Egypt on Tuesday, but was got off before midnight, and she proceeded on her voyage. The local gas company having refused to reduce their price for street lighting, the Corporation of Hythe have lighted the streets with oil as an experimeet. The English amateur cricketers have concluded their tour in America. In all they played eight matches against representative yams, and won every one of ttiem. THE GLADSTONE HOUSBHOLD.—Mr. GladStOrle'S Cold is better, though, owing to bad weather, he did not attend church on Tuesday morning. Mrs. Drew is also somewhat better.

BEACH'S RETURN TO ALSTIIALIA.—WiIIiam Beach the champion sculler, left Blackwell Pier in the tug Ajax on Thursday morning for Tilbury, where he embarked for Australia. A large crowd gave hearty cheers as the tug left Blackwall, and the band played "The Conquering Hero"

EVOLUTION AND RELIGION.—The Rey. H. Ward Beecher lecturing in London on Monday night, declared his full ac- ceptance of the doctrine of evolution. As an honest man, as a Christian man, and as a Christian preacher, he asserted that evolution was the greatest blessing, not to biology, not to physiology, not to sociology, but to religion. TERRIBLE ATTACK BY A CAT.—Mrs. John Black, of Southside, Glasgow, was attacked by a cat, on Wednesday night, terrible wounds being inflicted on the left leg and arm. Two policemen arrived, and after half an hour's ex- citing chase they killed the cat, which was affected with rabies, and which jumped several times at their heads before they could destroy it. GRAVE CHARGE AGAINST A CLERGYMAN —The Com- mission appointed by the Bishop of Carlisle to inquire into a charge against the Rev. F. Dwyer, vicar of Grayrigg,near Kendal, has presented its report. The charge is made by a servant girl, and improper conduct is alleged. The finding of the commission is to the effect that a prima fade case for further proceedings has been made enL SHOCKING RESULT OF GOSSIPING —The Newcastle Em- ben magistrates have committed James Morgan, farmer, to trial for the manslaughter of his wife, aged sixty-eight. Prisoner had quarrelled with his wife for gossiping, and she was afterwards found dead in a field with discoloura- tions on the throat. The doctors thought the woman had died from sanguineous apoplexy, produced probably by violence. TIM FIRE AT NEWTON PAPER MILT,—A. fair number of gentlemen assembled at Newton, on Thursday afternoon, when the salvage from the recent fire at the paper mill of Messrs, Gillespie and Mason was offered for sale by auction. The salvage consisted of jute—more or less damaged by fire or water—and buyers attended from Liverpool, Man- chester, dme The auctioneer was Mr. Mellor, of Oldham. Very poor p rices were realised. A (iAmEEI TYPER SHOT.—Consternation was caused in Alyth, Pertbst 'ire, on Saturday night, by the news that Mr. Wainwright, ee, slant of the mansion of Keith, near Blair- gowrie, had accielentally killed his gamekeeper. It is stated that Mr. Wainwrig ist was in the act of preparing to fire at a covey of partridges'. which suddenly rose behind him, when his gun went off and the contents lodged in the heart of his unfortunate attendant, who was standing not far off. Gil- ruth's death was instat ttaneons. He leaves a widow and a large family. A NOVEL USE OF T, 11? PARCEL POST.—On Friday, an inquest was held at Came 'en Town, London, on the body of a newly-horn female, whir it was discovered in a parcel en- trusted for delivery to the Post-office authorities. A wit- ness named Chapman said mewls things were sent through the parcel pest, a dead monk 9y being thus sent in this dis- trict a few days ago. The j' try, in returning a verdict ac- cording to the medical teatime' y adduced, stated that some person or persons unknown were chargeable with causing the child's death. A TERRIBLE EXECUTION.—At Canton, a Chinese aged 18, has undergone the "Lin. 1' Chi" execution. which is that one piece after another of the victim's body is cut away until the body is divided up it tto exactly 1,000 pieces. The victim, as in this case, always dies from loss of elood before the horror is completed. The woman here mentioned d was charged with having poisoned h, w husban and three relatives. Although it was shown t sn examination that she was innocent of the crime, the people of the dis- trict insisted on her execution, which t he Viceroy finally ordered. JOCKEYS' INCOMES.—It seems, says the "Standard," an amazing circumstance—evidence of the ext Int to which the times are out of joint—that a jockey should he assessed by ' the incornestax surveyors on an income of Li 0,000. That, however, is the figure at which it is stated t ht Frederick Archer was called upon this year to pay his t ightpenoe in the pound; and another Newmarket jockey, a man of lees ability but considerable shrewdness, is understot el to have sabmitted unrnurmuringly to a claim not much smaller in amount. It is of no advantage to the Turf, so far as its avowed object—the improvement in the breed of is - is concerned, that any jockeys should receive the in °Dine °f a Lord Chancellor or an archbishop. SEVERE PUNISHMENT AT SCHOOL. FATAL REST' 121,7, Dr. Churton held an inquest on Thursday night, at Ferry, Cheshire, on the body of Lilian Thompson, a, 'ced. three years. Evidence was given showing that, though of this tender age, the child was sent to school, and for som alleged offence she was put to stand upon a form. She fell off. alighting on her head, and sustained injuries causing concussion of the brain and death. The teacher swore that she did not place the infant on the form. The Coroner said he was determined to get at the facts, and summoned a number of the school children, who swore that the child fell off as alleged. The Coroner commented OR this barbarous conduct, and the jury' in returnine a verdict that the child's death reealted from afall, strongly condemned the Practice of punishing children in this manner. ROMANTIC ELOPE3fENT.—A romantic elopement has Net occurred in the neighbourhood of a village some twelve miles from Warwick. The young lady, who is well cennec- ted and about 30 years of age, has long been the ruling spirit of the Dissenting Sunday school in the parieh,and the happy swain, who is ten years her junior, was a member of her class. 'rho fair one left borne a few days since for an inland watering-place and was joined at the next station by the favoured one, whose occupation has latterly been that of a cowman on a local farm. For months past a belief has been current that the regard of the parties for each other was more tender than usually obtains between teacher and pupil, and the young cowman had occasionally boasted among his fellows that be intended to cross the water with a lady companion poosessed of £l,OOO. Nothing since has been heard of them. NARROW ESCAPE OF THE GREAT EASTERN.—On reach- ing Holyhead on Sunday night the Great Eastern narrowly escaped destruction. When she reached the harbour it was blowing a heavy gale from N.N.W. Orders were given to let go the anchors, hut some delay arose and the vessel was rapidly drifting on a dangerous shore. Great consternation e prevailed on board and signals were made for help. The sea was very high and the breakers dashed furiously on the rock bound coast. Just as it seemed impossible to save the vessel the ancllora were got down, and fortunately held. occupied chimney n e stack Tugs also came from shore and stood by until the big ship was taken into harbour and safely moored. All night these was considerable uneasiness on board as to whether the anchors would bold, which they fortunately did. It is stated that the vessel was only a fathom's length off the rocks when the anchors went down. HOUSES STRUCK BY LIGHTNING.—At about noon on Sun- day a heavy thunderstorm of brief duration passed over Heywood and the neighbourhood. lhe flashes of lightning were very vivid. The full force of the stermansdeceomnaesdirdaiteorlwabbealey felt at Sudden, a village between Heywood and Rochdale. It also entered the front bedroom, tearing the plaster, &c., from the wall, and going out by theevindow, smashed many panes of glass, tore the guttering off outside, and threw the outer wall out of s plumb. The electric fluid also enSered the parlour by meat ,9 of the flue, and after displacing the mantelpiece, smashi the ornaments, and throwing the fire-irons across the par- lour, made its exit by the 'window, which seems to have been open. The next house and another some little di. ,seesse away were also struck.
