div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 10, 1886.

THE CZAR is not an amiable man, and the news from, Bulgaria must make him unusually disagreeable to those who sur- round him, For it is clear that the Bulga- rians have testified at the polls that they re- pose entire confidence in their own rulers, and that they will not submit to Russian dic- tation. The elections„ have, moreover, affor- ded another proof of the self-contra of this gallant little nation. Although. Russiark agents did their utmost to provoke disturbances they failed in almost every case. At Sofia, the Ruasian Consul was conspicuous in his efforts to bring odium on the Regents by or- ganising a riot. He hired a number of peasants to break up the electoral bureau, and when they were beaten off he primed them with brandy, under the influence of which they fired their revolvers at the crowd. M. NEKLINDOFF'S explanation of "this re- grettable fact" ought to be enshrined as a curiosity in the history of diplomacy. "A Montenegrin who had taken refuge in the Consulate fired two revolver shots in the air against people who were throwing stones in the courtyard of the Consulate. I had the man arrested and locked up," A man who fires at people in the air is a. remarkable mis- creant, and certainly deserves to be locked up for such very original lunacy. M. NEKLIN- DOFF is evidently a 3 great a. IY.engler as General EXULBARS. M. DB GIEXS is pro- bably disgusted with the whole business; for the Russian Foreign Office has generally dis- played some judgment even in, its least credit- able enterprises. But the assertion that the CZAR has taken the whole coaduct of this. enterprise in Bulgaria into his own hands is, certainly borne out by the behayiour of hi 3. instruments. A gang of brigands could; I scarcely have acted worse. The CZAR has totally,misunderstood the character of the Bulgarians, and, General KArLDARS has not chosen to undeceive him. Bribes and thrsats have alike failed most ignominiously, and the men who are supposed by Russiansto have seized the reins of authority against the wishes of the people have been elected. to the: Grand Sobranje by such enormous majorities that the party of M. ZANKOFF can scarcely be. said to exist. This is the answer of Bulgaria. to fraud and intimidation. Of course Russia will declare the elections illegal, but as she has no right to do anything of the kind, this thunderbolt will be regarded by the Balga- rians with equanimity. They a:a not bound in any way to accept the CZAR'S judgment of their own affairs, and they havo brove,d to the satisfaction of Europe that they have exer- cised their undoubted rights with good sense and moderation. Even Prince BISMARCK) who has no love of "infant liberties," must be moved to admiration by the sturdy deter- mination and alert intelligence of a people who a few years ago were regarded as mere serfs, with all the vices of bondage. But Prince BISMARCK does not allow his judg- ment to be affected by any sentimental con- siderations. He would sacrifice the Bulga- rians without a qualm to any scheme on which he had set his mind, and lately it has looked as if this sac-

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: , rifice were really a part of his policy. His journals continue to explain that Russia is perfectly entitled to re-establish her influence in Bulgaria, and the conduct of General RAULBARS is viewed with comparative sere- nity at Berlin. The German CHANCELLOR has contrived so far to wring a sullen acquiescence from Austria in this attitude of indifference to Russian aggression, and it is even suggested that he would be content to . allow a military occupation of Bulgaria if Russia gave a guarantee to quit the country as soon as " order and tranqui- lity " were restored. But of the value of such a guarantee Austrian statesmen are as good judges as the CHANCELLOR, and they could not consent to this develop- ment of his cynicism without exciting an outbreak of popular wrath in Hungary which they are scarcely prepared to face. The attitude of England in this business is said to be "observant." Were Lord RAN- DOLPH CHURCHILL in Opposition we should be told that this observant attitude was due to the pusilanimity of a Liberal Government, which, as usual, was truckling to Russia. Lord RANDOLPH has used some energetic words about the Bulgarian question, but the only action on the part of the Cabinet that is yet known is Lord IDDESLEIGH'S Circular, 1 which seems to have been treated everywhere 1 with the utmost indifference. It is scarcely 1 a sign of strength that the SOLICITOR GENERAL should querulously complain of Mr. GLADSTONE for not using his voice to aid the Ministry in carrying out his own policy. But everybody knows that in befriending Bulgaria the Government will command the Support of all parties. Mr. GLADSTONE need not exert his eloquence to prove this. Ministers have public opinion at their backs, and we are all waiting to see what use they will make of this unusual advantage. Specu- lation is rife as to a possible league of Eng- land, Austria, and Italy, and there is much less reticence in the 'ltalian Press on this subject than in our own. An official organ at Rome discusses the contingency with a frank eye to Italian interests, but not with much hope that England will abandon her traditional policy of maintaining her freedom from Continental entanglements. Italy has every reason to desire that the present poli- tical equilibrium of the Mediterranean should be undisturbed by any intervention of Rus- sian power at Constantinople. "No one 1 doubts that an intimate entente between Italy and England would be useful for the attain- ment of this end, which we ought to propose to ourselves, and the knowledge of it would be received by the country with general satisfac- "" tion. Better still if to the said alliance other Mediterranean Powers were accessory; but to form an alliance contracting parties are necessary, as to marry needs a wife, and is anyone able to assure us that in London there is the same desire for this alliance as in , Rome? Concede the circumstances favour- able . . . what proofs has England thus pv far furnished of an inclination to abandon her traditional policy of liberty of action, to it. contract with us, with or without a third Continental Power, a positive alliance with distinct purposes and on deafly specified conditions ?" There is certainly no proof whatever, and most EnOishmen would be in- disposed to contract an alliance of this specific kind, with a view to so remote a con- tingency as a Russian occupation of Con- stantinople. But the gravity of the situation . is more immediate than this, and it is a • serious question whether, if Austria is really determined to resist the complete military absorption of Bulgaria by Russia, it is not ex- Ipedient for England, in conjunction with Italy, to give a very decided support to Aus- trian policy. Are we prepared to give material as well as moral aid to Austria if she should be involved in a great sauggle with tio Russia for the proctectorate of the Balkan States? There are many who say that this is really no affair of ours, that if Russia does actually go to Constantinople this will not seriously endanger British interests, and that to embark on a war which would affect our Indian possessions as well as our position in Europe, simply for the purpose of saving Bulgaria from Russian clutches, would be Quixotic. On the other hand, there is often no better means of preserving the peace than making it clearly understood that in certain clearly defined circumstances you will fight ; and a clear understanding of this kind as re- - gards the attitude of England might be a very wholesome factor in the calculations even of the CZAR. If Austria is to be not only the "sentinel on the ramparts," but the whole force of resistance to the invader, Russia may count on the benevolent neu- trality of Germany and risk everything. We very much doubt whether the apathy of the , Powers with regard to the indefensible tyranny of the Russian action in Bulgaria now is calcnlated to make the CZAR believe that he will be opposed by any league what- ever if he determines to recover Bulgaria 1 at one stroke by employing overwhelming force. -..

• THE collection of Consular reports in the " Times " will not be pleasant reading to many an Englishman. The general conclu- sion to be drawn from these documents is that British trade is in many cases passing into the hands of foreigners. In some cases the cause is want of enterprise. Mr. MERLIN says of the trade on the Levant that we are losing it, "because we have no commercial travellers, no organisation for ascertaining the credit of our customers, no enterprise, and we expect people to buy what we sell, not what they want, in our way, not in their own." In i Rio Grande, n Brazil, much the same reason is assigned for a loss which is measured by the fact that British exporting houses there Lave been reduced from six to two, and im- porting houses from four to two. The Ger- mans, who oust us, belong to a better class, socially and commercially, than our own mer- chants, and we have no commercial travellers. In the province of Sao Paulo, Mr. COWPER declares that where the productions of foreign industries compete successfully with, or are superseding, those of Great Britain, the fault is that of the British manufacturers them- selves, who are often too conservative in style and design, and obstinately ignore the tastes, wishes;, and requirements of the consuming markets, whereas German, French, and Aus- trian competitors, with a keener eye to busi- ness and more mobile in disposition, spare no pains to adapt and supply goods in accord-, ance with the wants and peculiarities of each country." Mr. YEATS BROWN, at Genoa, declares that the trade of Northern Italy is going away from this country. "In metals," he says, "we are being beaten out by the Germans, in machinery by the Swiss and Italian industries; in hardware and Birming- ham goods the United States have recently come to the front with a rush. In woollens Germany is underselling ; s u ; -rt cotton, the home industries in cured fish, the French." ; "The ptevailing impression here," says Mr. BROWN, "is that our people are too grand for

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: the present times of grand competition." In Reunion the story is precisely the same. " Formerly," says the Consul, "the British ttader had only to open his mouth for plums to drop into it. There is no disguising that now this happy state of things is at an end, and that it behoves us to look about and see how other nations are competing with us. I find that shopkeepers in these days of com- petition will not go in search of goods. Sam- ples must be brought to their own doors for them to select and give their orders, the same as in England." LA ROCHELLE gives a simi- lar report. "I have never," says the Vice- Consul, "seen a traveller going round for English makers of these materials." Mr. CRAWFORD, the Consul at Oporto, says that "English manufacturers rely on long tradi- tions of success, and often disregard the fact that to hold their own they must exhibit the same qualities as did those who built up Eng- lish trade." The loss of trade in Japan, where the fall runs into millions, is one of the most serious of all. The Consul at Yokohama re- ports that the principal import of nail-rods is from Belgium, where the makers "pay more attention to the smaller sizes usually taken by this market." These reports all go to show that England mu t look to her laurels in the matter of trade. It is a question mainly of knowledge and aptitude. Our Continental competitors have for the most part been late in the field, but they are making headway through their superior education and readi- ness to adapt themselves to the ever-changing conditions of the countries with which they are on a commercial footing. It is not a question of tariffs or of Fair Trade ; it is one rather of enterprise and intelligence. If we would keep to the front, we must—looking to the future—make elementary education free, and establish a technical school in every large town in the kingdom. Knowledge is power—in commerce as in everything else.

THE Mormons have come to London, have seen, and have not conquered. They do not appear to have excited much enthusiasm among the reporters or the audience, and the description of their appearance, and the speeches to which they treated their hearers in St. George's Hall, recall in many particu- lars ARTEMUS WARD'S immortal interview with that departed saint, BRIGHAM YOUNG. The star of the Mormonite troupe seems to have been Elder SLOAN. After Elder KITSON —who is described as a "thin, wiry person of solemn demeanour, with high forehead and clean-shaven face " had proclaimed the failure of Christianity, and Elder SHIPP had disappointed his audience by refusing to "go into full details " on polygamy, Elder SLOAN rose and volunteered to let the audience "have it." This naturally roused in the audience an ambition to -let Elder SLOAN " have it," and a very lively interchange of retorts went on between the Mormon apostle and the unsanctified portion of his hearers. Mr. SLOAN undertook to vindicate polygamy as the saving force in society, but he had to admit that the saving force had begun by using up all the females in Utah, and leaving a large number of men without wives at all, and a small number with too many. From Mr. SLOAN'S expressed satisfaction with this arrangement we are inclined to suspect that the distribu- tion of matrimonial plums in the Mormon Pudding has been favourable to him, and that he belongs to the second class rather than to the first. Mr. SLOAN'S success as a dialecti- cian was less conspicuous than ls capacity for low joking. His answers to the ques- tions indeed suggested to the reporter a com- parison with the corner man at the Christy Minstrels: "To a gentleman who elicited the information that a marriage contracted accor- ding to English law was not recognised by the Mormons, and who urged that there- fore in Utah he would not be con- sidered as married to his wife, Mr. SLOAN merely replied, Ido not know that you are married to your wife,' thereby (says the re- port) raising a laugh.' " After a few more quips of this kind, Elder SLOAN subsided and gave place to an " elderly lady of tearful aspect," whose appearance gave extra point to her remark that there were many happy homes in Utah. This naturally pro- voked inquiries of a personal kind, the audience being clearly of opinion that if there were such "happy homes ", the teirfut lady could not possibly have belonged to one of them. However, sh declined to state whether she was a member of what the re- porter euphuistically describes as a " poly- gamic household." This seems to have brought the performance to an end, and the i general impression was that it was a very I poor performance.

• SOME few weeks ago, we laid before our readers a copy of the Circular which Mr. Thomas Morris, as Chairman of the Com- mittee, had forwarded to a number of his fel- low-townsmen, and to subscribers to the Warrington Library. The object of the Cir- cular was to elicit opinion on the questicn of making the lending department of the library free to the public, and to ascertain how far present subscribers to the Library would be likely to continue their subscrip- tions under altered conditions. It is satis- factory to find that the large majority of those who have sent replies are wholly- in favour of making the lending library free. Indeed, fully two-thirds of thos-e who have written may be classed as supporters of the move- ment, and one gentleman gives proof of his earnestness by sending two guineas towards the expenses of till Committee. Existing subscribers WIIG nave written are pretty general in their intimation that they would be willing to continue their subscriptions if the Library were freed, and some go so far as to say they would, if need be, increase the , amount. Amongst the few who are opposed to any change, several of them state that, in any case,they will continue their subscriptions. It would seem, therefore, that if the Library and Museum Committee of the Warrington Corporation were to take the matter up with spirit and earnestness, they would find that many of the old subscribers would be with them, and that new subscribers could be obtained to take the place of those • who might fall off. Its curious to note that the majority of those who express their disap- proval of the project are lady subscribers to the Library. One of them remarks, by way of objection that "people place little value on that which costs them nothing." With- out disputing the truth of this observation, it may be remarked that it is scarcely perti- nent to the case. Suppose the books in the Library were lent out free to-morrow, could it be said that the ratepayers were having them for nothing? Certainly not ; the bulk of the money for the maintenance of the Library—more than three-fourths of the total—is already being provided by the ratepayers by the penny in the pound which is yearly levied for that purpose. In other towns where a library rate is laid, and where books thus purchased by public money
THE EXAMTNEPk, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 16, 1886.

I are lent out, they are lent to the public, in accordance with the Free Library Acts, free of charge. We question whether there is another Library in the kingdom, at work under the Free Libraries Act, which makes a charge for books lent out ; and it is there- fore high time that the Lending Depart- ment of the Warrington Library was brought .into line with other similar institutions and t made free to the public.

NEW POOR'S RATE FOR BOLD.—The Widnes magistrates on Thursday signed a poor's rate for the township of Bold, at one shilling in the pound, estimated to produce £794. UNITED METHODIST FREE Cietracx, RUNCORN.—The an- niversary was celebrated on eruncley, whea the resident pastor, the Rev. E. Hall, preached two sermons. The choir, under the leadership of Mr. J. Holford, sung special hymns, dee. LOCAL HoNorns.—Mr. W. H. Faulkner, now serving under the Liverpool School Board, and late pupil teacher of the West Bank Board Schools, Widnes, has obtained the 21st place on a list of 1.250 candidates for admission into training colleges. Mr. T. S. Lawley, of the Warrington-road Board Schools, was placed 69th. DEATH OF AN OLD DITTON RESIDENT.—By the demise of Mrs. William Roberts, of Brookfield, which sad event took place on Tuesday. the village of Ditton has lost another of its old inhabitants. Mrs. Roberts, who was 80 years of age, had for 16 years been a resident of Ditton. The deceased lady was the wife of Mr. William Roberts, a trustee of St. I Michael's Church, and formerly a churchwarden. Mr. Roberts has also attained a ripe old age, but, notwithstand- ing this, is a regular attendant at church. LAUNCH OF A LIGHTSHIP AT RUNCuRN.—A new lightship built to the order of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, from the designs of Mr. John S. Davies, was launched from the yard of Messrs. Brundrit and Co., Runcorn, on Wednes- day. The dimensions of the vessel are—Length 70ft.. breadth lift., depth 7ft. gin., and it is of great massiveness and strength. The work has Leen carried out under the direction of Lieut. M. A. Sweeney, marine superintendent to the Board, and Mr. E. C. Wheeler, Lloyd's surveyor, and has given great satisfaction. The vessel was christened " The Mars," by Master John Brundrit. It is to be stationed in the Upper Mersey, near Otterspool. Rutecoure DOGS AT LYTHAM.—At the Ridgway Club (Lytham) Coursing Meeting this week, Mr. J. Brundrit, of Runcorn, had several dogs competing. In the North Lan- cashire Stakes, Mr. Brundrit's Bullien beat Sir T. Brockle- banks's Benfold in the first round, but in the next succumbed to Mr. M. Fletcher's Feather. Mr. Brundrit2s Bletchley was knocked out the first round by Mr. Fawcett's Fauld'e I Farm. In the South Lancashire Stakes Mr. Brundrit had Bessie Lane, Bessie Muir. and Bessie Clifton (late Clifton Revile) entered, Only the latter, however, got through the first round, vanquishing Mr. E. Webb's Winnington H. In the second course she was defeated by Mr. S. Swinburne's Serab. L.I.INITARY PROPERTY AT WlDNES.—Before Messrs. John Brock and George Pilkington, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Edwin Ward, estate agent, Lacey-street, was summoned by the Widnes Lecal Board for permitting a agent, tnz to remain unabated on preperty of which he was street.—Mr. J. T. Allen, clerk to the I Board, prosecuted, and called Dr. Cooper and Mr. Dickson, who proved tt-at the property, six houses in Cromwell- street, was in a most insanitary conaition, and dangerous to health. The serving of the customary notices was also proved.—Tne defendant, who slid he commenced the work w:th all the despatch he could, was ordered to pay costs, 15s, and abate the nuisance. SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. S. ORME, AT RUNCORN.—Mr. Samuel Orme, manager of the copper works of Messrs Denis and Co, Widnes, who lived in Waterloo-road, Runcorn, died under very sudden and painful circuristances on Saturday night. For several months Mr. Orme had suffered from a disease which seriously impaired his constitution, and he bad been attended by Dr. Mangan. There was, however, no cause for apprehension. On Saturday afternoon Mr. Orme, who was a vice-president of the Football Club, and an enthusiastic admirer of the winter game, wit- nessed an exciting match between Runcorn and Rochdale. He was then in his customary health. About half-past eight in the evening, however, he was walking hurriedly up High-street, when he suddenly fell on to the pavement, and was picked up in an insensible condition and carried into the shop of Mr. Slater, butcher. Dr. McDougall arrived on the scene a few minutes' later, and pronounced life to be extinct, probably through failure of the heart's action. The facts were reported to the coroner, who, after a statement from Dr. Mangan, decided that an inquest was unnecessary. The deceased gentleman: who was 50 years of age, was highly respected in the town, and his demise was the cause et widespread regret. The Football Club has lost one of its most ardent and generous supporters, and the members of the club intend to-day, in the match against Liverpool Old Boys, to wear black bands out of regard to his memory. Mr. Orme held the highly honourable position of W.M. to the Macclesfield Lodge of Freemasons, and amongst the brethren of the craft both there and at Runcorn he was very popular and much respected. The funeral took place on Thursday at Macclesfie'd. The body was conveyed from the late residence of the deceased by the hearse of Mr. S. Yarwood. The ceremony took place in the presence of a large number of spectators, and the body was followed to the grave by many relatives and friends, together with the represen'itives of various institutions with which during his lifetime the deceased was connected. Mr. S. Taylor, of Rencorn, took part in the sad ceremonial. The body was borne to the grave by four members of the Runcorn Foot- ball Club—Messrs. H. Hughes (captain), W. Wright, W. Hughes, and J. Dunbavand. The secretary of the club, Mr. J. E. Langshaw, Mr. A. Riley, Mr. W. Riley, and Mr. Peter Riley were also present. Numeroas wreaths were sent as tributes of respect to the memory of the deceased. The wreath sent by the workmen at the copper works of which the deceased, prior to his death, was the manager, and the one sent by the members of the Football Club, were triumphs of floral skill. Handsome wreaths were also sent by the members of the Ellesmere Lodge of Freemasons, Mr. George Moss, Mr. A. Riley, Miss Taylor, Mr. Musgrove, and others. All these wreaths were supplied by Mrs. Stoll, High-street. The coffin was literally covered witb floral wreaths, and the proceedings were of the most impressive character. PENKETH WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.—On. Wednesday evening the members of this assooiation met in the Elementary School- room, when the evening was devoted to impromptu speaking, the chair being occupied by Mr. C. E. Parker. The subjects were drawn as follows : Hydropathy, Mr. B. Hobson; Is Matter Eternal, Mr. A. J. White; Is the Voluntary or Board School System best, J. Thompson; What do you think of Home Rule, Mr. J. Mainley ; Love, Mr. G. Randall; Bachelors versus Benedicts, Mr. Davidson; Leather, Mr. Po'snitt ; Dreams, Mr. C. E. Parker. The various subjects were well spoken about, and the evening was agreeably spent. There was a good number of members present. MYSTERIOUS DEATH AT PENKETH.-011 Tuesday afternoon, at the Fiddler's Ferry Inn, before Mr. Husband, deputy coroner, an inquest was held as to the death of a person named Joseph Smethurst, carver and gilder. The deceased's body was found floating down the river, and was got out by the crew of the steamer Prixey near to the Fiddler's Ferry Inn, and was taken there. There was found upon the body a lot of gilders' tips, cushion, pencils, and a letter, through which the police were able to trace his friends. It seems his sister, Miss Smethurst, is a school teacher at Wimslow, and she was present to identify the body. No clue could be got as to how deceased met with his death, and the jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned." The deceased was buried on Wednesday afternoon, at the , cenv3tery, Great Sankey, when there was a good number of his relatives present. The funeral requi- sites were supplied by Mr. E. Connor, Warrington, and Mr. James Hayes had the arrangements entirely entrusted to his hands.

_ NEW COMPANIES.—The following items appear in the "Investors' 0 dardian " of last Saturday : Whiteeross Company, Limited: This company proposes to take over the business of wire and iron manu- facturers and colliery proprietors, carried on by the Whitecross Wire and Iron Company, Limited, at Warrington, and at Peasley Cross and Sutton, near St. Helens, Lancashire. It was registered on the 6th inst., with a capital of £350,000 in £lOO shares. The subscribers are:—R. W. Murray, Belfast, 1 share; W. B. Ritchie, Belfast, manufacturer, 1 share; C. M. The number of directors is not to be less than five, nor more than seven; the company in general meeting will determine remuneration.—Fleetwood Salt Company, _Limited: This company proposes to acquire and work brine, mines of salt, rock-salt and other minerals, brine shafts and springs, in Great Britain or elsewhere. It was registered on the 4th inst., with a capital of £50,000 in £lO shares. The subscribers are Wethered, Clifton, Bristol, col- liery proprietor, 50 shares; C. Thomas, Soap Works, Bristol, 50 shares: 11. Rawcliffe, Chorley, Lanca- shire, brewer, 50 shares: Mt. Cochrane, M.E., Gos- forth, Northumberland, 50 shares; F. 11. Gossage, Soap Works, Widnes, 50 shares; T. S. Timmis, Soap Works, Widnes, 50 shares; A. W. Chalmers, 5, Fenwick-street, Liverpool, chartered accountant, 50 shares. The number of directors is not to be less than three; qualification, 25 shares.

21 candidates in the field little doubt cart be entertained that a contest of a somewhat excited nature will take place. ST. PAUL'S HARVEST FESTIVAL, WIDNES.— file collec- tions made at the harvest thanks?:iving services amounted to £32, which wi'l be added to the fund for the erection of

a parochial room. A RUNCORN FLAT SUNK.-011 S It:arc-I,w the flat Martin, of Runcorn. came into collision with the steamer Reginald, of Waterford, at the entrance to the Mersey, and the former sank outside the Rip Rap Buoy. The crew were saved. The steamer was not damaged. TRAP ACCIDENT AT WESTON, NEAR RUNCORN.-0(1 Fri- day, as Mr. George Bell, engineer to the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, was driving to the Weston works, the horse fell and the occupants of the trap were thrown into the road. Mr. Bell's shoetder was badly injured. FAILURE. AT WIDNES.—At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, on Monday, a petition was .filed by Henry Shell:Art, tailor and draper, 57, Mersey-road, Widnes, and a receiyine order was granted.by Mr. Registrar Bellringer, the 25th Last being fixed for the public examination. NARROW ESCAPE OF A SAILOR AT RCINCORN.—A sailor named Peacock, employed on board the schooner Eyelina, was walking along the locks on Saturday, when he fell into the Welsh-row basin. He was rescued by two boatmen, and was attended by Dr. Mangan, who found him in a very ex- hausted condition. MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN, RUNCORN The Rev. T. Patrick, M.A., chaplain to the Mersey Missions to Seamen, preached at the Runcorn Perish Church. on Sunday morn- ing, in aid of the funds of the mission. The sum of LG 103 was collected. In the evening Mr. Patrick occupied the pulpit at Halton Parish Church in furtherance of the same object. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORE.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mr. G. H. Denby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted the following persons for not sen- ding their children regularly to school :—Wieliain Hough- tore venis Malone, Pat Lawlor, John Bell, John Clegg (two cases), Peter Riley, A. Armstrong, John Hooligan, Edward Ryan, Charles McKenna, and Thomas Lalley. The usual penalty was imposed in each case. ST. MARY'S R.C. CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The anniversary services in connection with St. Mary's Roman Catholic Chapel, were held on Sunday. In the morning there was solemn high mass, when the Rev. Father Brennan was the celebrant, and the Rev. Father Dubberley, S.J., was the preacher. In the evening a sermon was preached by the Rev. Father Gerald Tarleton, S.J., and the rosary recited. At each service there was a large congregation. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT HALTON WESLEYAN CHAPEL.— Harvest thanksgiving services were held at this chapel on Sunday. The edifice had been tastefully decorated by mem- bers of the congregation. Large quantities of fruit, flowers, and vegetables had been presented. Two sermons were preached by the Rev. R. F. Hornabrook, and appropriate anthems were sung by the choir. The fruit and vegetables were distributed amongst the sick and poor of the village on Wednesday. RUNCORN Y.M.C.A. HISTORICAL CLASS.—The first meet- ing of the present session was held on Monday night, in the reading-roem of the Y.M.C.A. The Rev. Thomas Bell, curate of Holy Trinity Church, delivered a lecture on the "Ancient Codices of the Bible," to a good audience. The lecture, which gave evidence of wide research and thought- ful preparation, was an exhaustive description of the ancient manuscripts of the Bible. The Rev. George Wood, Wes- leyan minister, presided. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.— The anniversary of the school was celebrated op Sunday, when special sermons were preached in the chapel by the Rev. Wm. Evans, M.A., of Pembroke Dock, formerly of Runcorn. In the afternoon a'children's service was presided over by Mr. James Pritchard, and the Rey. William Evans gave an address. On Monday evening the Rev. John Jones occupied the pulpit. The amount collected at the various services amounted to £l7. FLORAL SERVICE AT WIDNES.—A. juvenile Templars' floral service was held in Malin's Temperance Hall, Widnes, on Sunday afternoon. Specially selected music was sung, and Mr. Thomas Reay delivered an address. In the even- ing Mr. Morris Jones preached a sermon to a good congre- gation. Collections were made in behalf of the Temperance Hall building fund. On Monday evening a harvest supper, consisting of roast beef, plum pudding, dec., was partaken of by a fair number, and subsequently an entertainment was given. CAMDEN WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN.—There was a large attendance on Friday even- ing last at the above class, Mr. H. Randle presiding. A very interesting and instructive lecture was delivered by Captain John Le Couteur, subject :—" Reminiscences of two voyages to Serie and Palestine." The lecture was lis- tened to with close attention thronghoet, and at the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, on the motion of Mr. S. C. Beckett, seconded by Mr. C. Norman, and supported by Mr. Kitto. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The usual forteightly meeting of this body was held on Tuesday after- noon at the Board-room, Dutton Workhouse. The chair was occupied by Lieut.-Col. Ashton, and there were also Present the Revs. J. J. Lockwood and J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Mclntyre, Percival, Lewis, Aaron, Brandreth, Far- rell, Hewitt, Hadfield, Parr, Smith, Wallington, Mounfield, and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—The Local Government Board wrote acknowledging receipt of a letter having refer- ence to Appleton Drainage, and stating that the subject was receiving the attention of the Board. The Local Govern- ment Board also acknowledged the receipt of a letter having reference to the proposed regulations for milkhouses.—Mr. Farrington, sanitary inspector, read his report. He referred to the pollution of a well at Bartington, and was instructed to communicate with the Inspector of the Northwich Union on the matter, it being alleged that the nuisance came from land in the district of that Authority. He was also instruc- ted to communicate with the Daresbury Highway Board as to the road drainage in that vicinity. Mr. Farrington also reported a nuisance at Appleton, which had, however, been removed.—This was all the business. RUNCORN BOARD ON GUARDIANS.—On Tuesday after- noon the ordinary fortnightly meeting of this body was held in the Board-room at Dutton Workhouse. Lieut -Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present the Revs. J. J. Lockwood, J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Aaron, Levis, Weir, Mclntyre, Wallington, Farrell, Hadfield, Brandreth, Parr, Baguley, Campkin Hewitt, Lowe, Percival, Taylor, Smith, Hamilton, Mounfield, and W. H. Linaker (depnty clerk).— The Committee appointed to consider the amount of super- annuation to be allowed Mr. and Mrs. Jones, late master and matron of the workhouse, recommended that, considering the efficient services of Mr. Jones, and his present state of health, five years be added to the number he had passed in the Board's service, making the term 34 years, and that £7l 83 be allowed him annually. It was also resolved to recom- mend that £4B 16e 4d be the amount of the superannuation of Mrs. Jones.—The Chairman, moved that the report be adopted. He stated that it was not until after a long dis- cussion that the Committee arrived at the sum fixed upon, which was at last unanimously agreed to. The Board had the privilege of adding a certain number of years to a per- son's service, when the work had in their opinion been well done, as in the case of Mr. Jones, and the Committee had resolved to recommend that five years be added to his 29 years' ssrvice. In the case of Mrs. Jones no additional years had been included. He was glad that the Committee came to a unanimous conclusion upon the subject, and he hoped the Board would adopt the report in a similar man- ner.—Mr. Weir, vice-chairman, seconded the motion, which was adopted.—The Rev. J. Lockwood proposed the adoption of the quarterly accounts of the Finance Committee, which, summarised, were as fellows :—Contracts £451 14s 2d, sala- ries £2513 15e 61. petty cash £7 19s 61—Mr. Mclntyre se- conded the proposition, which was carried.—The Board then proceeded to relief business. A WIDNES TRUSTEE CASE.—At the St. Helens Cennty Court, on Wednesday, Judge Thompson had before him an interpleader Case, in which John Lecomber, watchmaker, 139, Mersey-road, Widnes. and Ellen, his wife, claimed as joint trustees under a deed of settlement to recover certain property seized by the South Lancashire Loan, Discount, and Investment Company, Limited, Liverpool. the judg- ment creditors in respect of a debt owing by the said John Lecomber. Mr. Sparrow, barrister, Liverpool, represented the judgment creditors ; and Mr. Copeman, Liverpool, appeared for the claimants.—John and Ellen Lecomber, it appeared, were trustees under a deed of settlement of pro- perty amounting to £4OO, made by Mrs Ellen Crowther, of Liverpool, ha trust for Ellen Maria Lecomber and Alice Maud Lecomber, their children. The property claimed con- sisted of several clocks, which had been seized amongst other things, and which were in the hands of the high bailiff of the County Court.—Mr. Sparrow proceeded to ask the plaintiff, John Lecomber (who had been in business in Reservoir-street and Kirkdale-road, Liverpool), questions as to his arrangement with his creditors on several occasions. Mr. Copeman said the only question was whether one par- ticular upright regulator clock in the possession of the high bailiff was the one duly assigned to Lecomber and his wife. There was malice at the bottom of Mr. Sparrow's questions, and they were merely to annoy and disgrace Mr. Lecomber. Mr. Sparrow said his allegation was that the whole thing was a swindle from beginning to end, that the clock never was Mrs Crowther's (plaintiff's mother-in-law), but that all along, and by sham documents, he had been enabled to de- feat his creditors.—Mr. Copeman said that in each instance, although he had been unfortunate in business, he had ultimately paid 203 in the pound.—ln further cross-examin- ntion. Lecomber admitted that he had exchanged with a Mr. Wood, of Liverpool, the clock mentioned in Mrs Crow- tiler's deed for another one. He had also sold and ex- changed other goods at his discretion.—His Honour asked Mr. Copeman if Ve thought after that admission he could support the claim.—Mr. Copeman thought he could, inas- much as the will stated a at if property was sold the money must b 3 invested in the funds.—Mr. Sparrow said he ap• prehended that Lecomber bad committed a breach of trust by changing the clock.—His Honour gave a verdict for the judgment creditors.—Mr. Copeman asked for leave to appeal on the question of the right of a trustee to exchange. His Honour declined to consent, and said he would not help plaintiff in any way.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.

The triennial election of eleven members to the Widnes School Board will take place on Satur- day, the 23rd of this month. The list of no- minations was made public on Thursday, and is as fol- lows :—George Henry Bolton, Penketh, alkali manufacturer; George Bond, Farnworth, clerk in holy orders; Rd. Brad- shaw, Appleton, schoolmaster; John Brock, Farnworth, chemical manufacturer ; James Clark, Widnes, clerk in holy orders; Rd. Holden Davis, Liverpool, chemical manufactu- rer; Henry Wade Deacon, Appleton, alkali manufacturer ; Thomas Finegan, Appleton, clerk in holy orders; Roger Fogg, Appleton, cashier; Francis Heyes, Appleton, wire ' drawer; John Birchwood Imison, Bold, pawnbroker; Ed- ward Martley, Widnes, estate agent; Ales. div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Cemetery Office on Wednesday. Mr. W. Mellor presided, and there were present Mes,rs. W. Littler, W. H. Rogerson, E. Imison, W. Whittaker, H. Coleburn, R. Morris, and W. F. &Ikeld (secretary).

div.head: STATISTICS.
div.p: STATISTICS.

The Secretary reported that the interments for the six months ending September 25th were 157 ' • corresponding period last year year 168, decrease 11. The fees received during the same period amounted to £l5B 12s 6,1 last year £l7O 3s, decrese £ll lOs 6d. The Finance Committee re- ported that the cash account for the month ending 25th September showed that there had been received in fees £3B 103 63, and certificates £2 10s, total £4l Os 6d. After pay- ing wages, &c., £3l 12s 6d was paid into bank. Accounts amounting to £3 14s 5d were passed for payment.

div.head: CLERGY AND THEIR FEES.
div.p: THE CLERGY AND THEIR FEES.

The Secretary presented the following letters :—" Trinity Vicarage, Runcorn, September 13th, 1886. My dear Mr. Salkeld,—Now that Canon Barclay is deceased, .1 shall be entitled to officiate at such burials as may be required for persons who have lived in Trinity Parish, and to receive such fees for such services. My parish begins at the Royal Hotel, High-street, and terminates at Occleston's Tannery. I will be obliged if you will kindly arrange that information may be given to me of all funerals coming from my district and instruct your clerk that for the future my services will be required for the burying of those who have belonged to Trinity Parish. I remain, truly yours, W. Preston."—The Rw. J. Lockwood. vicar of Halton, wrote as follows, under date October 13th. 1886 : " Gentlemen, I read the " order for the burial of the dead " on Saiurday last in the consecrated portion of the Runcorn Cemetery, over the remains of the late Mr. George Hatton, one of my parishioners; and owing to altered circumstances by the death of the late vicar of Runcorn I beg respectfully to ask your Board for the fees which were paid by the relatives for the officiating minis- ter."—The Secretary stated that he had occasion as warder of Trinity Church to see the Bishop of Chester at the time Mr. Adams was the incumbent of that church. The war- dens were desirous of having the christening fees and the marriage fees that were paid for services rendered at Trinity Church, in order to increase the incum'rent's salary., The Bishop stated that the fees would belong to Canon Bar- clay as long as he lived, afterwards when there was an avoidance the fees would have to go to their various dis- tricts—the district of Trinity, of Halton, and of Runcorn. Mr. Salkeld added that he had paid the fees for the quarter ending September 25th to the family of the late Canon Barclay, with an intimation that the fees for the last month would perhaps belong to the next vicar. He had received a polite letter from Miss Barclay, to the effect that she bed handed over the last month's fees to Churchwarden Mr. Lake. On the 25th September he forwarded to Mr. Preston his portion of the fees, and last week he gave 6s, treble fees for Halton, to the gardener for Mr. Lockwood, if he;asked for them. Mr. Lockwood, however, did not take the fees, but said he understood there would ne an alteration, and would leave it to the Burial Board to determine what was right. He (the secretary) took it that each vicar would now be entitled to the fees of his own parish. He should be glad of informa- tion with regard to the fees for headstones and graves. Since the death of Canon Barclay a head stone had been erected on Church ground, and Mr Preston claimed that the fee would belong to him, instead of the repre- sentatives to the next vicar. He (Mr. Salkeld) paid that fee to Mr. Preston. He should be glad if the Board would de- cide what should be done with these fees.—The Chairman said Mr. Salkeld had not done anything amiss, but it would have been as well if the whole of the fees had been re- tained until a proper decision had been arrived at. There was a further question besides those propounded by Mr. Salkeld, and it was who would receive the fees in the case of a Dissenting minister officiating at a burial in consecrated ground? It was a question with which they ought to pro- ceed cautiously. Where was the law upon the question ? Mr. Coleburn said Dissenting ministers were provided for by Act of Parliament.—Mr. unison asked if there was a solicitor to the Board ?—Mr. Salkeld: No.—Mr. Imison Then are we always dependent upon amateur opinion ? Mr. Salkeld replied that he had been sent to consult with Mr. Marsh, of Warrington.—Mr. Coleburn suggested that the subject should stand over until the new vicar came. There would be one appointed in a month or six weeks.— The Chairman informed the Board that the reason all fees had to be paid to Canon Barclay was to compensate him for the closing of the church yard. This was for the canon's life only, and now a different state of things would exist entirely. Mr. Imison : We ought to have an authoritative opinion upon the subject. We are not competent to settle it.—Mr. Rogerson bad no doubt that each clergyman was now en- titled to his tees for marriages and funerals.—Mr. Handley pointed out that the Board were not bound to receive fees. Let the clergymen fight it out amongst themselves.—Mr. Salkeld said he had simply collected the fees as a conve- nience to the late Canon Barclay, and at his special re- quest.—lt was decided to refer the subject to a future meet- ing.

div.head: OFFICE HOTIRS.
div.p: OFFICE HOTIRS.

Mr. Littler stated that there was impression abroad that no money could be paid at the office of the Board after 12 o'clock noon. It was pointed out that the office hours were from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., and that money could be paid any time during that period. If Mr. Salkeld was not pre- sent, fees could be paid to Mr. Ford, the gardener.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD. An extraordinary meeting of the ?Vidnes School Board was held on Thursday, under the presidency of Mr. T. S. Timmis, J.P. There were also present the Rev. Father Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Bradshaw, Deacon, Robinson, and Danby (clerk). The chief business was the passing of the financial statement for the half-year ended the 29th September last. The receipts amounted to £5,061 15s, which sum included a balance of £667 5s 8d brought from March last, £3,600 from the rating authorities, and £777 13a 51 school fees. The total expenditure was £4,757 13s 10i. The chief items were—Salaries of teachers £2,352 Cis Bd, salaries of officers of the Board £314 lie Bd, books, apparatus, stationery £268 8s id, furniture and repairs to buildings £493 13 sd, contributions towards industrial schools £5l 188 id, repayment of princi- and interest of loans £l,OOl 12s 7d. The outstanding liabilities of the Board are—Loans from Public Works Commissioners £32,462 14s, other liabilities £376 88 81— Dr. O'Keeffe moved the adoption of the statement, and remarked that everything was very satisfactory. He was much pleased at the excellent way in which the books of the Board were kept. In his opinion it would be impossible to find better kept books and a more excellent statement of accounts submitted by any public Board of any kind throughout the United Kingdom.—The Chairman seconded the motion, and said it must be very gratifying to the Board to hear the remarks of the chairman of the Finance Com- mittee. Referring to the item of £3,600 received from the rating authorities, the Chairman pointed out that in the previous half-year nothing was received from that source.— The accounts were passed.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOLARS AT THE INTERNATIONAL
div.p: WIDNES SCHOLARS AT THE INTERNATIONAL
EXHIBITION.

By the generosity of Mr. G. H. Bolton, of the Wines Alkali Works, about 1,400 scholars from Widnes and dis- trict were enabled to visit the International Exhibition at Liverpool on Saturday. The schools were represented as follows :—Widnes Church Schools 100, Farnworth Church Schools 100, Widnes Board Schoels 400, Penketh and San- key Schools 400, Fae'er Clark..'s Schools (Widnes) 200, and Father Finegan's Schools (Appleton) 100. In addition to these there were 50 from Hough Green National School. The children were conveyed to their destination in two trains, one leaving S tnkey Bridges at nine o'clock, and the other leaving Farnworth at 8-55, both calling at Widnes. Accompanying the scholars were the R 3V. George Bond, Vicar of Farnworth; the Rev. Mr. Jackson, vicar of Great Sankey; with Mr. Ferguson, Mr. David Forster, and the masters, mistresses, and teachers of the various schools. Owing to the faulty arrangements of the railway company the trains ware very late in arriving at the Exhibition Sta- tion, and a project to photograph the young excursionists in a group was abandoned. After having gone down the to- , bogganning slide, the youngsters were distributed in tens under competent guides, and with wander saw the sights of the huge show. At noon each child was regaled with a large Melton Mowbray pie, a bun, and a large cup of coffee or milk, and at seven o'clock in the evening they were similarly treated. Mr. David Forster took a prominent part in ministering to the children's enjoyment. He treated them with sweets, and paid for their admission to the Indian village. Mr. Ferguson, who represented Mr. Bolton, was also indefatig- able in his efforts to promote the enjoyment of the large crowd of boys and girls, and thoroughly succeeded. Upon the arrival of the trains back at Widnes, three hearty cheers were given for Mr. Bolton for his munificent gene- rosity.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Messrs. John Brock and George Pilkington. BELLING BEER WITHOUT A LICENSE.— Jesse Yersley, a beerhouse keeper at Farnworth, was charged with ulawf tally selling intoxicating liquors without a license. The defend- ant pleaded guilty. Mr. Thomas Angel, acting supervisor, appeared on behalf of the Excise. He stated that on the , 18th March the •defendant received a temporary t ransfer from the Bench, but he had neglected to apply for the license from the Excise authorities. The defendant stated that he bad acted in iomorance, being under the impression that he was covered by the magistrates' authority. The Bench imposed a fine of 20s and 12s costs. ASSAULT ON A BLATMAN. A fiatman named William Griffiths was charged with assaulting William Summerfield, also a flatman. The defendant pleaded guilty. The com- plainant said that on the Bth October the defendant, who was in drink, came on board his fiat. He told him that he did not want to have any conversation with him, whereupon

the defendant knocked him down. The defendant was fined 10s. and 7s 6d costs. A RUFFIANLY POLE.—A Pole named John Tharaswitch living at 21, Water-street, was charged with assaulting Wm. Lowchitii, also a Pole, living at 56, Crounwell•street. The evidence of the complainant and his witnessea was inter- preted by Joseph GidZambi.—lt appeared that several Poles were together in their lodging-house, when the defendant became quarrelsome and attempted to strike the tomplain- ' ant with a knife. He warded off the blow, Lnd the blade entered his thumb—lnspector Wood said there were two previous convictions against the defendant. The man was a very unruly character, and he had had many complaints about him —The Bench imposed a fine of 40s and 12s costs, in default a month's imprisonment. ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A BOY.—A summons had been issued against Thomas Harrison, caretaker of the Mailns Temperance Hall, for assaulting a boy named Johnson P. Morewood, living with his mother in Widnes-road.—Mr. Knowles appeared on behalf the complainant, and Mr. Peters on behalf of the defendant.—Mr. Peters applied for the case to be adjourned, and the Bench considered the request a reasonable one, and adjourned the case.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at Alforde Chambers, on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Crossage, J.P.. presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. E. Carey, D. Wright, B. Brown, W. W. Gcssag., J. Mid wood, R. Cook, F. Heves, J. Taylor, J. Houghton, S. Sadler, J. T. Allen (clerk), W. lig.' ginson (surveyor), and I. Carr.

THE AUDIT. Mr. John Hazlehnrst, the district auditor, reported that he iv-Al completed the audit of the accounts of the Board for the year ended at Lady Day last. He observed during the prozres9 of the audit certain charges in respect of re- freshments supplied to members of the Board when engaged in discharging extraordinary duties within the district of the Local Board. For these charges he was aware of no authority in law, but before taking extreme measures with regard thereto, he had thought it right to notify that simi- lar cbazges would not be allowed from thia date. He had

made a report on their accounts to the Local Government Board, with regard to which they would doubtless be corn. mLnicf 'ed with in due course. He was strongly of opinion that a system whereby an efficient check upon the gas alid
water stores could be obtained was urgently required, and he would sukgest to them the desirability of referring the reatte7 to a smill comntittee. and their clerk to report upon.
—Dr. O'Kecffe remarked that he thought the auditor should pay for Js refreshments when he was in Widnes, then.—On the suggestion of the chairman the letter was referred to the
Gas and Water Committee.

THE MEDICAL OFF!CER AND NUISANCE INSPECTOR. The Chairman referred to the discussion which took place at the last meeting regarding an application for the Local Government Board to pay half the salaries of tbee3 officers, and argued that the Local Government Beard could exercise no more power than they did under the present _ . _ .

arrangement. At present if the Local Board did not do what the Local Government Board considered necessary they would ser3 down a man to make an inquiry, and Make them do it.—lt was deckled that the clerk should give in-
formation to the Local Government Board with respect to the applicltion for half the salaries of the medical officer
and nuisance inspector.
THE WASTE HEAPS AGAIN. The Clerk read a petition, handed in that afternoon by Mr. T. J. Peters, solicitor, of the owners of houses and land in

and around Violet-street and Victoria-road,Widnes. It stated that the Cheshire Lines Railway Committee are now, and have been for some time, depositing chemical waste so as to form a large embankment or siding adjoining their pas-

senger station at Widnes. The petitioners complain that the gases given off by the waste used in forming the em- bankment were injurious to health, and that the embank- ment was so near their respective properties as to be offen- sive by reason of the ill-odour, and also that paint and metals on their properities were injured by the formation of black metallic sulphides by combination 'with the hydro- gen sulphide, which is the principal gas given off. The effect had been very seriously to depreciate the property in the immediate neighbourhood. The petitioners stated that the deposit constitutes a serious public nuisance, for the redress ot which there were several remedies of a civil and criminal nature in the High Court of Justice and also in the Courts of Summary Jurisdiction. The petitioners pray that the Board would be pleased without delay to take steps to put in force sueh of these remedies as might be hest calcu- lated to remove and arrest the nuisance mentioned. The petition was signed by Messrs. Thomas Sadler, T. S. Swale, R. F. Baker, R. Booth, J. Kiddie, E. Kiddie, J. Matthews, J. H. Lee, C. J. Bennett, Ellwood, Smith, and Co., Richard Tibbutt, Edward Martlev, and David Davies.—ln reply to Mr. Brown, Mr. Carey stated that the waste could be laid without creating a nuisance.—Mr. Heyes : It is very seldom laid without making a nuisance.—The Health Committee were deputed to deal with the subject.
. _ GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.-A WIDNES FIRM TO BE PROSECUTED. _

The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee contained this minute :—" Gas furnaces. Letter, 18th September, from Bowden and Walker, re alleged infringement of patent. The Clerk reported result of interview, and instructions were given to agree to an injunction being obtained and to pay the costs, say about £6." The Engineer reported tha. at the recent exhibition of gas stoves a considerable amount of business was done and the cookery lectures were well attended. The mean rainfall for the month had been 3 587 inches. The illuminating power of the gas during the month bad averaged 1701 candles. It was recommended that the Widnes Foundry Company be prosecuted for illegal use of water. —ln moving the adoption of the minutes, Mr. S. Sadler said he disagreed with the suggestion to prosecute the Widnes Foundry Co., because he thought there wane leading features in the case that had not received the consideration they deserved.—Mr. W. W. Gossage seconded the motion.—Dr. O'Keeffe asked if the committee were unanimous in the matter, and Mr. Sadler replied in the negative.—ln reply to Mr. Midweod, who sought for further information on the infringement of a gas furnace patent, Mr. Sadler said the committee had agreed to pay costs to prevent further litigation, because they did not think it would be to the interest of tire Board and the gas companies of the United Kingdom fo contest the matter. There were also things in connection with the affair it would not be wise to make public, but Mr. Midwood could be privately supplied with all information if he desired.—Mr. Brown explained, with reference to the alleged illegal use of water by the Widnes Foundry Company. that the firm owned several cottages in Paul-street, and, prior to painting them, they wanted some plastering work doing. The firm engaged a man to do it, and the mortar required was sent from the works. The mortar was made from water that had passed through the works meter. The plasterer, however, used some of the Board's water from one of the houses to soften the mortar. Tots was done entirely without his (Mr. Brown's) knowledge or the knowledge of any member of the firm. By careful in- quiry they found that there had been used three halfpenny- worth of the Board's water. Whatever might be the action of the Board he wished it to be understood that the firm were morally perfectly innocent of any intention to rob the Board of any water. The man had even eight or ten yards away a tap from which he could have taken water from the meter.—Dr. O'Keeffe moved, and Mr. Houghton seconded a motion that the recommendation be withdrawn.—Mr. Carey said he felt great, sympathy for Mr. Brown. He was perfectly certain that neither Mr. Brown nor any of his fzienes were morally responsible for the taking of the water, and that they had not the r'ightest intention to de- fraud the Board. He, however, thought it would have a misch:evous effect if it was felt outside, that, although the offence was very trivial, and, in fact, no offence at all in a moral point of view, that the law was not to be carried out as strictly with regard to a member of the Board as any- body else. In his opinion, it would be a capital thirg for the neighbenrhood if Mr. Brown would take the thing good naturedly and good humouredly. In the interests of Mr. Brown and the public, it wes desirable that this recom- mendation should be carried out.—Mr. Sadler pointed out that there had been cases where the blame had been placed on the shoulders of the workmen.— Mr. Wright contended that the cases were not similar. He remarked that two months ago Mr. Gaskell stated that pro- secutions would be instituted without regard to persons or respectability, ant. he considered it would be a misfortune if this recommendation was withdrawn. He therefore could not support the motion.—Mr. Brown said he did not wish any favour to be shown by the Board—(hear, hear) or any member of the committee, but there had not been a prose- cation undertaken on such trivial grounds. He asked Dr. O'Keeffe to withdraw his proposition and allow the prose- cution to go on.—Dr. O'Keeff a : Very well, I do so. —The minutes were then passed in their entirety.

___ HEALTH COMMITTEE.—BUTTERINE OR BUTTER. The rninut s of this committee contained the report of the medical officer for September. There had been 86 births and 77 deaths, representing rates respectively of 37.52 and and 336 per 1,000. There were 33 deaths amongst children under one year, and 17 between one and fire years. Diarr- bcea caused 25 deaths, and whooping cough one. The medical officer complained of the following nuisances : 1 Sewage flowing on the highway near the Horns, Farn- worth ; pigs in the back yard, 38, Market-street; overflowing ashpits at Victoria-street, and near the river; hack yards and closet walls broken down at Nos. 60 tl 68, Cromwell- steeet ; back yards floodtd at Nos. 1 and 11, Violet-street ; ashpits at four houses in Gladstone-street; stagnant water near to Kaludah Terrace, Widnes-road, and Lugsdale-road. Nuisance from glycerine works : Complaints had been made to the committee of nuisances from the glycerine works,and from J. Hutchinson and Co.'s works. Instructions were given to take legal proceedings ha all cases where the notices had not been attended to, and against Messrs. N. Mathieson and Company, and J. Hutchinson and Co., unless nuisances were abated.—ln m ving the adoption of the minutes, Dr. O'Keeffe drew the attention of the II yard to the glaring manner in which several shopkeepeis were selling butterine as butter. This matter was brought before the Board some years ago by the then chairman of the Health Committee, and steps were talv,n at that time to have the evil suppressed. However, the sales were going en as much as ever, and he would call the attention of the medical officer and inspector of nui- sances to the sullect.—Mr. Heyes seconded the motion.— Mr. Carey said he took Dr. O'Keeffe to mean not that the Board objected to the sale of a wholesome article of food. Butterine was a wholesome article of food and very often might be better than bad or rancid batter. All they asked was that butterine should be sold as such and not as butter. —Dr. O'Keeffe : That is it exixtly.—The minutes were carried. The

, appointed to investigate the ..pail system for the die- posal of the sewage adopted at Warrington and Rochdale. The systems in operation were Oescitied and it was stated that thq cost per head at each place WAS about 25 per bead of the population. chid cost WAS the re- moval of the excrement, but at Warrington it was expected that with intercepting depots they were providing the cost would be reduced to something like 7d per head. The pre- sent cost in W'idnes was about 5d per bead. It was neces- sary, however, for the pail system to b.! at all events par- tially adopted in Widnes, as the Local Government Board had refased to sanction any byelaws unless such provision was made. At Warrington Aidermin Burgess and Mr. Longdin, the surveyor, and at Rochdale Councillor Cheet- haul and Mr. Platt, surveyor, showed the deputation every kindness and courtesy, and gave them every information.— A joint Highway anti Health Cemmittee had considered the report and recommended that clauses giving the option to property owners to provide for the pail system be inserted in the byelaws —Carried.
SANITARY CONDITION OF THE TOWN.
The LocA Uovernment Board wrote asking what steps :he Boaki h4d t aken with a view to the improvement of

the sanitary condition of the district. It was directed that the following reply should be sent by the clerk :—" I am directed to acknowledge yours of the 23rd September in- quiring what steps have been taken, or are proposed to be taken, with the view to the improvement of the sanitary condition of the district as regards the several matters re- ferred to by Dr. Page, and to inform you that my Board have been for a very cehsiderable time previous to Dr. Page's visit endeavouring to grarple with all the nuisances to which Dr. Page refers, and for the bctter enabling them to do so new bye-laws are being prepared, and will shortly be submitted to your Board for approval. It is expected th.t when these new bye-laws come into operation the subjects named in the recommenda- tions Nos. 1,2, 3,4, 9, and 10 will be much more easily dealt with. As regards recommendation No. 5 plans for the extension of the main sewer, and for new sewers are now being prepared, and as in the case of the main sewer lately constructed, ample provision will be made for ventilation. In respect to recommendation No. 6, the manufacturers have been requested to abate the emission of black smoke as far as poisible. Recommendations 7 and 8 relate to common lodging houses, and to slaughter houses, and are provided I for in the new hve-laws. Without, however, waiting for the completion of the bye•law, special instructions have been given to the officials to report all nuisances so that prompt action might be taken. Yry Board are, and always have been fully alive to the importance of the poin to which re- ference is made in Dr. Page's memorandum of advice, and you may rest assured no time will be lost in carrying into effect the various recommendations made by Dr. Page, as far as it is practical to do so."

div.head: LIBRARY.
div.p: THE LIBRARY.

The General Purposes Committee recommended that a committee of 10 should be appointed to manage the Library. The following were suggested to act with the members of the Board :—Messrs. R. H. Davies, H. IV. Deacon, Richard Lewis, J. Morrison, and S. Robinson—Mr. Carey, in moving the adoption of this recommendation, remarked that the Library would be soon completed, and the Board ought to make arrangements to have it open as early as possible—lt was decided that the Library Committee should consist of 11 gentlemen, including those mentioned, and the following members of the Board :—Messrs. E. Carey, Dr. Olieeffe, S. Sadler, B. Brown, W. W. Gossage, and F. Heyes.—There was no other business of public interest.
WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART SCHOOL. LECTURE ON PHOTOGRAPHY.

The annual distribution of prizes to the successful stu dents of this 'school took place on Tuesday night in the Baths Assembly Room, Widnes. The room was crowded to its utmost capacity. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., occupied the chair, and he was accompanied on the platform by Mr. E. Carey and Mr. J. Morrison (hon. sec.) The Chairman having expressed his pleasure at being present at that an- nual gathering, called upon Mr. Morrison, who read the twelfth annual report as follows :—" The committee have pleasure in reporting that the classes have been well attended during the past session. 41 students were under instruction in art and 130 in science. The results of thet Government examinations are as follows :
Examined. Passed. Per Cent: Art
Machine construetiou and drawing 19 10 Building construction and drawing 5 3 Inorganic: chemistry (theoretical) 41 25
Inorganic chemistry.(.piactical) 3U

The results of the examinations in science subjects, while better than last year, are far below our general aver- age and the percentage of passes in practical chemistry is very unsatisfactory, only 43 per cent passing as compared with 53 per cent in 1885, 77 per cent in 1884, and 88 per cent in 1883. The unusu- ally high results in the first years of the establish- ment of the practical chemistry class were no doubt due to the fact that the students had previously gone through a complete course of theoretical chemistry. Ibe students of the past session were much younger and more inexperienced than formerly, and most of them were taking theoretical as well as practical chemistry for the first time. Of the few who had previously gone through a coarse in theory, 79 per cent. passed in practical chemistry, but of the great majority who had no previous knowledge in theory, only 24 per cent. passed in the practical class. It is evident from these figures that it is unwise to admit students to the practical data before they have gained any experience in theoretical chemistry, and that the committee have decided that, for the future, no student can take any stage in prac- tical chemistry, unless, at the time of joining the class, he holds a certificate in theoretical chemistry. Students join- ing the elementary stage of practical chemistry must hold at least a second class certificate in the elementary stage of theoretical chemistry. Students joining the elementary stage of practical chemistry must hold at least a first-class certificate in the elementary stage of practical chemistry. The success in the art class is very satisfactory, the percent- age of passes is the highest since the class was formed in 1875, and is considerably in advance of the average of that of the United Kingdom. It is to be hoped that this success will stimulate art students to persevere in their studies, and the committee promise en their part they will render every facility to enable students to procure knowledge in the higher grades of art. The Library, which was opened to the public on Saturday evenings, has been very well attended, on some occasions the room being inconveniently crewded. The committee in their first report eleven years age, and fre- quently since that date, recommended the adoptien of the Public Libraries' Act. The ratepayers have at last risen to the occasion, and at a public meeting held in the Volunteer Hall, on December 29th, presided over by Mr. Ceossage, the necessary authority was given. The Local Board are now erecting a suitable building for a •free public library and reading-room, and as soon as it is ready the committee of the Science and Art School will hand over to the proper authority the greater portion of the books in their possession. As regards finance, the majority of the manufacturers have, notwithstanding the great de- pression in tiade, subscribed with their usual liberality, and the committee have been enabled to maintain the efficiency of the school. The Government inrpector, Major Hill, RE, visited the school in February last, and expressed entire satisfaction with the arrangements made by the committee for conducting the classes." The report frequently elicited applause. Mr. Morrison added that only eight students had entered for theoretical chemistry, and if no more put in an appearance next week, the committee would be obliged to dispense with this class. The distribution of prizes to the students was then made by Mr. Gossage in a genial manner. —Mr. V. C. Driffield, of Appleton, whom the chairman in- troduced as an amateur photographer, now delivered a most instructive and entertaining lecture on "Photo- graphy." The lecturer evinced an exhaustive and prac- tical acquaintance with his subject, and in very lucid style he traced the history of the art from the earliest period step by step. He explained the methods and apparatus now used in producing views of landscapes and portraits of indivi- duals. showing that in all cases the impressions were ob- tained through the influence of light in inducing changes in chemical compounds. The popular part of the lecture was the numerous views thrown upon the large screen by means of a limelight by which the lecturer's observations were illustrated. A great proportion of them were of local interest, and fine examples of Mr. Driffield's skill. Great interest was exhibited in those taken by the instantaneous process. A beautiful picture was that of an express train dashing under the bridge at Farnwerth Central Station. A number of street scenes in Widnes and neighbourhood, taken by a little instrument of Mr. Driffield's own c mstruc- tion, were provocative of much amusement. Alluding to instantaneous photography. Mr. Driffield slid those persons who so frequently spoke of exposures of one thou- sandth part of a second would, if they looked into the mat- ter, find that as a general rule the shortest exposure of the sensitive plate was one•fiftieth part of a socond. He de- scribed an instrument he had invented for measur.ing the time of the exposure accurately, and his explanation was much applauded. He also mentioned at length an invention by Dr. Hunter for measuring the power of the I,ght for photographic purposes, and said it bad made photography possible in regions as yet unexplored by the camera. The statement was received with loud applause. In Ole presence of a delighted audience, Mr. Driffield produced from a nega- tive about four inches by three, a portrait of the chairman, about 14 inches by 12, and he was warmly appl,uderl. It is to be hoped that on some occasion in the near future Mr. Driffield will repeat the lecture to a Widnes audience.

While a train was running from Longhope to Grangecourt, a distance of three miles, the wife of a non-commissioned officer stationed in Dublin gave birth to a child. There were with her in the compartment—a third-class--one or two females and a young girl. Dr. Heane happened to be at Grangecourt çstation at the time, and he proceeded with the woman to, Gloucester, where her parents reside. PRINTING OF EVERY DESCRIPTION, executed by John S. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Mos')Ay.—Before Alderman Davies (in the chair), Council- lor Francomb, and Councillor Greening. DwrmaßtNG THE POLICH.—DAnieI Kenny and Thomas Flannery were charged with creating a breach of the peace by fighting in Bewsey-street on Saturday night. They were each fined 78 6d and costs, or seven days' imprisonment in default of payment. Tunrr.—William Smith, a lad, was charged on remand with stealing a black worsted coat, value 101, the property of his father, who lives at 21, Bestock-street. and also with stealing a pair of boots, value ss, the property of James O'Brien. He was sent to prison for two months with hard labenr. &Harm Otrr.—Ellis Johnson, who was charged with sleeping in an unnoccupied house:in Glazebrook-St., without having visible means of subsistence, was discharged with a caution. HIGHWAY ROBBSIIY.—Joseph Connor was remanded to the Lancashire County Police on a charge of being con- cerned in a highway robbery at Golborne. Prison was ap- prehended by P.C. littonagitan through a description that had been given to the poffce. DRUMM/MEM—The following persons were fined for this offence :—Edward Griffin. in Horsemarket-street, 5s and costs; Michael Daley, in Old-road, 5s and costs; Mary Tay- lor, in Vernon's-yard, 51 and costs; John Rooney, in Bridge street, ss, including costs. James Carley, Bridget Higgins, and John Maloney were each sent to prism for fourteen

days. CRC/SINE TO • 'Bus Hons.—John Dumbell was charged with ill-treating a horse on the 29th ult., and Richard Col- lier, who did not appear, was charged with causing the horse to be ill-treated. Inspector Aplin kR.S.P.C.A.) saw Dumbell driving a 'bus in Sankey-street, the horse was very lame and was suffering great pain. The defeadanta were each fined lOs and costa. OVBROROWDING.—John Platt, Wharf-street, was sum- moned for creating a nuisance by having his premises over- crowded. The case was adjourned for a fortnight to give defendant an opportunity to obtain a larger house. TUESDAY—Before Ccuncillor Francomb and Alderman Webster. A STartox LOAFRIL—William Shields was charged with being found on the premises et the London and North- Western Railway Company, at Bank Quay Station, it being suspected that he was there with intent to commit a felony. Chief Constable Hunt said that prisoner was one ef a num- ber of lads who gave a great deal of trouble by loafing about Bank Quay Station. Detective Harvey said that he ordered the lad away, and he thereupon became abusive. The magi- strates discharged prisoner with a caution. WEDNRSDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairelough and Alderman Chandley. DRUNICENNESS.—Annie Daley and Margaret O'Brien were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street on the evening previous. From evidence given by P.C. Wil- liams, it appeared that prisoners had behaved in a most disgraceful manner. They were each sent to prison for fourteen days. FRAUDULENT Etrasalannir. George Baker pleaded guilty to fraudulently enlisting in the 3rd Liverpool Regi- ment, by declaring that he had never been in Her Majesty's service before. He was afterwards found to have served in another regiment. Prisoner was sent to gaol for six weeks. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley, Dr. Gornall, and Mr. R. Garnett. A BEERROUSE SQUABBLE.—A young man. named Alfred Stokes, was summoned for assaulting William Corker, land- lord of the Star Inn, Longford-street, and further with assaulting Thomas Derbyshire, a waiter at the same place. Mr. H. J. Longton appeared for Corker, and Mr. A. Browne defended Stokes. It appeared that on Sunday last defend- ant visited the beerhouse, and owing to a quarrel which ensued, the defendant was turned out. During the structgle the defendant struck the landlord and the waiter. Defend- ant was fined 5s and costs for assaulting the landlord; the other case was dismissed. BEGGING.—John Cain, a middle-aged man, was charged with begging in Elizabeth-street, on the previous day. Chief Constable Hunt said the prisoner was an "Incorrigible beg- gar," and was a terror to the neighbourhood of Lovely-lane. He asked for a remand of the prisoner until Saturday, which was granted. WOMEN'S QUARREL.—Margaret Clement was summoned for assaulting Mary Ann Goodchild on the 2nd inst., and a cross-summons was issued by Clement against Goodchild for using threats towards her at the same time.—Both cases were

dimissed. ASSAULTS —David Jones, employed by Mr Wm. Heaton, contractor. was summoned for assaulting Robert Lewis, I another employer' on Saturday last. The men had some , words, and complainant alleged that defendant struck him, ' knocking him to the floor. The defendant then struck him again. He was bound over to keep the peace for six months. —James Sherrard was summoned for assaulting James Wilke on Sunday last, and was ordered to pay the costs.— James Warburton, a young man, was charged with assault- ing a girl named Letitia Hunt, four years old, in a closet, and was committed to prison for two months.—Thomas Oates was summoned for assaulting Bridget McDonough on the 13th inst. Case dismissed.—Mary Ann Leicester was summoned for assaulting her sister, Margaret Draper' on the 4th inst., and was bound over to keep the peace for six months. WILFUL DAMAGE.—Elizabeth Patchet was summoned for damaging the door of a house to the amount of 2s 6d, the property of William Woods, on the 9th Octeber.—She was ordered to pay the damage.

LYMM PE FLY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. P. Stubs and Mr. C. Lister. DRUNKENNESS. Thomas Baskerville, labourer, High Leigh, for being drunk and disorderly at Lymm on the 19th tilt., was fined 2s 6J and costs.—Thomas Worrell, fustian cutter, Lymm, was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly on the 19th nit. BRE&CH OF nut PFACE.—William Clark, brick-setter, was hound over to keep the peace for six months on a charge of making a disturbance by fighting 011 the 19th ultimo.

CART Wrrnour NAM-E.—William Callen, hawker, Hol- lins Green, was charged with using a cart without having his name painted upon it, on the 22nd ult. He was dis- missed on promising to have his name painted on his cart. _

OBSTRUCTION.—WiIIiam Broadbent, Alderley Edge, fur- niture remover, was summoned for obstructing the highway at Lymm by allawine a furniture van to remain there for four days. He was fined 5s and costs. ASSAULT ON AN OLD WOMAN.—Emma Newton was sum- moned by Mary Faulkner, an elderly widow, for assaulting her on the sth inst.—Complainant said that a boy of the defendant's had left a water tap open, and she reproved him. Thereupon Mrs. Newton came up, seized her. by the hair, dragged her to the floor, and then, whilst kneeling upon her, thumped her round the neck and on the head.—Defen- dant said that the proceedingf, had been taken through spit!. —She was allowed to go on her husband entering into his own recognisances of DB for her good behaviour for six months. He had also to pay lie costs. SCHOOL ATTENDANCH.--Thomas Lee was summoned for neglecting to obey an order of the magistrates that be should send his child to school.—He was fined ss, includit.g costs.
