DREN'EENNESS.—WiIIizm Loftus, a young man, was sum- moned for being drunk and disorderly on the licensed pre- mises of Mr. Forster, the Ram's Head Hotel, on the 2nd Inst. Police-constables Lloyd and Hunt stated they were called to put out the defendant. The defendant denied their statements, but the Bench inflicted a fine of 5s and costs.—Michael McLoughlin was charged with being drunk and disorderly on the 3rd inst., and was fined Sc and costs. —William Travis, for drunkenness in High-street, Gol- borne, on the 4th inst., was fined Sc and costs.—Thomas Travis, summoned for being drunk and disorderly in Queen. street, Golborne, on the 2nd iest., was fined Sc and costs.— Thomas Bates was also fined Si and costa for being drunk and disorderly in High-street, Golborne, on the Ist inst.—A like penalty was Imposed on Jonathan Pelling, Ashton, for being drunk and disorderly in Ctipslev-lane, Haydock, on the 21st September.—John Kilialea, and Patrick Carey, summoned for being drunk and disorderly in Penny-lane, Haydock, on the 26th alt., were each fined 50 and costs.— George IfVeywell, Haydock. was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Clipaley-lane, Haydock, on the 22nd Ult. BREiCH OF TEE TEAM—Richard Steel, of Golborne, was summoned for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in High-street, Golborne, on the let inst. The Bench said there was a doubt in the case, and it would be dismissed.— Patrick Duffy and Thomas McLoughlin were charged with a similar offence committed in Legh-street, Golborne, and were bound over to keep the peace for six months.—William Hibbert, Golborne, was also similarly dealt with. CHIMNEY FIRING.—John Ward was summoned on the

Ryan, John Sharratt of Ecclestoo), James Renny, Thomas Malloy, Phillip Sullivan (Sutton), and William Tinsley (Liverpool). BREACH OF THE Pnecn.—For this offence the following persons were ordered to be bound over to keep the peace:— Michael Dinnan, Joseph Dinnan, and Andrew Carr (Sutton), Ann Martin, Mary RutchforJ, and James Jackson (Ec- cleston). Scrtoor, ATTENDANCH—The following persons were eatla , fined ss, including coots, for neglecting to send their chil- dren to school :—Joseph Watkin and Henry Sephton (Windle). TRESTASS.—Jeremiah Rear, an aged man living in Ec- cleston was summoned for trespassing in pursuit of game in ,Sherdley Park, belonging Mr. Wtlliatn Longton, on the 2ad , inst. QUARRELS.—Richard Harvey was summoned for assanit- 'lag John Smith; and Elizabeth Hull, Ann Molynaux, and Emma Harvey were summoned for assaulting Ellen Smith. The parties live in Eccleston. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messes R. Houghton and 'r. J. Gillespie, an elderly man, named Matthew Littler, who was a principal party in a series of cases at the last Petty Sessions, arising out of a domestic squabble, under circumstances reported a fortnight ago, was again summoned by his wife, Harriet, to show cause why he bad not contributed to an order of the magistrates directing him to pay a weekly sum towards the support of his wife. Complainant produced an order of judicial separation between her and her hpsband, dated the 4th April, 1883, and under which the husband was ordered to pay 12s 61 per week to- wards his wife's maintenance. She said her husband had I never paid her a penny under the order, and the arrears, consequeetly, now amounted to the sum of £lO5 12s 6d.— In reply to questions by the magistrates' clerk, complainant said her husband had been previously committed to prison for three months for failieg to contribute to her support. He was a collier in good work, and getting good money. He WSLB "swaggering about," not long ago, that he was getting £2 per week.—The Magistrates' Clerk: Have you given her anything P—Defendant: I have never given her anything, and I never shall.—The Clerk: You would rather go to pri- son ?.—Defendant: 06, no, I shall not go to prison in this case. (Laughter.)—The defendant afterwards stated that after the separation order, he and his wife "made it up" between themselves, and they agreed to live together for a time. He left good work to live with her at Haydock, but when he came to her she refused to live with him, and she said she had not room for him at her house, and he had bet- ter go and get lodgings somewhere else.—The C:erk pointed out that the complainant had taken out a summons fo? the whole of the arrears, including those for which the defend- ant had been in prison. Tne summons would have to be dismissed, and the complainant must make out a calculation as to the amount of the arrears since defendant was in pri- son* The Bench promised to give the complainant a free summons, as suggested by the Clerk, in consideration of her , being a poor woman.

At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton and T. J. Gillespie, James Henry Far- mer, landlord of the Houghton toms, Houghton-street, Earlestown, and John Plumpton, a labourer, living at Earleetown, were summoned for commitaing a breach of the peace by being disorderly on the 2ad inst.—Defendants pleaded not guilty.—Police Constable Hunt stated that about half-past six oa the previous Saturday night he, in company with Police-constable Hughes, was at the bottom of Houghton-street. They heard a great disturbance, the sound coming from the direction of defendant Forster's beer- house. On arriving near to the beerhouse they saw a crowd of people, numbering over 100, and including, men, women, and children. Amongst the numlier were the two defend- ants. Plumpten was cursing and swearing, and Forster shouting and creating a great disturbance. Witness Broke to Forster about his conduct, and Forster told him to mind his own business. He (the officer) had aseertained that Forster had got up a "sweep" at quoits, and a dispute kad arisen as to which quoit was nearest to the peg. The defen- dant Forster was the referee, and that appeared to have caused the dispute. The defendant told the memto take no notice of him (P.C. Hunt), but to go oa quoit pitching. The defendants and other men went inside the house and he followed. In the first room they found a crowd playing dominoes, in the back kitchen they had what is called a French bagatelle and a "puff and 4art." They had every room occupied. They had had many complaints about the beerhouse ever since the license was granted, and they had had a great deal of trouble with it.—ln reply to the defen- dant Forster, witness said the land was formed for a public street —The Clerk (Mr. Nicholson) : Have you a claim to this land ?—Mr. Forster: Yes.—The Clerk said the claim had better be stated then.—The defendant Forster then said the parties had been quoiting for two or three hours, and the officers had gone by singly whilst it was go- ing on. They came together about half-past six and then interfered. He (defendant) was trying to do all he could for everything to go off quietly, and there was only a little disturbance about one of the quoits. He had an indenture in his possession from a gentleman sitting on the Bench (Mr. Houghton) and a letter written by that gentleman to show that the place where they were quailing was not a street, and it was not public land. It was private land, bought and paid for by the lessee. On the lease it was stated to be for an intended street.—The Clerk said if it was marked out for an intended street it might be dedicated to the public at any time. Certainly it was not the place to play queits upon.—The Chairman said the Bench had care- fully considered the case, and they wished the defendant Forster to remember that his license might be stopped next year if he carried on in that way. There had been several complaints with respect to the house which had not been noticed by the police, and while they would dismiss that case they advised the defendants to be more careful in fu- ture.—The Clerk : Whether this is an open street or not, if you allow people to come there and play quoits to the annovance.of the public, the magistrates may refuse to re- new your license next year. That will be worse for you than if you are fined to-day.

BRUTAL CONDUCT TOWARDS A WIFE.—At St. Helens, on Friday week, before Mr. Sinclair and Mr. Walmsley, an elderly man named John Earlam was summoned by his wife, Ellen Earlam, for assaulting her.—Mr. Mearns, who appeared for complainant, said this was a case scarcely beard of in respectable matrimonial circles. The parties, who lived in College-street, were married thirty-four years ago, and for the last thirty years they had lived in a state of continual strife on account of defendant's bad behaviour. On five occasions he had been up before for assaulting her, twice for aggravated assaults, for which he was committed to three months' imprisonment. On Saturday last Mrs. Earlam. who keeps a shop, was serving several customers, when defendant interfered and zefused to allow them to be served. Four or five customers were sent away and their money returned. Mrs. Earlam was sending some goods to one of them by the servant, when defendant put his back to the door. Complainant remonstrated, upon which he seized her by the hair, forced her against a flour sack, and with an iron scoop struck her repeatedly on the head and shoulders, injuring her severely. She asked the magistrates to impose a small line and grant her a separation order, as she could not live with him any longer. He got drunk be- fore breakfast, then went to bed, and afterwards got drunk again. He robbed her of all the money he could get and illtreated her.—Mrs. Earlam corroborated this statement, and in reply to Mr. Sinclair said she was afraid of her life. He was so treacherous she never knew when she was safe He had not been sober for two years.—Defendant admitted having committed the assault.—Mr. Mearns said com- plainant did not ask for alimony.—The magistrates im- posed a fine of Zl. and costs, and granted a separation order.

WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE UNION. MEETING AT WARRINGTON. In connection with the Warrington Temperance Union. an Alliance meeting was hold in the Public Hall on Weinesday evening. The chair was taken by Dr. Gornall, J.P., and there were also on the plat- form the Rev. Prebendary Grier (of Rugeley), Rev. J. Yonge, Rev. R. Pitcher, Rev. S. Wilkinson, Rev. G. E. Cutting, Rev. J. H. Joneo, Rev. R W. Samuel, Rev. Father Cullen, Mr. P. Hardy (Manchester); Councillors Greening, J.P., J. Pierpoino, and J. H. Fleming; Major Wateret-n (Edinburgh) ; Messrs. R. Garnett, J.P., H. Thornton, E. Twise, J. Summers- gill, C. 11. Pigott, E. Ford, R. Tate, T.Dale, J.Shaw Green, J. Bayley, J. P. Jones, J. Muiline' D. Hough- ton, P. Clare, J. Swift, J. Skelland, G. Weaver, W. Wright, T. Mayhall, H. Mills, J. Gandy, F. Jen- kins, J. L. Swailes, A. Cook, A. H. Dunn, J. E. Richardson, T. Garnett, W. Beswice, W. Nicholson. J. Hallison, J. Hodgins, J. Bromley, W. Isaacs, T. Evans, T. Ashley, J. Owen, C. George, G. Bagley, T. Crampton, &c. There was a large attendance. Mr. HARDT mentioned that be had received letters of apology for non-attendance from the Rev. Father Thompson, Latchford, Alderman J. Crosfield, J.P., and Mr. John Fair- clough. J.P. The Ceternetex, who was received with applause, said he considered it a great honour to preside over that meeting. What he lacked in fitness for that honourable position would be more than compensated for by the character, eloquence, and sincerity of the speakers whom he should have the privilege to introduce to them. The various phases of the tempe-ance question would be spoken of by their friends, and he should not occupy much of their time. That, he went on to eay, was not an essen- tially teetotal platform. The great purpose they had in view, the reduction of the number of houses licensed for the sale of intoxicants, and the promotion of temperance amongst the people, was worthy of the support of every right-mindsd citizen. (Hear, hear.) They were aware that magistrates were invested with despotic power in the re- newing of licenses to houses for the sale of intoxicants. That system dated from the time of Henry the Sixth, but who could eoubt that if public-houses had been recognised in Sasen times the regulation of them would hare been ves- ted in the township, the hundred of the county, and local option would have been established. They asked for the same power as the landowner possesses who owns a whole parish, for he may suppress the sale of liquor by simply refusing to allow a public-house to be built, thereby assur- ing the same control over the liberties of the inhabitants which is claimed for the majority of ratepayer.). They claimed that the control of all new licensee and the renewal of existing licenses should be dependent on the will of the inhabitants of the district for which such licenses were granted, and they appealed to all classes, and especially the masses, to give them the power to strike at the root ot the evil, and to regulate or control a traffic which, as at present conducted, was a prolific source of wretchedness, misery, and woe to vast numbers of the people. (Applause.) On that question even the brewers were being convinced that there were too many public-honses. At the recent eireerster sessions in the town a firm of well-known brewers, through their solicitor, offered to the magistrates to give up the licenses of a cer- tain number of public-houses—he thought it was three—if the magistrates would only grant them one in a new dis- trict. Fortunately the Licensing Committee did not accept the bait, as it was in the monied interest of the firm that the offer was made and not for the public good. (Heat, hear.) As a politician he saw no reason to be discouraged, for though from his point of view their cause naturally be- longed to the reformers it was important to note statements by members and supporters of the present Government. Ii the debate on the address, in reply to the Queen's speech, in the early part of this year, Mr. Balfoer said there was one question greater than the question of allotment, namely, the question of temperance, and that, he said, wonld be dealt with in the new local government bill. Mr. Johnston, a memuer for Bel- fast, a devoted supporter of the present Govern- ment, has said that as a pelitician he was prepared to put the temperance question first, and even to support or move an amendment to the address. Then in the recent speech of the leader of the House of Commons at Dartford, he said that the question of local government would include another very large and thorny question—the licensing question—end he believed it possible for local bodies to settle the main difficulties which have arisen. "At any I rate," said this consistent politician, "I think with the agreement of all parties, except enthusiasts and fanatics, a real and genuine move forward can be made." They, the chairman went on, did not object to that sneer, and the time was coming when "enthusiasts and fanatics" must press forward that question independent of all political par- ties, and they should perhaps have the same courtesy shown to them by Her Majesty's Government as at present is be- ing shown to another section of politicians, and they will say "We will do everything and anything to keep you with us ; you have made sacrifices, and so will we. You have flung over your party ,and supported ours; we will fling over our principles and carry out yours." (Hear, hear.) He would say in conclusion to the political minority in this town, of which he was a member, that unless they showed sympathy with the great social question that tended to the general good of the public, they never need to expect to win Warrington. (Loud applause.) The Rev. S. Wixoeisson said he was very glad to see there that night so many ladies, who, by their presence counte- nanced the great movement they had met to further. He did believe most sincerely that if they could only get the women of England heart and soul on their side in time they should succeed in that temperance movement. (Ap- plause.) He then moved :—" That this meeting is con- vinced that the traffic in intoxicating liquors, however re- stricted and regulated, produces social disorder, political corruption, and wide-spread moral degradation; and that while it continues it must be a great factor in the production of in- temperance, pauperism, insanity, impurity, and every form of crime and outrage ; the meeting is therefore of opinion that the traffic ought to be prohibited by an efficient legis- lative enactment resolutely enforced." (Applause.) Mr. R. GARNETT, J.P., seconded the resolution. He was sure, he said, the resolution would commend itself to their judgment as it did to his. It had his very earnest support. ',Applause.) The Rev. PREIII3NDART Galen, who was received with applause, supported the resolution. It was true, he said, all the world over where strong drink was used that a certain proportion of the population was addicted tp drunkenness. Do what they would if they went on drinking alcohol a certain number would get drunk. They were differently constituted. Some men had strong heads and some men had weak, some men had good digestion and some bad, and unquestionably there were persons who were fascinated by that drink, and corrupted by it; persons whose whole consti- tutions seemed to be changed by it, and if the great bulk of mankind used and promoted the sale of strong drink, then nothing in the world could prevent a very considerable part of the population from being converted into drunkenness. Now, what was to be done if that was the case? He knew what would be done if that strong drink were not pleasant to the taste of man. It would not be tolerated. It was only tolerated because, unhappily, it was pleasant to the taste of man. It came to this, then, that men are selfish, and being selfish they will not abandon that which is an injury and a curse to their neighbours. What they had to do. then, to get rid of that plague was not simply to be total abstainers themselves, but to diminish, to entirely abolish if they could, the temptations to the use of it. (Applause.) They had I tried every other method. The resolution said that "the traffic in intoxicating drink, no matter bow regulated or how ' restricted, produced social disorder, political corruption, and wide-spread moral degradation." As to political corruption, they knew right well that beer bad been used to bribe man- kind for many generations in this country, and he was afraid it bribed them still. What was more, they found that even the highest in the land were not proof against the political corruption of strong drink. They remembered some time ago Lord Salisbury actually converted Sir Henry Allsopp into a peer. Why, he (the speaker) did not know. Sir Henry Allsopp had rendered no very eminent services to this country. He had, it was true, brewed an enormous amount of beer, and grown enormously rich, but what more he had done he did not know. He was shocked when he saw that he had been created a peer. (Hear, hear.) He did not know why he had been made a peer, but this he did know, that Sir Henry Allsopp gave a very considerable sum of money to- wards the electioneering expenses ef the Conservative party. Where did he get the money from? He got it, of course, from the drink of the people, and after he had done that he (the speaker) did not say on account of that he was made a peer. (Hear, hear.) It was very shocking of Lord Salis- bury, wasn't it. (" Shame.") Quite so; he had no busi- ness at all to break up the old traditional distinction between the " beerage" and the peerage. (Laughter.) Then they knew how immaculate the Liberals were. Shortly afterwards Sir Arthur Bass gave a considerable sum of money in the same wayto the electioneering expenses of the Liberals and he has been elevated somewhere. He said a plague on both their parties. (Applause.) He said this distinctly that he could gather from the whole of the political career of Mr. Gladstone that he cared no more for the great movement than did Lord Salisbury. Let there be no mistake about it. He had hoped better things of Mr. Gladstone and of the party to which he belonged, but he was utterly hopeless of them now, and those who cling to that party simply be- cause it chose to call itself Liberal were making the grandest mistake Christian men could make. What they had to do was to form another party that would be above I all political corruption, and would attempt to clear them- selves of all the evils which flow from the liquor traffic. (Applaese.) If they were Liberals, ho supposed they were in favour of the progress of the people. He was, and he wanted to see them vastly improved, much more highly educated, their homes much brighter, and he wanted to see them far more intelligent than they now were; but be knew that they should have very little improvement until they got out of their way these multiplied temptations of a degrading vice. (Hear, hear.) He hoped there were some Conservatives there, and he should like to plead BCV:itthßtiOtEhSen%o They preserved to if prefshereve the institu- tions of the country, s but how werepeotphioese weinre- dissatisfied and discontented because they were miserable. Why were they miserable? Because they were drunken, and they were druneen because of the temptation to which by the law of England they were exposed. The measure for which they contended was a great Liberal measure and a great Conservative measure and all ought to join them to put down that accursed trade. (Applause.) It had been pointed out that a diminution of the number of public- houses did not lead to a diminution of drinking, and he

agreed with that. No matter how the traffic was regulated it would lead to the same evils. Mr. Chamberlain thought he had found a way of regulating it by which it might be rendered perfectly innocuous. He proposed intro- ducing the Gothenburg system under which Town Councils were to buy the public-houses, and then they would see that they were properly officered. But they found that in Gethenberg, and in all the towns of Sweden in which this system prevailed, the people were actually more drunken than they were in Edinburgh. (Laughter.) They did not think, therefore, that that was a very hopeful scheme to introduce into England. (Hear, bear.) Some people thought the matter would be all right if the licenses were issued by elected hoards, but he was not aware that they would b• 3 any better than the magistrates. In Wolverhampton the Town Council had been selling sites tor gin palaces ; in Birmingham the

Town Council had done precisely the same thing, and the other day, at Derby, a friend of his bad to oppose the Town Council, who wanted to transfer licunses into his paris..t be- cause it would be pecuniarily advantaireous to the Corpora- tion. He believed it was quite possible if licenses were issued by town councils the councils might be given, no doubt for the benefit of the places they govern, a certain pecuniary interest is the licenses, and if that was done be was of opinion it would be fatal to the morality of the whole country. (Hear, hear.) They might depend upon it that if town councils were allowed to handle any of the money that came from licenses they would never get rid of one. His advice to them was tc have nothing to say in favour of transferring the control of licenses trom the magistrates to Town Councils. It was not the licenses that did the harm. It was the drink that made people ;drunk, and nothing but the drink. This, then, was the con-
• clasion he came to, that •• the traffLo ought to be prohibited by an efficient legislative enactment resolutely enforced." (Applause.) What was an efficient legislative enactment?
Of Course, it would be possible to abolish the trade in song drink by an imperial enactment all the country over, and this had been done with the best results ipt the State of

Maine. Bnt they were willing to try another plan, which was simply this, that wherever the people ask that there might be no strong drink sold in their parish, if they asked it by a sufficient majority, no Town Council, no Licensing Board, no magis- trates, and no power on the earth or under the earth should have the right to force the liquor trade amongst them. (Loud applause.) The resolution was then put to the meeting, and carried unanimously.

The Rev. G. E. CUTTING proposed "That in view of the enormous public evils and calamities, directly and indirect- ly caused by the traffic in intoxicating liquors, this meeting calla upon the Government, Parliament, an apon all pa- triotic statesmen to put forth united efforts to frame and pass such a measere as shall remove the evil traffic front the Commonwealth, and enable the people in their respective localities, if so minded, to vote it out of existence by direct veto." The resolution also, he said, called upon the minis- ters and members of the Christian churches to combine in their efforts to carry out that grand object. They local men, he said, were that night to show their faces,clear their throats, and sit down again, and it was quite right that in the presence of many eloquent strangers, local speakers should occupy as little time as possible. But it was impor- tant that they should show their faces, and as a respected and esteemed minister of the Church of England had al- ready addressed them, he was there to show his Methodist face—(applause)—and to say that the Wesleyans in War- ! rineton were to a men in sympathy with the objects of the I United Kingdem Alliance. (Applause.) He went to a temperance meeting whee four or five years old, and then ! imbibed temperance principles, and he was glad to say, on his birthday ;that day, that he was a teetotaller of 85 years' standing. (Cheers.) He wanted them all, as temperance workers in Warrington, to be encouraged. The magnificent meeting held the) day previous at Manchester, and that en- couraging meeting that night, should stimulate them I !to do and dare more in Warrington on behalf of that cause. There were workers, but what was wanted was work of a more imposing kind, in order that a public im- pression might be made. He wanted those who were co- workers, and who were in sympathy with the work, to be ! stimulated. That was a terrible word to be used at a tee- total meeting. But they did believe in stimulants of some I kind. Not all stimulants were to be condemned, and they I needed the stimulation that meetings of that sort were cal- culated to give, so that they might add to their zeal. If , they meant to make an impression in Warrington, they must have a little more enthusiasm on this question. They must be a little more coarageoas and audacious. To be a little awkward was a dieagreeable thing, but to be very awkward was productive of a good result. There were those who classed all temperance workers as fanatics and enthusiasts, but had it not been for the enthasiasm and fanaticism of the temperance party, they would not have promised to them even the vestige of political help that was offered to them. Thank God for the wrek of enthusiasts. Since tbe time of enthusiasm in connection wtih Murphy's Mission, the temperance movement in Warrington seemed to have been like a shorn Samson. They had been in the Delilah lap of indifference and miasma.% but he thought that the time bad been sufficiently long for Samson's hair to grow again, and he thought that there were signs that Samson was about to move and put forth his strength. (Laughter and applause.) He trusted that the Samson of temperance would put its arm round the temple of Bac- chus, and pull it down—(applause)—and, without having any political meaning, he prayed that it might pull down the significant representation of that borough in Parliament. (Applause.) If they sent a Tory to Parliament, let him be a teetotal Tory. He had no personal or political feeling, but it did grieve him, and exasperated him, when he remem- bered that he was represented, and that they were repre- sented, in Parliament by some one who did not represent them on that most important matter of all. They were hoping soon to celebrate the jubilee of the (*teen, and he wished they could celebrate it by striking off the fetters of the slaves to drink, and redeeming the people from that cursed bondage. (Applause.) The Rev. J. H. dorms seconded the resolution. He was, he said, pleased to find so many members of the church to which he had the honour of ministering among those I present that eight. He also was pleased with the appear- ance of the platform. He was, however, a little disap- pointed that they had not their member there that night. ! (Laughter and cheers.) If they only had the genial ' presence of Sir Gilbert Greenall on that platform he should be pleased, and he should be still more pleased if the? had their Liberal candidate on the platform. (Cheers.) He was hoping to see the day when the churches of the land would take up that matter, for, as Christian churches, they held both political parties in the hollow of their hand. It would be pretty well known that—coming as he did from North Wales—that he was a good, strong Liberal, but he would tell them honestly that he was first of all a Christian, a temperance man, and a social reformer: then he was a Liberal. (Cheers.) He would sell his party the next day if he found the Liberal party bringing forward a brewer as a candidate for Warrington. He wanted to say a word or two to the Liberal and Coeservative electors who were at that meeting. They must see to it that at the next elec- tion their vote was not given to any man who was not pledged to the hilt to the principles of the United Kingdom Alliance. (Applause.) To they Christian people, to him as a Christian minister, this was the first question, far more important to him and to them as the people of England, than any other question on the programme of either political party. They must, as far as ever they could, push this question to the front. He wanted the Liberal electors, before the next election time came, to see to it that the Liberal candidate was pledged to the principles of that Alliance. (Applause.) He had great faith in the squeezeability of the candidates for Parliament. They could bring them round to their own :opinions. He would rather see Warrington—though he was a strong Liberal—represented by a Tory than by a Liberal who wouli not promise to do his utmost to bring about the downfall of the liquor traffic. (Cheers.) The state of our licensing laws was a disgrace to the Christian community; and they had themselves to blame for the present state of things. If they could take the matter up heartily, they could soon change the aspect of affairs. He would mention an occur- rence that took place in Liver Pool a few years ago. A new dock was being opened in the northern portion of Liverpool, and it was found that a piece of land in the neighbourhood had been secured for the purposes of a public-house. The neighbourhood was alarmed, and the magistrates were petitioned. The owner of a line of steamers appeared per- sonally before the magistrates to implore them not to put that plague spot in the midst of his workmen, bet in face of all this the magistrates granted the license for that public- house. That was a thing that might happen anywhere. Warrington people might object to having plague spots near their doors, but if the magistrates were so disposed, they could do it. Were they willing that this state of things should last much longer? It had lasted long enough. (Hear, hear.) Or would they, in the name and fear of God, record a vow that they would do all that lay in their power to sweep those disgraceful laws from the British statute book? (Cheers.) That would indeed be a noble way of celebrating the Queen's jubilee. (Cheers.) Mr. HARDY at this juncture read a letter that had been received from Mr. Joseph Leicester, whom it was expected would have been present. Mr. Leicester wrote—" I deeply grieve to say how sorry I am at not being able to be at your meeting on Wednesday. I had fully hoped to have been able to have taken my part on your platform, in my native town, but my nerves are so unstrung with over work that I am utterly unable to address meetings just now. At some future time I pray God I may once more visit my native town, and say a word upon the grand old cause of temper- ance and prohibition." Major WATERSTON, of Edinburgh, then supported the re- solution. He said that upon that platform he looked very much upon Liberals as tweedle-dee, and upon Tories as tweedle-dum. (Laughter.) He had, practically, a kind of contempt for political parties. He was a strong political economist, however, and it seemed to him that if voters were to consider political economy, and leave party politics aside a little, it would he a great blessing for the nation at large. The results of Sunday closing in Scotland were such that the people of Scotland were so copvincel that one day in the week was a blessing, that he believed the great majority of the country, if they had the power, would go in for prohibition for the whole seven. (Cheers.) In the boroughs of Scotland, the licensing was entirely in the hands of the Corporation, hut were they much better because of that; he said no. His opinion about town councillors and magistrates was that they were just ordinary men, and were susceptible to back door influence just like other mortals. (Applause.) He hoped that his remarks had no local significance. (Laugh- ter.) He was entirely looking at the matter from a Scotch point of view. The question must be submitted to the
MM.

great democracy of the land. It was said that the traffic was for the public convenience: if so, the public knew their wants better than anyone else, and should control it. One thing that bad struck him in Scotland was that the magi- strates there were much in favour of local option. He did not know any magistrate who had a public-house next to his own house. (Laughter.) If a public-house WA3 a blessing, wlay do not the magistrates take a share of the blessings? Would they believe that magistrates were so philanthropic AS to deprive themselves of blessings ? No ; if theca were any blessings they would have the first place. But they knew the evils that followed from public-houses, and kept themselves from them. He (the speaker) did not only ob- ject to magistrates thinking for him, but he objected to any laws, passed by either Whig or Tory Government, that sought for a single moment to confer upon the wealthier classes of the country power that it did not give to the humblest of the subjects. The law of Scotland at present gave to the landed proprietor the power to defy the law in granting licenses if they oppesed them. They had the power to veto the license by virtue of their property right. Why should not work- ing-men, who had no property, have the same privilege? Had the Father in Heaven any law that dealt with one class more than another? He had no respect of persons. If the law of this land was to be based, All it should be, on the law of God, then the law that gave to the rich of the land power and protection, and did not give it to the poor, was contrary to the divine law, and he (the speaker) took his stand, as a Scetchman, against it. (Applause.) He did not say anything against the people who held licenses. In Scotland publicans had to have the very best characters, and he believed that in the town from which he came there was a larger percentage of c,,urch-going people amongst the pub- licans than in any profession in the town. At the same time, he drew a great distinction between church-going people and christiana. There were 802 drinksellers in that town, and out of them there was only 27 who were not mem- bers of one church or another—yet they had 8,000 people drunk last year. That proved that the difficulty was not as much in the men as in the shop. Therefore, they must grapple with the traffic, and take the licensing power from the magistrates to give to the people. Trust the people ; give them a right to assert their manhood. He believed that the hearts of the people were tight, if the temptations that surrounded them could be removed. If they could succeed in that what a blessing it would be. (Cheers.) The resolution was then carried with applause. The Rev. J. YONGB proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, and asked him to be good enough to on their behalf send copies of the resolutions passed to the member for the borough, and to Her Majesty's Government, that they might know what they in Warrington thought upon that question. It was too late for him to say much, but there was one thing he should like to call attention to. A good deal had that night been said about the desirableness of transferring licensing power from the magistrates to the people. They were all at one, he believed, as to that, but he should like to make a reference to the conduct of the local magistrates upon this particular matter. They were all aware, he presumed, that every year applications for new licenses were made to the magistrates by various persons in the berough. He thought he was correct in saying that it was now some time since the magistrates for Warrington sew their way to grant any such application. (Cheers.) IHe could like to testify—as he could do from personal ' knowledge—to the exceedingly courteous way in Iwhich the Mayor and the magistrates had always listened to the representations made to them on this subject by various temperance organisations in the town. It was due to the magistrates that they should acknowledge by that expression their gra- titude for the way in which the magistrates had dealt in the matter. He was mare that the magistrates themselves would be delighted if they were relieved of this duty, but he was sure they would be glad to know that they had the cordial support of the right thinking people of Warrington, in pursuing the course they had done for some years past, and from which he hoped they never would in the future depart. (Cheers.) Mr. HARDT seconded the resolution, which was carried with applause, and the meeting then terminated.

2ND V. 13. SOUTH LANCASHIRE REGIMENT (LATH 21ST L.R.V.) The competition for the second series of Subscription Prizes, value £lO, presented by friends of the corps in St. Helens, Widnes, Prescot, and neighbourhood, took place on Saturday. The prizes in this series are only open to those men who bare never previously won a prize over the value of 15s; hence the best shots in the corps are debarred from competing. The distances shot at were 200 and 300 yards, fiva shots at each. Regulation targets. Position, standing at 200 yard., and kneeling at 300 yards. A rather cold and strong wind blowing across the range severely tried the skill—or rather the want of skill—of a great number of the more inexperienced shots who entered, and made the shoot- ing very difficult for even the more practised hands. There were 123 entries. The first prize was won by an old mem- ber of the Widnes company, the second and third by mem- bers of the St. Helens companies, and the fourth by a Sutton volunteer. IMPORTANT ALTERATIONS IN ENGINEERING WORES.— During the past few weeks extensive alterations have been carried out in regard to the works of Messrs. T. and T. Vickers, engineers and brass founders, Earlestown. The firm had its head quarters at Liverpool for many years, and the Earlestown works were opened as a branch department. The local works have since been considerably extended, and the firm lately decided to carry out alterations necessary to enable them to have their head quarters at Earlestown in- stead of at Liverpool. The Liverpool portion of the works has consequently been given up, and nearly all the men employed there have been removed to Earlestown, where alterations in the works are being made to find the required accommodation for the machinery and men.

EARLESTOWN. -UNITED Missiox.—A series of special services, under the united support of local clergymen and ministers, and arranged by Mr. G. Dring, the Earlestown town missionary, wilt be commenced next week in several places of worship. Drtmrx.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Tuesday, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, Walter Hughes, a labourer at the Viaduct Works, was charged with being drunk and disor- derly at Earlestown on the previous day, and was fined 5s and costs.

SUCCESS OF A LOCAL SITIDENT.—At a /want Government examination held in London, tha results of which came to hand last reek, Mr. Edward Corlett, of Marketrstreet, Earlestown, has been successful in obtaining a First-class Queen's Scholarship, which entitles him to two years' free education at Borougb-road Training College, London. FIIIEWOIIK-9. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Samuel Kershaw and Thomas Lawson, boys, were summoned for letting off fireworks in the public street at Earlestown, on the 2nd inst.—P.C. Hunt deposed that about a quarter past nine on the previous Saturday night he saw the defend4nts letting off fireworks in Market-street, Earles- town. Lawson climbed up a lamp post and handed a light down to Kershaw.—The parents of the defendants promised to see that their children did not again commit the offence, and the summonses were dismissed.

Tun RECENT HARVEST HOME- FEsTrvAL.—On Mon- day evening a meeting of the society members connec.ed with the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legh-street, was held in that place of worship, to receive a report upon the recent Harvest Home Festival. Mr. Thomas Clarke presided. The secretary (Mr. T. Ormand) submitted the report, which showed that the festival was a success. After paying all expenses there was a balance of over £l5 in hand. Thanks were accorded to Mr. Ormand for his exertions, and a vote of thanks was passed to all friends wha had COa- tributed their support. THREATENING LANGUAGE.—James Waterworth Was summoned at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, be- fore Messrs. R. Houghton and T. J. Gillespie, for using threatening language to Samuel Brown, at Earlestown, on the 3xl inst. Complainant stated that while he and his wife were at home on the date named the defendant knocked at the doer, and on it being opened, he used abusive and threatening language. He (complainant) had previously had tbe defendamt bound ever to keep the peace for three months for a similar offence.—The Bench ordered the de- fendant to be bound over for six months. QUARRELSOME NEIGHBOURS. -- Before Messrs. R. Houghton and T. J. Gillespie, at the Town Hall, on Satur- day. Mary Houghton was summoned for assaulting Mary Ann Ellis, wife of Aaron Ellis, a moulder at the Viaduct works, at Earlestown, on the 30th September. The defend- ant pleaded not guilty. Mr. Stuart, solicitor, Newton, ap- peared for the complainant, and stated that the defendant put her fist in his client's face, and exclaiming" This is my bench of fives, and I will give them to you," struck her with her fist. The defendant afterwards put her two hands into his client's face and said "Here's the ten command- ments," and she struck her agaia.—The complainant corro- borated this statement, and in reply to the defendant said she did not take a long brush and threaten to push it down her (defendant's) throat. The Bench imposed a fine of 2s 6d and costs.

DISTURBANCE ON THE MARKET PLACE —At the New- ten Town Hall, on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton and T. J. Gillespie, Isaac Haskins' a .young man, was summoned for committing a breach of the peace by being disorderly on the Market-place, Earlestown, on the Ist inst. It was stated that the defendant, with others, was coming from the direction of the Alexandra Theatre, when they be- gan to curse and swear. They also used abusive language to Market-Inspector Crabtree.—Mr. Stuart, who appeared for the defendant, urged that the defendant was not disor- derly, and alleged that the market inspector had pushed the defendant, said the inspector had exceeded his duty.— The Bench remarked that they thought the market inspec- tor would not have interfered with the defendant without any cause. He had been a constable, and knew his duty. The Bench, however, would not record a conviction against the defendant if he would agree to pay the costs of the ero- ceedings.—The defendant agreed to do this, and the case was dismissed. • SCIIOOI, ATTENDANCE.—At the Newton Petty Ses- sions on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton and T. J. Gille%pie, Richard Beere, of Newton, was summoned for neglecting to send his child to school.—The defendant pleaded not guilty, alleging that his child was unwell.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Nicholson): What isithe matter with her? Defendant: There are many illnesses. The child has been unwell since birth. It is a weakly, sickly child.—The Clerk: You have no doctor's certificate to that effect? Defendant: No.—Mr. John Ball, school attendance officer, was then sworn, and he stated that he had visited the de- fendant's house and complained of the irregular attendance of hes daughter at school. He admitted that the child was not a very strong child, but it was well enough to run about the streets.—ln reply to the chairman, the defendant added that he had not a doctor's certificate. He had no means to be always running to a doctor for certificates, which meant more expense. He bad now a bill for £2 17s from Dr. Wat- kins, which he could not see himself clear to pay, and last year he had a bill of £4 17s 6d to pay. He could net al- ways raise the money—it wanted saving and working for.— The defendant was fined ss, including costs. HARVEST FESTITAL A.T Newrore—Services of thanks- giving for the harvest were held in St. Peter's Church, Newton, on enelilay last. In preparation for the occasion the sacred edifice had undergone an elaborate decoration with fruit, flowers, vegetables, wheat, corn, ttc. The vicinity of the communion was bedecked ley Mrs. Jones. the Misses Pearson devoted their attentions to the pulpit, the front of the choir stalls was attended to by Miss Westhead, Mrs. Birlev and Miss Russell were in charge of the arrange- ments for the eagle lectern, Miss Pennington set out the reading desks, Mrs. Gillespie attended to the font, and the windows and gas standards were decorated by the Misses Devereux. The morning preacher was the Rev. Canon Lefroy, M.A., and the evening preacher the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, 8.A., vicar of Holy Trinity Church, War rington. The choir of the church, under the leadership of Mr. P. ' Fairclough (who accompanied on the organ), sang the anthem "0 taste and see" in the morni4g, and in the evening the choir rendered "I will magnify Thee, 0 God." There were very large congregations, and the offertories, which were is behalf of the National Society for the educa- tion of the children of the poor in the principles of the Church of England, amounted to over £l2. PRIILEOSH LHAGEN MEETING AT EARLESTOWL-0U Monday evening a lecture and entertainment, under the auspices of the Newton and District Habitation of the Prim- rose Leaeue, were given in the Viaduct Institute, Earles- town. The room was crowded. The first item on the Pro- gramme was a lecture by Mr. M.eßrown-Westhead, who said he thought the aims of the Primrose League would meet with the approval of all who had thee:interests of their free country at heart, and its success would afford intense gratification to its originator, Sir Drummond Wolf, a mem- ber of the Fourth Party. He gave a brief outline of its objects, which he said were to preserve the maintenance of religion, the estates of the realm, as well as to upheld the supremacy of the imperial ascendency of the British ern= Dire. In religious matters, they wished to'avoid all .bigotry and intolerance, and to be on one side in successfully coping with the common enemy, the atheism of the present day. (Applause.) In the entertainment which followed, the fol- lowing ladies and gentlemen took part :—Mr. John White, the Dame President, Mrs. Rovse, Mrs. Seton, Mr. George Wright, Mr. H. F. Gooch, Mr. H. Thomson, Mr. T. Stone, and Mr. C. E. Pearson. Mr. W. Thompson proposed a vote of thanks to the performers, which was seconded by Mr. Catterall, and carried. Mr. T. H. Pearson responded, and Captain Seton proposed thanks to Mr. Westhead for his lec- ture. Mr. W. Mawdsley seconded the resolution, which was agreed to, and Mr. Westlilad suitably responded. Mr. Thomas Stone, hon. secretary of the League, announced that the number of members of the Habitation was 550.

div.head: LIBERAL CLUB GATHERINGS. INAUGURAL CONCERT.
div.p: LIBERAL CLUB GATHERINGS. INAUGURAL CONCERT.

The first of a series of free entertainments to be held in connection with the Earlestown and District Liberal Club, Fairclough-street, was held on Thursday night, at the club. The room was crowded. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. D. Burdis, and among those present were Messrs. W. Urquhart, B. Corlett, J. Newton, P. M. Campbell, C. Kelly, W. Younger, Mr. T. Morris (secretary), and others. The Chairman said that last year a series of discussions were held in the room by the members of the club, but this year it was thought desirable to somewhat vary the pro gramme. The committee of the club had decided during the ensuing season to have not only lectures, but concerts as well, believing that by combining pleasure with profit they might promote the interests of the club. (Hear, hear.) Hav- ing referred to the presence of the ladies at the meeting, he said that the members were desirous of forwarding the in- terests of Liberalism in the division, and afterwards to cul- tivate that social comfort and friendship which in a country place like Earlestown tended very much to make life more agreeable. He wished that the session upon which they were entering might be a great success, and that a much larger, better, and more convenient room would soon be required for the club. (Applause.) Messrs. E. and C. Corlett then gave the pianoforte duet "The Bohemian Girl," Mr. S. Swann sang "Out on the deep," Mr. John Gibbons sang " Nora, the pride of Kil- dare," Master B. Tripp gave a violin solo entitled" Home, sweet home," and Mr. P. Hastie sang " Over the rolling sea." Mr. C. Hallas created amusement by an American recitation, and Mr. J. Williams was encored for his kumourous song "My Wife's relations," and gave "The jolly little nigger." Mr. E. Corlett gave a selection on the pianoforte. Mr. T. Morris (sec.), in the interval, announced that the first meeting of the discussion class , would be held next Thursday night, when Mr. W. D. Bur- dis would read a paper on "The duties of Liberals in this , division." He hoped the discussion class would be success- ful, as was the case last season. (Applause.) The second part of the programme included songs by Messrs. Hastie, Swann, Gibbons, and Williams. a duet by Messrs. Swann and Hastie, a violin solo by Master Tripp, and a recitation by Mr. Holland. The entertainment closed with a vote of thanks to the entertainers and chairman.

MII. SIMS REEVES AND " ENCORES."—A ballad Conceit at the Philnarmonic Hall, Liverpool, on Tuesday evening, wag (in the language of a contempory) "turned into a b3ar- garden" by the noisy and preposterous deman s of a por- tion of the audience for an "encore" from Mr. Sims Reeves. The great tenor, with the other vocalists engaged, had gone so far as to sing twice as many sengs as they had engaged to give, but so persistent was the unraannerly section of the audience that tbe concert terminated in a most abrupt manner.

ST. HELENS. ONE lIITNDEED AND TEN CONVICrIONS.—At the Town Hall on Monday, before Aldermen Harr son and Cook and Dr. Twvford, Elizabeth Tithtr, an elderly woman, was charged with druukenneu on Saturday night. It was her 111th appearance, and she was committed to prison for a month.

Tilt MAYORALTY. - The members of the Town Council who attended elmmittee meetings on Wednesday signed a memorial to Colonel Gamble asking him to accept the Mayoralty next year. A special meeting of the Coun- cil will be held next week to elect two aldermen to the va- cant chairs.

TITTYTON TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION.—The usual weekly meeting of the above took place on Tuesday even- ing. Mr. E. S. Eccles presided, and gave a brief address on the "Ravages of drink." An entertaining programme fol- lowed of songs and recitations by Mrs. Eccles, Miss Martha Mason, Dr. Capper, Mr. H. Capper, Miss Turner presiding at the pianoforte.

PLANCTORTE- -RECITAL —On Friday evening Mr. Hague Kinsey, of Liverpool, late of .the Conservatoriuna der Musik, Leipzig, gave a pianoforte recital at the Town Hall, to a small but appreciative audience. The programme was a classical one, and contained selections from the works of several of the leading comp6sers. At the close several ladies and gentlemen congratulated Mr. Kinsey upon his efforts PRESBYTERIAN entiam BA Z &AM —Next Thursday, as stated in an advertisement in another column, a grand bazaar in connection with the Presbyterian church, Hard- shaw-street, will be opened in the Town Hall. The object is to raise ..-Cl,OOO for the enlargement of the Sunday school premises, repairing the church, and placing therein an organ. Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P., will attend the opening cere- mony.

CAUTION TO DRIVERS —At the Town Hall, on Mon- day, before Aldermen Harrison and Cook and Dr. Twyford, William Sephton, a resident of Windle, was summoned for allowing a horse and conveyance to stand in Brownlow.. street longer than necessary, en the 25th ult. P.C. Cannee deposed that he saw defendant's horse and conveyance with- out anyone in charge, and he afterwards met the defendant c(.ming out of a puhlic-house. The defendant ran his ye-

hide from St. Helens to Havdock and plied for passengers. Mr. R. W. H. Thomas, who appeared for the defendant, contended that the vehicle did not stand for more than ten minutes, which, he urged, was not an unreasonable time. The magistrates imposed a fine of 53 and costs.

MISSIONARY SERMONS AND MEETINGS.—OR Sunday, special sermons in connection with the Church of England Foreign Missionary Society were held at the Parish Church, when sermons were preached by Dr.Weithreight, formerly a missionary in the Punjaub. H pleaded the cause of foreign missions in an earnest manner. On Monday evening Dr. Weitbreight addressed a well-attended meeting in the Girls' Schoolroom in connection with the Ckurch Missionary Society. The annual services in connection with the Wes- leyan Home Missions were held in the Wesleyan Chapel, Corporation-street, on Sunday, when two impressive ser- mons were preached to large congregations by the Rev. Geo. Hammond, of Rathdrum. At the close of each service, a collection was taken in aid of the Wesleyan Home Mission- ary Society._

BunrAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of the St. Helens Burial Board was heist at the Town Hill, on Thurs- day week, when there were present—Alderman J. Harrison, J P. (in the chair), Messrs. N. Lacey, J. Lewis, Green, T. C. Wilcock, T. Brewis (clerk), and Knighton (assistant clerk.) —The financial statement showed there was a balance of £2O 15s 2d in hand from last month, and the cash received during the month amonnted to £46 0.3 2d. The payments had been :—WagPs £2B 5s sd, deposited in bank £2O, bal- ance in band £lB Os 11d. The interments during the year up to August 25th were 665, during September 123, total 785. The number of intern-lents during September last year were 66.—Mr. Wilcock asked the clerk if a member of that Board who had not paid his debts was competent to act as a member. He knew it was not allowed in regard to the Town Council.—The Town Clerk said a man who had merely not paid his debts was still a member, but if he was a bankrupt he forfeited his pesition on the Board.—This was the only business.

BANKRUPTCY OF A PUI3LICAN.—At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, before Mr. Regiatrar Bel!ringer, the case of James Liptrot was called. The debtor, until very recent- ly, kept the Cowley Hill Tavern, but is at present a glass- cutter at Nottingham. Mr. Gittens, the official receiver,, stated that he had received a letter from the debtor, in which he explained that he had no • money to bring him from Nottingham to Liverpool. He had therefore to ask for instructions respecting the proceedings to be taken in the future.—Mr. Mearw, St. Helens, who appeared for several creditors, said Mr. Liptrot had already put them to a great deal of inconvenience by having called them together at. Liverpool on two occasions, and not having been present himself. He suggested that the examination should be adjourned for a short time, for the purpose of giving the debtor another opportunity of attending the court, as it was very important that he should be examined concerning his dealings with the estate.—On the suggestion of the of- ficial receiver, the registrar adjourned the hearing until the 21st inst..
FAILURE OF A. TRADESMA.N.—At the Liverpool Bank..

ruptcy Court, en Monday, before Mr. Registrar Cooper. William Pimley, who carried on business as a tailor and draper at 70, Bridge-street, St. Helens, came before the coert for his public examination. The statement of the affairs showed liabilities £1,359 8s 7d and assets £631 103 34. Tho amount due to preferential creditors is £l5, leaving a deficiency of £742 185 4d. The debtor was ex- amined by the official receiver. He stated that he com- menced business in 1878 as a draper and dealer in ready made clothes at a shop in Sutton-road. St. Helens. He had no capital at that time. He remained there until December, 1884, when he took his present shop, and he estimated that he had at that time a surplus of £52 103. He borrowed £3OO from his mother-in-law to pay for the stock on the premises in Bridge-street. He attributed his failure to his having "over bought" himself, his capital being, with the exception of a few pounds, locked up in stock: The Official Receiver remarked that the debtor appeared to have very properly stopped trading in good time, as soon as he found himself in difficulties. The examination was adjourned to October 25th. JUVENILE THIEVES.—At the Police Court, on Satur- day, before Alderman Harrison and Alderman Cook, John Grady and Thomas Grady. of Bold-street, and James Led- with, of Wright-street (all boys), were charged with steal- ing about a dozen tobacco pipes, value fourpence, the pto- perty of Plerriet Millett, of Westfield-street. On being charged with the theft they all pleaded guilty.-John Grady ThomesGrady, John Reid (Bold-street), and William Hunt, (Canal Bank East), were then charged with stealing a quantity of fruit from a stall in the Market-square, belong- ing to Mrs Strandring. All the boys pleaded guilty. John Grady was sentenced to receive nine strokes with the birch- rod; Thomas Grady and Ledwith six strokes .each. Reid and Hunt were each fined 105 and costs, or seven days' imprisonment in default. Pa'rick McTague, 3 Court, High-street, was charged with stealing two balls of twine, value eightpence, from the shop of Mr. P. McKinley, small- ware dealer, Bridge-street. Prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to reoeive nine strokes with the birch-rod.— Michael McTague, brother of the last-named prisoner, was charged with stealing a pipe and a quantity of;cigarettes from the shop of Mr. C. D. Fothergill, tobacco manufac- turer, Church-street. As the prosecutor did not appear, the prisoner was discharged with a caution. WIFE DESERTIONS.—At the Town Hall, on Friday, Thomas Dudley, of Eccleston, was charged with neglecting to support his wife and family. The defendant's wife said she and defendant were married seventeen years ago. In February last he deserted her, and had never given her any support since. She at present lived in Copperas-street, and supported herself by washing, sewing, and working in the fields. Defendant had previously deserted her. He was a labourer, but would not work regularly.—Defendant said his wife had told him to leave the house, as she would rather have the lodger than him. She took his money to the beer- house and drunk it.—Complainant denied this, and in answer to the bench said she had six children.—An order for the payment of 85. per week was made upon the defendant. --At the Town Hall, on Monday, John Cossins, a resident of Windle, was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute to his wife's maintenance. The parties were married in Flint in 1378, and there were three children liv- ing. The complainant alleged that her husband deserted her a fortnight ago, when h came home drunk and created a disturbance. In reply tb the defendant, she admitted that her mother had ordered him out of the house, but she her- self did not do so.—The defendant said his wife had not applied to him for any money since he left the house, but she went to the relieving eflicer. He declared his intention not to give his wife any money while she stopped where she was at present.—The case was afterwards adjourned for a month to give the parties an opportunity of coming to an arrangement. HARVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICES.—COND'OgIitionaI Chapel : In celebration of the ingathering of the harvest special services were held in the Congregational Chapel Ormskirk-street, on Sunday. The Rev. R. J. Ward (pas.. tor) preached both morning and evening. In the morning he took his text from the sth chapter of Mark. 26th, 27th, and 28th verses, concluding with the words—" First the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear ;" and in the evening his text was 25th Matthew, 24th verse, " And he also that had recsived the one talent came and said, I knew that thou wert a hard master, reaping where thou didst not sow' and gathering where thou did'st not scat- ter."—St. 'lark's Chu) ch : The special services in connec- tion with the harvest thanksgiving were continued at St. Mark's Church, Cowley Hill, on Sunday, when the Rev. G. , LakPman conducted the service in the morning, the preacher being the Rev. J. W. Williams, Vicar of Widnes. At the close of an interesting sermon the preacher remarked that it was a great privilege for him as a stranger to come and preach in that beautiful church, and to see and fully realise 'the vitality of the grand oil church in the town of St. , Helens. It gladdened him to see the efforts they were all making on behalf of that church. He urzed them all to do their utmost for the purpose of entirely clearing away any debt which remained upon it. The choir then rendered as anthem entitled—" Thou visitest the earth and blessest it" in an excellent manner. In the evening the Rev. G. Lake. man (Vicar) preached to a crowded congregation.—Victoria Hall: Ihe Baptists worshipping at this hall, in Cropper'S Hill, held their harvest thankseing festival on Sunday. The Rev. W Harris preached in the morning, and in the evert- ing the Rev. W. Arthur, past ee conducted the serviee. the afternoon, a special musical service was held. Theeo was a large congregation at each service. The hall was beautifully adorned with a profusion of fruits and flowers, which had been presented for the interesting oocasion bY several members of the congregation and friends.

-- A WOMAN FROM AUSTRIA. NEAR THE VILLAGE OF ZILLINGDORF, in Lower Austria, lives Maria Haas, an intelligent and industrious woman whose story of physical suffering and final relief, as related by herself, is of interest to English women. "I was employed" she says," in the work of a large farmhouse. Overwork brought on sick headache, followed by a deathly fainting and sickness of the stomach, until I was unable to retain either food or drink. I was conapelled to take to my bed for several weeks. Getting a little better from rest and quiet, I sought to do some woik, but was soon taken with a pain in my side, which in a little while seemed to spread over my whole body, and throbbed in my every limb. This was followed by a cough and shortness of breath, until finally I could not sew, and I took to my bed for the second, and, as I thought, for the last time. My friends told me that my time had nearly come, and that I could not live longer than when the trees put on their green once more. Then I happened to get one of the Seigel pamphlets. I read it and my dear mother bought me a bottle of Seigel's Syrup, which I took ex- actly according to directions, and 1 had not taken the whole of it before I felt a change for the better. My last illness began June the 3rd, 1882, and continued to August 9th, when I began to take the Syrup. Very soon I could do a little light work. The cough left me, and I was no more troubled in breathing. Now I am perfectly cured. And oh, how happy I am! I can- rot express enough gratitude for 6eigel's Syrup. Now I must tell you that the doctors in our district distribu- ted handbills cautioning people against the medicine, telling them it would do them no good, and many were thereby influenced to destroy the Seigel pamphlets ; but now wherever one is to 'be found it is kept like a relic. The few preserved are borrowed to read, and I have lent mine for six miles around our district. People have come eighteen miles to get me to buy the medicine for them, knowing that it cured me, and to be sure to get the right kind. I know a woman who was looking like death, and who told them there was no help for her, that she had consulted with several doctors, but none could help her. I told her of Seigel's Syrup, and wrote the name down for her that she might make no mistake. She took my advice and the Syrup, and now she is in perfect health, and the people around us are amaied. The medicine has made such progress in our neighbourhood that people say they don't want the doctor any more, but they take the Syrup. Suf- ferers from gout who were confined to their bed and could hardly move a finger, have been cured by it. There is a girl in our district who caught a cold by going through some water, and was in bed five years with costiveness and rheumatic pains, and had to have an attendant to watch by her. There was not a doctor in the surrounding districts to whom her mother had not applied to relieve her child, but everyone crossed themselves and said they could not help her. Whenever the little bell rang which is rung in our place when somebody is dead, we thought surely it was for her, but Siegel's Syrup and Pills saved her life, and now she is as healthy as anybody, goes to church, and can work even in the fields. Everybody was astonished when they saw her out, knowing how many years she had been in bed. To-day she adds her gratitude to mine for God's mercies and Seigel's Syrup." Maitta Haas.

I may state plainly that I tried every medicine that I ceuld hear of, and all in vain, until I was induced to try Seigel's Syrup, and found myself quite well and in good health when I had used the bottle. Ido recommend it to every person as being B miraculous medicine, and you may use my name, if desirble. A. Davidson. WORTH A POUND A BOTTLE. 100, Hollinwood Lane, Clayton Road, Bradford, Yorkshire October 12th;1885. Dear Sir,—Having had a very bad digestion, and a very sour stomach, dizziness in the head, and pains be- tween the shoulder-blades, I could not get any relief from any kind of medicine I have tried until I took Mother Seigel's Syrup, and have been completely cured. I have had bad digestion four years, and it has been worth a pound a bottle to me.—Yours gratefully. D. Mitchell.
Upper Carr, Liversedge, Yorks., November 29th, 1885.

Sir,--41 friend of mine living in the country near here has been a sufferer for more than two years from liver complaint, and at times been unable to follow his employment. Having tried dozens of different medi- cines, but of no use, I procured him two bottles of your Syrup in Bradford, and he assures me that he never felt so well in his life, and will be pleased to recommend your medicine to anyone who may be suffering from a like complaint. If you have any circulars I should be pleased to circulate them in this district.—Yours res- pectfully, Walter G-arside. Twyn-y-Medw, Fleur-de-Lis, Via Cardiff, March 22nd, MM. Dear Sir,—l feel duty bound to relate to you what a wonderful cure my wife has attained by the use of your Curative Syrup. After years of suffering with indigestion, she is now quite well. lam never without it in the house. There are, I dare say, twenty families take it with my introducing it them. You may make use of this with pleasure. I travel about a great deal in Wales. Not a day without I meet somebody or other that is troubled with .some disease or other.— Yours obediently,
David Williams.
MOTHER SEIGEL TAXES THE LADY'S CRUTCHES.

A lady writes us from Sturton-le-SteePle, last De- cember, as follows :—" I have great pleasure in testify- ing to the benefits received from using Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. In November, 1881, I had tried several prescriptions, and suffered much from a dis- ordered system. Before taking your medicine I wa- brought down so low and weak that I could not pos- sibly get along without the assistance of crutches, so it took a considerable time to bring a perfect cure. I can thankfully and confidently say that it effected a cure by`the spring of 1882. I have since then recommended it to several friends, and, whenever they have given it a fair trial, it has proved a blessing. Like myself, they would not be without it. "Newton-heath Supply Stores, 574, Oldham-road, Dec. 21,1883.

"Gentlemen,—It is astonishing what a sale I have for your Seigel's Syrup; it keeps increasing. It has worked wonders in the neighbourhood; there is scarcely a day but someone is praising it. Several of my customers say, had it not been for SeigePs Syrup they would have been in their graves. In fact, I have a case in my own family; my wife had suffered for years with Dyspepsia, and tried a good many remedies without effect ; but after taking two bottles of Cura- tive Syrup she was completely cured.—Yours respect- James A. Hall." 3. 8. Woodruffe, Chemist, of 71, Queen-street, Hull, sends the following "To Mr. J. Woodruffe, Chemist and Druggist, Sut- ton-on-Hull. I purchased from you a bottle of Seigel's Syrup, which after three doses began to make me feel a new man. I have suffered for this last seven years from weakness of the bowels and body, and being constantly purged, but thanks to your Syrup, I feel a new man.— Yours truly, " H. MASTRIIMAN." Joseph Goddard, Druggist, 48, Castle-street, Edgeley, Stockport, December, 1884, writes thus: "As regards your medicine, 1 have sold more of it this year than last, and I find whoever tries it asks for it again, be- cause they derive so much benefit from it. Several of my customers keep having it again and again, simply because it does thsm so much good. They don't want their names published, but saw they should not keep spending 2s Oct if they did not get a pound benefit from it.

• WIT AND HUMOUR. Tom: "why: are some Government bonds called Consols ?" Dick: "Because they are such a consolation to a man." Why are younc, ladies nowadays like bells ?—Because you can never find out their metal until you have given them a ring. "Is it true," asked the professor, "that a trombone player saved the life of Frederick the Great ?" "It is," replied the student. " How ?" "Frederick killed him." "Isn't it heavenly ?" ejaculated Miss Gush, in refe- rence to Miss Pedal's performance on the piano. "Yes," replied Fogg; "it is indeed heavenly. It sounds like thunder !" "What do you grow on this land?" he inquired of the farmer who was leaning over, a fence inspecting a par- ticularly barren piece of ground. "Grow lazy," was the satisfactory reply. Husband, handing his wife some money: "There, dear, is ten pounds, and it has bothered me a little to get it for you. I think I deserve a little applause." Wife " Applause ? You deserve an encore, my dear !" Scene--Poulterer's shop. Lady: "You can put aside about half a dozen of your plumpest partridges." Poulterer: ".Yes, ma'am. When shall I send them." Lady: "sot at all; my husband is out shooting par- tridges to-day, and he'll call for them this evening." "Sir," said a Custom officer to a tourist, "I thought you told me you had nothing but your personal wearing apparel in this trunk." "So I did." "Well, how do you account for the presence of a dozen bottles of brandy ?" "Oh, that's all right! They are 'night

caps.'" Longfellow and Fields, the publishers, were making a short pedestrian tour, when, to their surprise, an angry bull stood in the pathway, evidently determined to attack both poet and publisher. "I think," said Fields, "that it will be prudent to give this reviewer a wide margin." " Yes, ' replied the poet, 'Sit appears to be a disputed passage." A little girl, very much excited, rushed into the par- lour, which was full of company, and exclaimed: "Mam- ma, just think of it !" "Think of what, darling ?" "Our cat has a whole lot of twins, and I didn't even know she was married !" _ _ _ ,

A Chicago boy, the other day, hacked a railway tor- pedo with a hatchet. Like George Washington. when lie hacked the cherry tree, the boy, or what was left of him, couldn't tell a lie about it, but he wanted to be awful bad. .

Policeman, to a man who had fallen over a bridge, and is up to the neck in water: "Your name? Your address ?" " Yes ; but—" "Not a word; it is for- bidden to bathe in this river, and I am not here to listen to extenuating circumstances." An editor's business is to do editorials, grind out poe- try, sort manuscripts, keep a mighty big waste basket, steal matter, fite other people's battles, take white beans and apple sass for nay when he can get it, work nineteen hours out of twenty-four, and be condemned by every- body.—Josh Some years ago, at the Derby, when the grand prize was won by a French horse, the Frenchmen present cheered most vociferously, and, in addition to other ex- pressions of triumph, one of them shouted, "Waterloo avenged !" "Yes," said Sir William Harcourt, who was standing by, "you ran well in both cases." "Well, Mr. Robinson, and how does your son get on with his violin?" "Astonishingly; there were fourteen of us playing together last night, and he took the lead." "Capital—admirable !" "Yes, and he kept it so well, sir, that none of us could catch him." Mr. Le Jones: "Well, Miss Coldcash, I suppose you received a good many Easter cards?' Miss Coldcash (sweetly) : "Oh, yes! and there was one particularly dainty and artistic. I am sure it came from you.', Mr. Le Jones (delighted): "What makes you think so ?" Miss Coldcash: "Because I sent it to you last year." "There is much religious teaching to be gained from Nature," solemnly remarked a young clergyman while calling upon a lady of his congregation one summer evening. "There is," was the quiet reply. "We should never forget that there is a sermon in ever blade of grass." "Quite true. We should also remember that grass is cut very short at this season of the year." "Halo, Sambo ! Hab yer lef yer master dat you's libbin with now ?" "Yes I hab ; he's so mean dat I couldn't lib with him no longer. Would yer beliebe it, Ike, I went inter de parlour yesterday wid a letter, an' dere was two ob his darters playin' on de same pianur— an' him rich enuf to buy dem half a dozen apiece. Oh, he's mean, Ike, berry mean; I couldn't stay wid such a niggardly master." A Russian seaman who had deserted gave himself up once, on the guano island of Lowe, to a crew of British seaman, expressing his desire to renounce his allegiance to the Czar, and become one ailrhe stibjects of Queen Victoria. "Jack" was zled how to naturalise him, and a conference was held to siftle tffelrinotty guestion. The result was that, after thorlussian ha d4blured his country, every British seaman threw a bucket of water upon him, and thus was he washed of his nationality. HOOKED AND LANDED.—Bride's Little Brother to Bride- ' groom : "Did it hurt you much when she did it ?" Bridegroom: "What hurt me ?" Bride's L. B.: "The hook. Did it go in your lip ?" Bridegroom: "I don't know what you mean, Johnnie." Bride's Mother: "Leave the table this instant, Johnnie !" B.'s L. B.: "What for? I only wanted to know if it hurt him. You said Sis had fished for him a long time, but she hooked him at last, and I wanted to know if—" B.'s L. B. is yanked out of his chair and hurried from the room, and the bridegroom becomes meditative. HAD'icr EATEN ANYTHING.—A negro in great pain sent for a physician. The doctor, upon arriving, asked: "Have you been eating anything calculated to hurt you ?'"*Oh, no, sah, not er talL" "Any fruit ?" "No, sail, not er tall." "Well, tell me what you did yester- day." "Well, sah, yistidy mornin' I went down to mer daughter 'Tildy's house. She wasn't at home,van' I sot down ter wait fur her. While lookin' er roun' I seed er big watermilon in er tub o' water, an' I tuck it out an' eat it. Den, ez 'Tildy didn't come I went ober ter Unk Ab Moore's house. Da wuz eatin' watermilon,, an I j'ined in. Arter this, I went down ter de cotton 'War house. Foun' er ha'f or watermilon on er box, an' ez it 'peered ter be sufferin' I eat it. I come home 'bout this time, but ez I didn't hab no appertite fur dinner I went out an' got me er watermilon. Erbout er hour arter cliS I went ober ter Unk Bill Gray's an' he'p em eat water- Dat's.erbout all. No, sah, didn't eat nuthin' ter hurt me, lessen it wuz er couple er mush milons dat I eat la.s' night. Hole on or mink. Lernme see. Oh, yes, I did eat erbout or dozen years o' b'iled co'n an' erbout Or tofu peck o' peaches.'
