A NSW CONET.—A comet was discovered by Mr. Finley, the astronomer at the Cape Observatory, on September 28. Its present position is about 28 degrees below the equator, SO that it is not visible in onr latitudes. The comet is des- cribed as circular, with central condensation. Its bright- ness is equal to a star of the eleventh magnitude, and its diameter to the second arc. As it appears to be travelling in a nortberlY direction, it promises to be an interesting visi- tant to our evening skies. THE GOVERNMENT HOME RULE BILL —IEII BASIS OF sETTLEmsrer.—Whatever doubt may linger round the authenticity of the programme set forward by Lord Randolph Churchill at Dartford, on Saturday, we are in a position to state that his announcement of the intention on the part of the Government to deal in the coming session with the question of Home Rule in Ireland is founded upon accom- plished facts. The matter has been decided upon by the Cabinet, and a committee is preparing the lines of a bill. The basis of the measure is the establishment of four national councils representing the provinces of Ireland. Ihe bill differs from Mr. Gladstone's proposal chiefly in the omission of a legislative body seated in Dublin. Otherwise the scheme will meet the fullest aspiration of Home Rulers in respect of transferring to local bodies in Ireland the direc- tion of Irish affairs now dealt with at Westminster. We understand that the Government have been in communica- tion with Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain, and have secured the promise of the hearty co-operation of these gentlemen. It will, we believe, turn out that the real author of the Home Rule scheme which the Government have finally decided to adopt is Mr. Chamberlain. Our own information at the present moment is limited to the fact that the Government have proposed to introduce a Home Rule Bill on the principle of provincial councils, and that it has so far reeelved the approval of Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain. The Government must have ad- vanced in details to meet Mr. Chamberlain's declaratian that over and above his groundwork of national councils, "it is only a very large proposal which can in the future be ac- cepted as any solution." As far as we have been able te ascertain it by personal communication, the Government scheme will be contemptuously rejected by the Irish Par- nellites. This will probably be fatal to it from a Liberal point of view, since the first condition of an acceptable Rome Rule Bill is that it should satisfy the aspirations of the Irish people.—Daily News. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. OCTOBER 16,1886.
A 11EDNIGHT ALARM. A STORY OF A VOLUNTEER ENCAMPMEII7. By C. Mc.MANts. _
"Let's see, thow once come varra nigh hevin' to feight th' Russians, didn't tha, Bob?"

"Will tha let me be quiet when lam quiet? Tha hes never done praytin' abeaut thad thee; an' aw dar say as iv thow'd bin i' my shoes thow'd nooan ha' shaped better then aw did." " Wod's thad? lies he bin a sowger ?' was the in- quiry from various parts of the room in which the friends were sitting. The house was a well-known inn, not far from Manchester. The scenery out there is rugged and grand, and besides this, it is over three , miles from the place• where the hero of the following story resided. Thus he and his neighbour, after a plea- sant Sunday afternoon's travelling, were considered by the law to be bona fide enough to be able to obtain alco- holic refreshment at otherwise unauthorised hours. John Harmer, for this was the name of the person so vociferously alluded to by the company, was some time before he made any reply, but on it's being jestingly insinuated that he was ashamed of his colours, he made reply: "No! I never listed i'th' regular army, but aw were wonst i'th' volunteers, an' thad browt abeaut th' affair at he's powin' at." " Wod's thad? Aw never knew as th' volunteers lied bin co'd eawt to war" ejaculated another bona fide who occupied a seat near the window, and who had for the last half-hour posed as the joker-in-chief to the com- pany. "But aw did hear at there were a gret mony give up a year or two sin. Wor thad abeaut th' time that yo're speykin' abeaut ?' "Now, it worn't ! There were no war agate at I know on, except a bit ov a war wi' th' factory masters as put a deal on us eawt o' wark for awhile; so me an' a tooathree others as hed joined th' rifles a year or two befoor geet a good opportunity to goa up to camp as were held that year at Raycastle in a field. This field were a gret way fro' any- where else exceptin' th' ruins ov a great castle that had stood theer mony a century, and that wer said to be haunted. Among eawr officers there were Tom Blake. He ran three factories i' them days, an' he were one o'th' promi- nent men among volunteers when Setterda neet sowd- gerin' were summat new i'th' land. He were a captain , o' my company, an' when we were ordered eawt for , active service at Raycastle, be bid us o behave eawrsels, an' nod ged drunk an' disgrace eawr uniform. Besides thad he towd us that there were no tellin' heaw soon we mit be called on to defend eawr country fro' enemies that would invade it an' try to drive us into slavery. I'd allus thowt 'at Owd England were safe enough among the waves, bud when aw heea,rd Captain Blake tell how th' Russians could come in i' disguise like traders or ordinary travellers, an' then spring up o at once an' seize our fortresses an' arsenals, aw begun to quake a bit an' to think that volunteerin' wornd o fun and spreein'. Well, we went deawn, and it happened that th' varra fost neet aw were put to walk sentry reet at th' top ov th' owd castle wo. _ _

Id were a derk neet an' o' were still, and when ths leets hed o popt eawt i'th' tents, aw sterted thinkin' to mysel as aw walked abeawt wi' mi gun o' my showder heaw aw should act if some o'th disguised Russians were to spring up an' try to seizeeawr camp. Aw were quite sure as aw could behave like an Englishman should aw be required, an' when aw thowt o'er it a' bit, aw med up my mind as if there were on), military glory to be getten thad way, aw were th' mon to ged id. Id wor lonely though walkin' abeaut at th' top o' thad wo, an' aw were fain when th' best half o' my turn were done. Id hed getten not far off time for me to be relieved, when aw thowt aw heerd a seaund—like a climbin' or scram- blin, or summat that way. I stopped an' listened, bud for a minute or two there were nowt, bud just as aw we gooin' to set off walkin' ageon I heeard it come at th' other end o'th' wo. Neaw then," aw thowt, "there's somebody tryin to ged o'er th wo. Whoever con id be comin' in as late as this?" Aw walked a few yards i' timid direction, bud aw could see nowt. Aw sheawt,ed, "Who goes there ?" bud nobody went far enough to answer me. To tell th' plain truth aw began to get reyther feared. Th' noise went on wos than ever, an aw started o' believin as there were a dozen or soa tryin to ged on th' wo. They were foreigners too aw thowt, or else they'd ha known as bi gooin reawnd a bit they could ged in witheawt o thad bother. Aw were geddin gradely ill freetend as they were Russians becoas Captain Blake wodn't hey towd us for fun. He wer a mon that read th' pappers a deal an knew o' abeawt their gooins on i' foreign parts. I went, as fast as I could walk to the other end o' th' walk an sheawted eawt "Guard turn eawt"—an id did turn eawt—an when I'd towd th' sergeant o' abeawt my hearin' these noises he ordered th' guard to fix bayonets and follow him in his search for th' marauders. Bud we fun nowt, an just as we geet back Captain Blake come up. He were th' officer o' th' day, as they co' th' officer as coom reawnd every neet, an when he heard wod aw hed to say he towd me to listen for id ageon, an iv aw heard id to co' on id to come forrut an let idsel be sin. If id didn't come eawt when id were ordered aw'd to fire on id, an wi them in- structions aw were left to keep sentry ageon till time should come for relief. In a minute or two, just when th' others had getten nicely eawt o' hearin, aw were herkenin fit to strain my ears when aw could hear th' seawnd ageon come—scrape, scrape, scrape, ageon th' wo—as iv there were somebody wi' clogs on tryin' to 'Crab o'er th' wo'. Aw were so flayed for a minute or two aw couldn'd go forrut to give id a challenge. Aw'd heard 'at th' Russians wear heavy boots wi wood soyles, an aw couldn'd see bud wod it must be them trying to ged into 'th' camp. In a while, when th' noises were gedoiin' leawder an' leawder, aw pushed forrut abeaut a hup- dred yerds, an' sheaWted eaut to know whoa went theer. There were no answer, an' no stoppage o' th' climbin' noise, soa aw fired my rifle met into wheer th' noise ODOM fro'.
_ Th' noise echoed ageon, an' neon th' owd ruins, an' th' sargant runteawt wi' th' others afterhim, an' wanted to know wod aware shootin at.

Aw towd him, an' we went to'art wheer th' deeod body should ha' been. Bud there wur nowt—an' thad were vast queer, an' med me begin to think as there were boggarts th' business, an' aw towd th' sargeant soa. Bud he only laughed, an' sed as aw'd never heard no noise, only aw were nervous, when just at thad minute we beard th' same scrapin' an' climbin' at another part o° th' buildin'. " Theer id is !" aw says, an' we o' seet off at a double to wheer th' seavvnd wur. When we geet within a hun- dred yerds or soa on it we walked more cautiously. Just then a cleawd shot away fro afore th' moon an' theer, reet at eawr feet, wur a gret black thing, seet on it sending o' my blood to my heart. Aw should hey run away at once—aw'll own thad bit—but th' sargeant jumped deawn, an' co'd on us to assist him i' catchin th' animal what hed freetened us soa.
An' wod dun yo' think id wur? Id wur nowt bud a donkey as hed getten into th' habit o' strayin', soa id owner hed put a booard i' front of id eyes, an id wur tryin' to get rid o' this ageon th' wo.
This were th' last aw heard o' th' Russians, an afore th' next campin' eawt time coom aw'd a touch o' rheu- matism as sent me upo' th' sick list, soa aw geet th' long furlough, an' left.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The sensation created by the disclosure in the "Daily News" of the Government Home Rule Bill testified to the profound interest attached to the question. How the secret got out remains untold. But the "Pall Mall Gazette," which knows every- thing, accounts for it on the ground that though the "Daily News" has stood steadfastly by Mr. Gladstone and his great scheme of Home Rule, the personal relations of the Editor and Mr. Chamber- lain have not been altered by political differences. Whether the statement was well founded or not will doubtless appear in due course. It is suggested that public opinion having almost unanimously de- clared against the proposal it will not be carried further. But if Mr. Chamberlain is really con- cerned in the matter, it would not be safe to assume that. There is about the member for West Birm- ingham a certain dogged tenacity of purpose, a ruthless and relentless pursuit of fixed determina- tion that is not easily to be turned aside. It was no small thing for him to break with Mr. Gladstone and array against himself that active antagonism which pervades a large and influential section of the Liberal party. But Mr. Chamberlain, once moved to take the step, has pursued it unfalter- ingly at whatever cost to his own political pros- pects, and to the feelings of others. If, as I shrewdly suspect is the simple explanation of the whole matter, he has exacted from Lord Randolph Churchill a pledge to bring in a Home Rule Bill, the basis of which shall be the establishment of pro- vincial councils in Ireland, you may depend upon it he will demand the uttermost fraction of his pound of flesh. Lord Hartington, called upon by a news agency to stand and deliver his testimony on the question of the day, declared with curious precision of phrase that he had never given his consent to a Home Rule Scheme establishing four provincial councils in Ireland. But it is noteworthy that, though for three days political attention was centred upon the alleged disclosure no sign was made by the Government. The " Pall Mall Gazette" succeeded in extracting a telegram from a membe • of the Cabinet, who, however, did not deny the statement. "I know nothing about it," he pettishly said, which may be quite true, for Lord Randolph when he settles what course the Government shall take upon particular questions does not always consult or even inform his colleagues. One ()the: striking feature in the episode has been the attitude of the Conservative press. This unfortunate branch of the community has had a very bad time of late. There was, first of all, the Dartford speech, upon which for the most important part it took refuge in silence. Now there is this Home Rule Bill. What are they to say about it? If they were sure the whole thing were an invention of the enemy they would jump on the scheme. But supposing after all it were true, where would they be in February next in face of the Ministerial programme, suppos- ine• in October they were to denounce its leading feature?'' The " St. James' Gazette," which ought to know, will not undertake to say that Tory scribes would not servilely support the Dartford pro- gramme, supposing it were proved to express the full mind of the Cabinet. In the same way they will support the Home Rule Scheme if, or when, it is formally adopted by the Government. In the meantime they speak -very guardedly of it, whilst on the other hand it is almost unanimously de- nounced by the Liberal press as miserably inade- quate. Whilst, save for this episode of the Government Home Rule Bill. there is a lull in politics, at home there are ominous mutterings which seem to threaten war abroad. Russia has met with a de- cided rebuff in Bulgaria, where the people have re- fused to elect Russian nominees to the Parliament. In the case of some nations this rebuff might be ac- cepted with more or less grace. But it is a differ- ent thing for the Czar who lives only upon the re- putation for invincibility. If the great sovereign is to be flouted by an insignificant state like Bul- garia he will lose caste in the eyes of the Asiatic hordes that own his sway. There is an uneasy apprehension in well informed quarters that the Czar will feel bound to vindicate his authority by the occupation of Bulgaria. Such an act would be a violation of the Treaty of Berlin, and would Russia in direct collision with the signatory powers. This is the prime danger of the situation, but it does not comprehend all. The relations of Germany and France at the present moment are suggestive of a train of gunpowder over which a torch is con- stantly flashed. The bombastic Boulanger has the torch in his hand just now, and no one can say at what moment he may not bring about an explosion. The situation .is in fact exceedingly e•rave. I mentioned the other week that next year every- body is going to make a holiday in the Australian Colonies. Meanwhile everyone is going to India. Lord Rosebery's intended visit has long been an- nounced. At first it was not intended that Lady Rosebery should accompany him. The countess is not so fond of travel as her husband, and found their journey of three years ago to Australia a weari- ness to the flesh. But it is finally decided that she will accompany Lord Rosebery, who will also have as travelling companion Mr. Munro Feigusson (generally known by his territorial title " Novar "), a pleasant-faced young gentleman, recently elected for Leith. I heard two months ago that Lord Har • tington was going to India. But it seemed an in- credible effort on the part of the noble marquis. But when we hear that the Duchess of Manchester is going, the report of Lord Hartington's journey may be received without reserve. Lord Fife, like Novar, a popular Scotch landlord, will also make India his winter holiday ground, so will Mr. Herbert Glad- stone, who is going on a visit to his brother. These are well-considered movements, for there is no place more delightful or more interesting as a win- ter holiday resort than India. In December and. January the climate is delightful. Lord Harting- ton's arrangements for this distant journey confirms what was stated in this column a week or two ago, that in high political circles there is no anticipation of Parliament meeting before the usual time in February. In spite of the attractions of India the United States still manages to secure its fair average of autumn visitors. Lord Lansdale is there, as every- body knows, and the American people have not for the first time the opportunity of studying samples of our hereditary chamber in the flesh. A rumour is buzzing about of the re-appearance of another noble lord, being none other than the Earl of Ayles- ford, whose death was reported more than a year ago, and whose body was actually brought over to this country and buried in the family vault. The romaneists will have it that this was quite another body, and that Lord Aylesford is still alive and en- ioyincr the advantages not only of freedom from overaelming mass of debts, but the actual benefits of the large sums paid by insurance comp lilies upon alleged proofs of his death. This is, of course, all nonsense. But it serves to make a little talk in America. Amongst other commoners now in the States is Mr. Stewart Maclver, formerly member for Plymouth, and proprietor of a West of Eng- land paper. Mr. Macliver, when I last heard of him, was at Niagara. Sheen, the pretty little riverside village near Richmond, is cheered by the prospect of the proxi- mate arrival of the Comte of Paris and his family. The Comte has taken Sheen Ilou e, a fine residence, in which the Prince may, if he pleases, live in as i absolute seclusion as if he were n the midst of the desert of Sahara. A large old-tashioned garden is attached to the house, and is surrounded by a high wall that keeps at arms length theouterw of Col. I. knew it very well when it was the property Beresford, the member for Southwark in the Par- liament of 1874. On slimmer evenings many plea- sant dinner parties hastily made up in the House of Commons, took place at Sheen House. All the doors
bring

and gates were thrown open on boat race day, and • nearly the whole of the Conservative party were assembled in the house and grounds. Since then islence and night has fallen over the place. Colonil Beresford sold it to the trustees of Sir Henry Meux, a poor afflicted creature who had a million of money and never an hour's perfect health. It was a curious, piteous case, a man half-made as it were, and rather existing as a vegetable thanliving as a human being. For nearly ten years the high stone walls of Sheen House shut in this miserable tragedy. Now it is all over,what Carlyle might with more of literal truth than pertained to the general application have called a "forked radish" has returned to mother earth, and now Sheen House will be graced with the presence of royalty, and maintained with some- thing of the splendour of a court. The great forthcoming scandal will be settled early- next month. Settled is not exactly the word; for Lady Cohn is determined to fight, and so is Lord Colin. The briefs are out, and tilere will be a very strong bar. One can see from the counsel retained that there will be powerful appeals to the jury. In the Divorce Court there are certain bar- risters who are well up in all the technicalities of the practice. They have the ear of the Court, and know what to say and what to do. But when you see counsel whose practice does not lie exclusively before Sir James Hannen or Sir Charles Butt briefed that means a pitched battle and a jury case. Lady Colin sues for a dissolution of marriage. Lord Colin sues for a divorce. At first he had a long string of co-respondents. At present he seems to think that four are quite enough. Their names were commu- nicated to you some weeks ago. Three of them are men of distinction. The Duke of Marlborough has rank; Colonel Butler is an aide-de-camp to the Queen; and Captain Shaw is Captain Shaw of the Fire Brigade. The fourth is a doctor who used to attend Lady Colin. Colonel Butler is the husband of the Miss Thompson, who painted the Roll Call, and one of the most intimate friends of Lady Colin is Mrs. Butler's sister. That intimacy has lasted several years, and still continues. Lady Colin, since these divorce proceedings commenced, has retired almost exclusively into private life. One of the few houses at which she may be met is Mrs. Mey- nells.

CLAIM FOR MISSING PROPERTY

AT WARRINGTON. On Thursday his Honour Judge Ffoulkes was oc- cupied a considerable time in the hearing of a jury case, in which Joseph Grice, of 73, Knutsford-road, Latchford, was the plaintiff, and Adam Mort, land- lord of the Eagie and Child Inn, Bridge-street, was the defendant. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Longton for the defendant.—Mr. Browne told the jury that the claim was as to the return of certain goods stored by the plaintiff with the defendant. In February, 1885, Mr. Grice deter- mined to give up housekeeping, and desired to store his furniture somewhere. He thought the Eagle and Child yard and premises the most likely place. He then-saw the defendant. Mr. Mort, who kept the hotel, and asked him if he could store a quantity of articles. Mr. Mort said that the goods could be placed in some loose boxes in the stable, and to this plaintiff agreed, selecting the one in which they were to be placed. Plaintiff said that he did not know how long he should require the storage, and defendant said he would charge for it as reasonably as possible. The goods were packed in five boxes, four of which were nailed, the fifth being locked. The boxes and other articles of fur- niture were removed to the Eagle and Child pre- mises on the 28th of February. Defendant on several occasions gave up the key of the stable to plaintiff, in order that he might inspect the articles, and take things out which he required. In April, Mr. Mort sent for Mr. Grice, and told him that he wanted the loose box for stabling purposes, and asked if there would be any objection to the goods being removed to another room. Mr. Grice did not object, and the plaintiff said that the articles would be perfectly safe. In the December follow- ing plaintiff discovered that the goods were mi- -'ng. 'A case was tried at the Police Court in which tper- sons were charged with stealing and receiving gome of the goods, but the case was not brought forward with regard to any of those goods. as they were re- covered and handed over to Mr. Grice. When plaintiff wished to remove the rest of the goods defendant said that he must not do so until the sto- rage had been paid for. Defendant said that his charge for the 52 weeks was 18s, being at the rate of 4d per week. The amount was made up to £1 3s 6d, for which credit had been given. The goods sued for were still missing, , and were of the value of £l6. Evidence was given on behalf of the plaintiff, and Mr. Long- ton then intimated that his defence was that Mr. Mort was nut a bailee of the goods. He then called witnesses for the defence.—His Honour, in address- ing the jury, said that this was an action brought for the detention of certain goods that belonged to Grice, which, he said, he had entrusted to the care of Mort. The point of dispute between ne parties was as to the terms upon which the goods went to Mort's premises. It was said that Mort undertook • to store them under his own control and charge, and on the other side, it was said that the defendant did not take them as a caretaker, but simply let the room to Grice for a certain amount. If Mort under- • took to store the goods he was responsible; but if he only let the room, and Grice was to have charge . of them in the room, Mort would not then be responsible.—The jury .gave a Verdict for the de- fendant.

ALLEGED ROBBERY AND FORGERY AT ORFORD BARRACKS. A peculiar case of robbery and forgery came be- fore the magistrates (Mr. R. Garnett and Dr. Gor- nall) at the Warrington Police Court yesterday. Charles Fianna gan, a private in the South Lanca- shire Regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks, was charged with entering the quarters of Major Brown, at Orford Barracks, on Wednesday last, and stealing therefrom a post letter containing a cheque for about £7 Bs, and a blank cheque; and he was fur- ther charged with forging and uttering a cheque for £7 at Parr's Bank, on Monday last, in the name of Major Brown.—Chief Constable Hunt said the prose- cutor in the case was Major Brown, of the Ist Liv- erpool Regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks. Major Brown had quarters at Orford, but his resi- dence was at Lymm. The prisoner, Charles Fianna- gan, was a private in the South Lancashire Regi- ment, and was 18 years of age, and was a native of near Liverpool. They found, from letters in his possession that he had been brought up and edu- cated at the St. George's Industrial School, Liver- pool. From what they could gather it appeared that after leaving the industrial school the prisoner by some means or other was recommended as a servant, and acted as valet, travelling, among other places to Italy. On coming back to England, the prisoner about two months ago enlisted into the Ist Liverpool Regiment. He was somewhat well behaved since he joined the corps and had latterly been acting as a waiter in the officers' quarters at Orford. About ten minutes to eight on Wednesday night last the prisoner was waiting at the "mess," and he was suddenly missed by Sergeant Byrne, who was then in charge. A short time afterwai Private Francis Percival, a trusted servant of 20 years service, had occasion to leave the room in which the officers were dining, and to enter Major Brown's bedroom. He noticed that his superior officer's portmanteau had been disturbed, and a bunch of keys was hanging in the lock. The portmanteau was opened, and Percival saw a number of sove-feigns lying about. He looked around the room and nis- covered the prisoner under Sergeant Brown's bed. He dragged the prisoner out and asked him to ac- count for his presence there, and the prisoner re- ' plied "All right, I thought it was Major Brown coming, and I went down there out of sight." The prisoner was then seized and was taken before Ser- geant Byrne, whereupon he feigned to be drunk, l_le (Chief Constable Hunt) had evidence to prove that the prisoner was " shamming " drunkenness, and when he was searched in the plan-1 -room by Sergeant Devonport £5 in gold, and 6s 6d in silver, one franc piece, and a number of keys, such as would open drawers and portmanteaus were found in his possession. At the time defendant was being searched another officer's servant named William Fox saw the prisoner drop a piece of paper to the floor. It was picked up and was found to be a eheque for £7 in the envelope, made out by Major Brown in favour of a Manchester firm, and which the prisoner ought to have posted on either last Sunday or last Monday. This discovery led to other inquiries, and it was ascertained that the prisoner had stolen a blank cheque from the cheque book of Major Brown, and he had filled it up for £7, and the £5 6s 6d found in his possession was a portion of the cash for that forged cheque. He (Chief Constable Hunt) asked for the prisoner to be remanded for a week.—The prisoner was then remanded until next Friday.

div.head: Weaerg to the gditor.
div.p: Weaerg to the gditor.
THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE.

Sir,—l for one quite agree with the remarks made by your cerresoondent " Clifford Dix" concerning the approaching celebration of her Majesty's Jubilee. Such an outspoken, but nevertheless correct, way of putting the matter comes as a relish to those who like myself can look at the tinsel of the throne without becoming blind to the things around us ; aye, things that compare badly with the so-called "happy reign." If royalty wishes to retain the affections of the masses, it is nothing unreasonable of the people to expect in return for the liberality shown by them in providing so handsomely for one member after another of the Royal household, some substantial token of concern. No doubt the opening of an exhibition, or an art gallery, may be con- sidered a sufficient duty twy some, yet such acts will not— however pleasing they may ba to a class—add much com- fort to the tens of thousands of her Majesty's subjects who will be brought during the coming winter to the brink of downright starvation. Would it not be a good memento of her Majesty's Jubilee if, out of her superabundance of wealth which she is known to possess (part of which she has derived from her subjects), she devoted a few thousands towards relieviEq: some of her destitute subjects P—l remain, yours, &c., PLEBEIAN. Kingsley, October 14th.
"TITHE RENT DAY" AT LYMNI.-A FAIR OFFER.

Sir,—lt is the " tithe rent. day" at Lymm on the 29th Inst. Already I hear among the farmers strong murmurings in respect of having to pay such an 'impost. One farmer said—" It took 150 loads of potatoes to pay his tithe." I have been thinking we might justly make a proposal to the Rector somewhat as follows.:—

If he (the rector) would foYego his tithe money, we on our part would relieve him from all "spiritual oversight" over us-; ie., we would (so far as in us lies) do as we Promised (or someone for us) when we were christened, "Renounce (does renounce' mean to fight?) the devil," individually and collectively. _ _

If our skulls are somewhat thick we are nevertheless brave men; such an enemy as I have referred to would not frighten us. I would have you to remember, sir, we are the descendants of the heroes of Peterloo. Surely if our fathers could put down the." Reds" in double quick time, I cannot see why we their sons should not be able to make a decent onslaught on that most subtle and expensive enemy the d—l without the aid of the clergy. Peroaps, sir, either yourself or some one of your readers will give me their ideas as to whether my scheme would be likely to work smoothly. You will excuse me reminding you that th.re are two big ideas in it—the elimination of .4 tithe rent day" and being left to fight (without the aid of the clergy) a subtle enemy.

div.head: FARMER. " WESLEYAN METHODISM AND THEATRE
div.p: FARMER. " WESLEYAN METHODISM AND THEATRE
GOING."

- Sir,—lt is clear from the mistake which "W. E. S." makes, as to the pieces recited at the Wesleyan School, that he was not present, and is somewhat presumptuous in writ- ing on the subject. His lette , however, starts a wider issue upon which I ask leave to say a few words. There is urgent need in our Sunday schools of opportuni- ties for social enjoyment, and that the character of that enjoyment should be as high intellectually as it should be pure morally. The competition of outside and less worthy entertainments would force this upon our attention even if common sense did not. We need, therefore, to seek our material in the noblest authors, and to take count of the higher standard of taste of to-day. I would put it to our friend whether he does not see all the difference in the world be- tween a number of scholars reciting for the amusement ef their fellow scholars, and a number of actors who do the same for gain, and with no idea of instruction whatever. Is there not as much difference as there is between a school room and a theatre to which attaches an evil influence which the best friends of the drama equally recognise and deplore? I further would ask—" What difference is there in principle between singing and reciting a piece ? " Two, at least, of the songs would. had they been recited as admir- ably as they were sung, have been very amusing. I hope "W. E. S." will reconsider the matter, and not needlessly hamper Sunday school managers who are trying to interest as well as instruct their young people, and so keep them from every kind (or form) of evil.—l am, sir, yours truly, R.P. Warrington, Oct. 14th, 1886.

div.head: MAYOR AND "TRIFLING" AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE MAYOR AND "TRIFLING" AT WARRINGTON.

Sir,—l was pleased to notice in a recent issue of your paper a slight review of the sayings and doings of several of our Town Councillors at one of their recent meetings. Criticism, when fairly offered, should be welcomed by our public men, and the fear of giving offence should sot cause ratepayers to withhold their opinions. It is generally held to be a sian of the possession of a large amount of worldly wisdom when a man refuses to have a tilt with those gen- tlemen who happen to be clothed with the garments of authority, therefore the present writer's opinions touching the question so ably introduced by Councillor Roberts at the recent meeting of the Town Council, may be a sign merely of the writer's vacuity of mind. My purpose in writing you this note, sir, is to point out to the Watch Committee that neither the CHef Constable (Mr. Hunt), nor yet the men under his control, are looked upon as being without sin; they are not infallible; we do not expect this much from them, any more than the public expect the magistrates to bend and bow to every decision a chief constable may in his wisdom arrive at. When it does happen that the guardians of the peace go wrong, we may fairly be charitable to their sins; but it scarcely, follows that the Mayor should condone such sins by term- ing them "trifling." As I understand your report, P.C. Niell having searched a prisoner and found £7 and a gold watch upon him, kept possession of the property "for an unreasonable length of time ; " he had previously been guilty of unreasonableness by withholding the " trifling " sum of 17s. Most people would say such a man ought to have been more severely dealt with as an example. It is well known to be a dan- gerous thing for a man to have enemies in the police force, and therefore many complaints are never made. I must add that I think the Warrington police force are fairly well kept to their duties by Mr. Hunt, yet the case to which I have referred proves how necessary it is for the Mayor, Watch Committee, and the bench of magistrates to be on their guard is the Borough Court, when advice and evi- dence are tendered by members of the police force. Let us have the guardians cf the peace as near as possible like Canes wife—above suspicion.—Yours,
W. CAUTION.
THE POLITICAL "RIGHT-ABOUT ,TURN."

• Sir, Political events just now justify one in slightly varying Shakespere's phrase and saving that "he is a wise Tory who knows his own leader." Riven as has bean the heralding banner of Radical reform, great the upsetting of parties, regretful the cessation of English legislation, yet all these events are compensated for bv the appearance of a Rldical—not new born certainly who has resolutely shaken off the fetters of Tory, servitude, and has inscribed, in letters of indelible chart cter, on the Tory banner the motto—not of " Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform "—oh no, that would really ha coming a little too closely in con- tact with Kilmainham conspirators—but the motto of " Local option " (poor Sir Wilfred !). " Land reform" (poor Joey !), " Three acres and a cow " (poor Jesse !), "The recognition of the right of self-government," " The foreign i policy of that arch traitor, the G.O.M,'" "The closure of debate."
Oh ! what a mighty reformation! Truly "".this Hebrew

has turned Christian." Was it but the taint of Hebrew 1 origin that kept the glorious apostle of Toryism—the Primrose League hero "—from turning Christian and giv- ing us a Christian policy instead of a Jingo fallacy, and is it because our new ally has none of the Hebrew taint that he follows not, in his foreign policy, the example of his glorious leader ? In hypocrisy, in deceit, in the sinking of principles enunciated with all the fire of self-seeking ambi- tion, in the sacrifice of the ancient principles of the party he professes to lead, in all these he has faithfully followed his master's lead, and has guided that innocent and confid- ing flock of Tory sheep into a fold surrounded by Radical fences, guarthd by Socialistic watch dogs, covered with the kindly protection of Liberal "principals." Solacing themselves with tbe assurance that surely the Radical physic, being administered by Tory ducal hands, becomes thereby the physic of Toryism, pure and unadul- terated, clean and undefiled, what a mighty change these poor sheep will have undergone. The wool of Tory hue has been shorn and has been made into garments of Radical shape. True, it is a Tory garment, but the shape is Radi- cal, and the bands that shaped it are dyed in the darkest ye of Radical heresy. Well may we Radicals congratulate ourselves. Where is the dividing line now? It can only be traced as being 'twixt the honest and the dishonest politicians. Of the latter this new school of Toryism belongs.

The Radical measures will in the interval of repose be stirred together in one huge pot, even the coals that feed the flame will be from Radical coal pits. The band that stirs the pot will aloue be Tory, and then without any in- gredients of a purifying nature, the savoury liquid shall be poured into Tory moulds—which were once too weak for such strong measures—and on the re-assembly of that august body in St. Stephen's measures in Tory moulds, but of Radical texture, will be presented to a flock of stupid Tories, who in their ignorance are as blind as bats, and the country will be made to ring from north to south with the tender regard which the "guardians of ancient liberties" have for the democracy. Oh! blessed hour, heralding the Utopia of political life, when politicians shall vie in their struggles to be just to all men, and particularly those who have laboured wader the lash of autocratic rule let all men, of all shades, sing your praises, and laud and magnify the name of scion of the spotless (!) house of Marlborough. "A RAD."

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 16, 1886.

div.head: CHURCH CONGRESS.
div.p: THE CHURCH CONGRESS.

Sir,—The church has just held its parliament, and after most serious delibeiation has, I suppose, decided to allow matters to drift alcng as they have done hitherto. I won- der what would happen were our church dignitaries, lay and clerinl, to decide upon doing a little bit of real work. What a hubbub there would be if it were decided say, to compel us all to put in an appearance at the Parish Church every Sunday morning, and by this means prone to the world that the Established Church was indeed a national church.

Yet I suppose it must be allowed that these especially privileged gentlemen did not meet day after day without doing something. Like their masters, who meet in St. Stephen's, they managed to get through a fair amount of talk, what the result of it all will be is another matter. Some of the questions brosight under their notice are likely at no distant date to be dealt with by men of a different stamp, who will not be so very diffident about the conclu- sions they may arrive at. There is, I sin pleased to see, a very strong opinion forming itself amongst leaders in the church that they cannot hold together much longer as an establishment. At a meeting of the Evangelical Protestant Union, presided over by the Rev. Canon Taylor, the chair- man said "he foresaw disestablishment ; it was a part of the Radical programme, end with disestablishment would come disendowment." I take this to be very encouraging, Mr. Editor, to the Radical party. Ido more, sir, I insist that it is that party's duty to do all in its power to scatter abroad the men who fritter away the nation's earnings. The rev. chairman gives his reasons for saving disestablishment is upon them. "The ehurches were turned into places for flower shows and ecclesiastical pantomimes, all to please the giddy and the worldly." Another speaker at the same meeting hoped for nothing from either political party, as Mr. Gladstone with his support of Ritualism was no worse than Lord Randolph with his appointment of dk Roman Catholic Home Secretary. Good! Our friends are between the proverbial two stools, and it is to be hoped the usual result will come about, more especially as another speaker asserted that the churches were "teaching the Devil's re- ligion." Surely the nation need not be taxed to give sup- port to his Highness with the hoofs. Of course at the church congress matters were scarcely se bad as this. There we had the usual congratulations given and received in quite a loving spirit. Altogether the brotherly love exhibited was so beautiful in its unanimity that it was quite a pity to see one enthusiast, Mr. Theo- dore Dodd, declare that they "should begin their reforms by cutting down the salaries of the archbishops and bishops." Mr. Dodd was quite right in this suggestion. but he might have spared his listeners the most unpalat- able. yet truthful sea ment, that the bishops "by faculties, alienated the masses and robbed the poor." Well we know this is so, and the statement has been repeatedly made, only to be repeatedly contradicted. The manufacturers and working-men of wealthy England have, for a number of years, been struggling hard to maintain a position of inde- pendence and respectability. The creators of the wealth have thought in their simplicity that they ought to enjoy some of its sweets, vet how are the workers faring to-day ? We are dreading and fearing to face what promises to be one of the most cruel winters on record. No fear, sir, of the workers dying, like one speaker says the church is, "of too much reseectability." Is it not a burning shame that one speaker giould have it in his power to protest against servants of Him who had not where to lay his bead, re- ceiving £5O and £3O per day? To tbe roost dense it ought to be clear that these men do not produce anything in return for the enormous wealth they are enabled to lay no. The Rev. Mercer Davies has published a pamphlet in which be states that the friends and members of the church believe the bishops ars " rolling in riches." The Bishop of Liverpool deplores "the ignorance of the people" and con- fesses that we have had " two and a half centuries of ne- glect. Of course, this is a mistake on the Bishop's part; had the people been. neglected—that is, left to themselves— be would not to-day have had to deplore their igeor- ance. Nor would Mr. Davies have had such a disgraceful list of fortunes, left by the Bishops during the last thirty years, from 1855 to the close of 1885,t0 record;"the average being about £54,000 a-piece, and the total personality of the 39 bishops being over two millions sterling; this being exclusive of any real estate they may have possessed, and exclusive also of any same invested is policies of life assur- ance or otherwise settled for the benefit of their families." I submit, therefore, sir. that Mr. Dodd: was quite justified in urging upon the attention of the Congress the question of financial reform among the clergy. We have been told times without number that the clergy in the rural districts acted upon the squirearchy in a benefi- cial manner; that the presence of a cultivated gentleman amongst a rude and ignorant population was, in itself, a de- sirable thing. Well, I have looked far some proofs of this. 1 cannot find them, where are they? Reading over the Report of the Poor Law Commissioners of 1832, I find that at the very t;.me when the power of the clergy and the squire was supreme the peasantry of England were sunk in the very lowest depths of pauperism and ignorance. It was not only that the people were igrorant, but their moral nature was completely destroyed. Throughout rural England a premium was paid on idleness and illegitimacy. An un- married girl, leaving the workhouse after her fourth confine- ment, said to the master," Well, if I have the good luck to have another child, I shall draw a good sum from the par- iah; and with what I can earn myself shall be be better off than any married woman in the parish." Truly in those good old days the the teachings of the church did work wonders, such won- ders indeed, that had they been :allowed to have continued, England would have been to-day one vast centre of pau- perism, brought about by clerical bigotry. Thanks to the freethought radicalism, the snake was sc,tched. On sanitary matters what was the influence of the "culti- vated gentleman?" I have before me evidence that you would scarcely care to print, Mr. Editor, it is so revolting, and resulting in such a state of moral leprosy,that least said about it the better, and yet it must be referred to, inasmuch as speakers at the Congress were bound to confess "that al- though a great improvement had taken place in recent years much remained to be done." A lady speaker, Miss Mason, giving her experience, well illustrated the degraded and unhappy state in which the peasantry vegetated. Quite recently she paid a v it to the house of a man who had just re-married. The bride at once explained her presence, and without circumlocution, "I marriel him," she said, because I had rheumatism in my knees, and this was a dry house." This statement, which contained volumes, was re- ceived by the clergy present with "laughter." It may be, as one speaker stated, "a pity and a token of a frivolous ago" that people's " hearts had to be reached through their heads, and their heads through their recreative reading." This will be altered shortly, and instead of mere recrsative reading, and reaching people's hearts through the over- seers, men will be taught the responsibility of life.
CLIFFORD DIX.

CONCERT.—On Thursday night, Mr. George Bvion gave his first concert of the season in the St. Helens Town Hall. The artistes were Madame Andersen, Madame An- toinette Sterling. Mr. Seymour Jackson, Mr. Bantock Per. point, Mr. W. H. Jude, and Mr. T. A. Barrett. There was a large and appreciative audience. Madame Sterling's rendering of Sullivan's "Lost Chord" was exquisite, and in response to an encore that lady gave "Darby and Joan."

THE COLLINS GREEN STRIKE.—The strike at Col- Has Green Colliery still continues, and there are no indica- tions of an arrangement being come to. The appeal to the miners in the district on behalf of the men on strike has been liberally responded to. A meeting to consider their position was held in Parr Methodist School, on Thursday week, when about 400 colliers attended. The chair was oc- cupied by Mr. Thomas Glover, the miners' agent, who de- livered an address, in which he put the circumstances before the meeting.—Mr. Woods (miners' agent) delivered a lengthy address. He urged the men to organise themselves, so that in future they would be better able to meet any aggressive measure made by their employers.—A resolution pledging those present to de all in their power to support the men on strike was passed with great enthusiasm.—The collieries are closed, and it is stated there is an unwritten agreement entered into on the part of all the colliers of the district not to apply for work whilst the dispute is existing.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTION.
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTION.

• It is not yet definitely known whether or not there will be a contest in Warrington at the forthcoming November election of Town Councillors for the borough, in the place of those who retire. The retiring councillors are: Liberals—Messrs. John Platt, Charles Broadbent, John Brown, and John Greening. Conservatives— Messrs. Richard Walker Francomb, James Cave Whittle, Thomas Jolley, Thomas Sutton, and William Tinsley. The Conservatives held a meeting to consider the matter on Thurs- day evening, and we understand that an in- timation has been received by the Liveral party from the Conservatives making an offer not to con- test the wards if two seats were given up to them. The Liberal party, however, .seeing that their op- ponents have already a considerable majority on the Town Council, are naturally averse to such an ar- rangement. On Tuesday evening a meeting of the Liberal workers of North-West 'Ward was held at Wycliffe Hall, when it it was decided that Messrs. Brown and Greening, the retiring members, , should be asked to submit themselves for re-elec- ' Con. At a meeting of the Liberal captains of the North-East Ward, held last evening in Brick-street School-room, it was unanimously decided to ask Messrs. Broadbent and Platt to again submit them- selves for election. Should hostilities prove inevi- table, it is understood that the Liberals intend to contest all the Conservative seats.

23, Old Broad-street, E.C. This has been a week of fluctuations in the Stock and Share Market. It opened with every prospect ef a series of startling rises in many of the most speculative Stocks, and has closed with a general disappointment. The reason is not far to seek. The crowd of speculatos for the rise who rushed in at the first sign of an improving market have not proved strong enough to hold on, and were forced to realise at the settlement just concluded, which has been a very heavy one, and most disastrous to many. American and Home Rails have relapsed considerably. Early in the chap- ter there was a big run on Brighton A's, which, however, have kept up their character for uncertainty, and hundreds of plungers have been heavily hit. Chatham and Dover also, for which there was a "Bull," have relapsed, leaving the speculators heavy losers. _

The Stock Broker; have -adopted a new method of charg- ing for "carrying over" stocks, which is not likely to meet with popular favor. Instead of charging, as heretofore, the market percentage, they now charge from 9d to is 6d per share, which means to the client something like ten per cent, for an accommodation previously costing only two. It is difficult to realize the spirit which impels thousands of English investors to cling so tenaciously to Mines as an investment. In spite of the notorious fact that the dividend earning mines can be reckoned on the fingers of one hand, there is rarely a new venture floated that does not receive a larger share of support than is accorded to any purely commercial enterprise. This week the public have offered to them various schemes of this class, and in spite of con- stant warnings the money is pouring in, though the chances of a penny being returned are thousands to one against it. We are apparently passing through a gold fever which has not yet reached its crisis.

A case has occupied the Courts this week which empha- sises the point I have always insisted on—the necessity of investors seeing all the contracts in undertakings to which they are asked to subscribe. By acting on this advice I have saved the public thousands of pounds which would otherwise have gone to swell the barming accounts of swindling promoters. A man who bought a business with- out examining the books would be regarded as insane, and yet investors do this eN ery day.

BAZAAR.—In aid of the minister's house fund in connec- tion with the United Methodist Free Church, a baztar was held in Frodsham Town Hall on Tuesday and Wednesday. The opening ceremony was performed by Mr. G. Slater, of Northwich, who delivered an appropriate address. The stalls were presided over by Mesdames Lewis, Webb, Noden, Earlem, Percival, Roscoe, Jones, Clays, and Jackson. Vari- ous attractions were provided. The amount realised from the sales, Sic., was £43. PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES.—A meeting of the Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship Parochial Committees was held on Friday, in the Town Hall, Mr. A. Thomas in the chair. On the recommendation of the Inspector of Nuisances, levels were directed to be taken, and a length of the sewer repaired under the superintendence of a sub-committee. The In- spector reported that the Frodsham and Helsby Drainage Board had refused to grant permission to the Committee to tap three manholes in Brook-furlong-lane sewer and place pipes in the watercourse. This matter was left in the hands of the Inspector.

MISSIONARY MEETING.—On Thursday evening a meeting was held in the Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, Frodsharn, in aid of the Foreign Missionary Society. Mr. Thomas Rigby, of Overton, occupied the chair. It was reported that the fol- fo wing ladies had collected the undermentioned amounts in the Frodsham district : Mrs and Miss Proud, £8 44 4d • Mrs Collinson, £3 12s ; Mrs W. Lowe and Miss M. 'Edmunds, £lB is 6d. Juvenile collectors, £7 5s 6d. Total, £37 3s 4d. There had also been collected the sum of £l7 3s 4d for the Zenana Missions. The Rey. J. E. Sowerbutts. a returned missionary from India, was present as the deputation and delivered an ad- dress. Votes of thanks were given to the secretary and treasurer of the Missionary Society and to the deputation. The amount realised by this and the services of Sunday was over £B.

WESLEYAN IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—A meeting of the Frodsbam Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Class was held on Friday, when the Rev. E. Mosscrop, president, reads paper on " Christianity, its evidence from prophecy," in which he stated that in the Patriarchal, Mosaic, and pro- phetic ages there were predictions which related to a Sa- viour, the coming of a mightier prophet than Moses, the final dispersion of the Jews, and the great blessings which are yet in store for the Hebrew race. But while prophecy dwelt upon these and other events it made its predictions a preparation for Christianity. The advent, office, and work of the Messiah were prominently noticed, and Christianity was its supreme subject. The attention of the class was directed to specimens from upwards of one hundred predic. tions given in clear and explicit language, w filch referred to prophecy in its relation to Cbriitianity-anc: the Christian Dispensation.

WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF !ART VACATION SKETCHING CLUB. On Tuesday and Wednesday the • drawings and paintings executed by the members of the above club were on private view to students and friends in the School of Art, Museum-street. This is the second year of this club's existence, and we are pleased to note that evident strides had been made by the members during this short period, the standard of the work all round being considerably above that of the work exhibited on the last occasion. The quality and quantity of this year's work testifies to the healthy stimulus given by the club to this interesting and important branch of study. Congratulations are due to the committee for this year's results, and credit is also owing to Mr. C. B. Aylward (second master), and Mr. G. Toft, who as the hon. treasurer and secretary respectively worked assiduously. Prizes were offered for general competition by the committees, these being supple- mented by special prizes by Mr. John Rylands, Mr. , Brewtnall, and Mr. 11. D. Barkas, headmaster, and other prizes by various co itributors. In review- ing the prize list we notice that Mr. G. Toft takcs the prize for the best landscape painted in either oil, water colour, or tempera. This subject is well chosen, the drawing and painting of the cottage which forms the central feature being carefully drawn and pleasant in colour. Other sketches ex- hibited by tilt. same student call for praise, owing to their being all more or less creditable transcripts of nature. A very carefully painted group of white roses, painted in oil by Miss A. Chrimes, secures for her the special prize offered for this branch of study. This work evidences considerable artistic ability, the flowers being nicely arranged. A prize has been awarded to Miss Dobson for a very sunny bit of landscape scenery. The light atmospheric effects introduced into this student's work are very agreeable. Miss C. Broadbent takes a prize for a vigorous study in water colour of a foreground tree with sky and distance. Some very good studies of flowers in oil colours are contributed by Miss E. Brewtnall, for which she is awarded the prize for plants treated decoratively. Mr. F. Warburton takes a prize for a neat set of architectural drawings of a portion of St. Thomas' Church, Stockton Heath; and Mr. Kendrick and Mr. Downe also exhibit some highly creditable work in this section, namely, drawings of the Lych Gate, Walton, and the Porch of Grappenhall Church The appearance of the interior of a cottage is well depicted by Miss Spinks, who takes a prize. Miss Calvert also takes a prize for landscape paint- ings, and Miss Johnson for a very careful study of roses in water color. Honourable mentions are awarded Miss V. Fleming for study of roses, and to Mrs. Downe for plant studies. In the general competition (advanced section) Miss L. Hulmes takes a prize for a very clever set of sketches of landscape scenery and plants painted from nature ; as also do Miss P. Garnett for a clever set of sketches in black and white, Miss Brookes for several neatly drawn studies in pictorial architecture taken from Warrington and neighbour- hood, and Miss M. Burgess for a pleasing study of a child's head in black and white. lathe elementary secton prizes have been awarded to Miss C. Flem- ing, Miss N. Birtles, Miss Thompson (for studies in flowers), and to Miss Parker, and Miss Cooper

TO THE BUR- GESSES OF EAST SUTTON' WARD. LADIES AND Gime LEMEN,—My term of office as your repre- sentative will expire in a few days. I have faithfully en- deavoured to represent your interest and discharge the duties imposed upon me as a member of the Town Council. I have been requested hy many and leflueetial residents of the ward to again represent your ward. In deference to this mark of continued confidence in me, I again consent to bestome a candidate at the forthcoming election, and should I be re- elected, I shall, to the best of my ability, attend to the in- terests of your ward and those of the borough generally. Thanking you for your former support and soliciting a renewal Of it, I remain, Ladies and gentlemen. Your obedient servant, JAMES FISHER. Olive Mount, Mill-lane, Sutton, Oct. 14th, ISS6.

On Friday evening a Privy Council order prohibiting landing in England, Wales, or Scotland of animals brought Um Norway was published. SELLING UNSOUND PORK —At Derby, on Friday, the manager of the Longeaton Co-operative Society's Stores was fined £l9, including costs, for having prepared and I offered for sale over 100 pieces of pork which were unfit for human food. It was stated that a family became ill in con- sequence of eating the meat. THE KERRY MooxLiGHTEns.—lt is reported from Castle- island, on Friday, that the police there have had an im- portant informer in their barracks for several days. He is kept in close quarters, and he is stated to be a nephew of a notorious informer named Biddy Brosnan. The news has caused great excitement in the district. A SOLICITOR CHARGED WITH FRAUD —The Manchester magistrates en Friday granted a warrant for the apprehen- sion of Frederick Huxley, solicitor, for obtaining half a crown by false pretences from a woman who had consulted him. Mr. Huxley had been summoned, but failed to answer. On Thursday he was severely reprimanded by the Recorder, in the Session Court, for not instructing counsel when paid to do so, and also for appearing in court drunk. BRAVERY REWARDED. It was announced on Friday evening that the Queen has conferred the Albert medal of the second class upon Edward Scullion, a chemical labourer, in recognition of conspicuous gallantry displayed by him on the 9th August last in attempting to rescue two men and a boy who had been overcome by sulphur in the air shaft of an unused sulphurretted hydrogen sewer connected with the works of the Newcastle and Gateshead Chemical Company. A " BARBARIC DOCTRINE."—The Rev. Henry Ward Beecher delivered an address at the City Temple to minis- ters on Friday morning. He dwelt on the aid rendered to the preacher by the newspapers. After the address Mr. Beecher, answering questions on the doctrine of retribution, caused considerable sencation amongst his hearers by say- ing that any man believing in the doctrine of retribution who married, entered society, or smiled was a monster. He ' preferred working through fear springing from love rather than fear engendered by the barbaric doctrine of retribu- tion. THE TICHBORNE CLAIMANT. L NEW YORK, FRlDAY.—Arthur Orton, the Tichborne claimant, is ill and destitute here. THE BULGARIAN CRISIS. ! VIENNA, THURSDAY NIGHT. A Lemberg payer to-day • publishes news from Bessarabia according to which Russia ,is energetically mobilising its army in those parts. The railways are said to be hastily completing preparations for the transport of troops and war material.
